1 Grothendieck topologies

Originally, Grothendieck topologies appeared as underlying his theory of descent (cf. SGA 1 VI, VIII); the use of the corresponding cohomology theories came later. The same approach is followed here: by formalizing the classical notions of localization, local property, and gluing (1.1, 1.2, 1.3), one brings out the general concept of Grothendieck topology (1.6); to justify its introduction in algebraic geometry, one proves a faithfully flat descent theorem (1.4), a generalization of the classical theorem of Hilbert (1.5).

The reader will find a more complete, but concise, exposition of the formalism in Giraud [19]. M. Artin's notes: “Grothendieck topologies” [1] (Chapters I to III) also remain useful. The 866 pages of Exposés I to V of SGA 4 are valuable when one considers exotic topologies, such as the one giving rise to crystalline cohomology; to use the étale topology, so close to classical intuition, it is not indispensable to read them.

1.1 Sieves

Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{R}\) a real-valued function on \(X\). The continuity of \(f\) is a property of local nature; in other words, if \(f\) is continuous on every sufficiently small open set of \(X\), then \(f\) is continuous on all of \(X\). To formalize the notion of “property of local nature,” we introduce a few definitions.

A set \(\mathscr{U}\) of open sets of \(X\) is called a sieve if for every \(U\in\mathscr{U}\) and \(V\subset U\), one has \(V\in\mathscr{U}\). A sieve is said to be covering if the union of all the open sets belonging to this sieve is equal to \(X\).

Given a family \(\{U_i\}\) of open sets of \(X\), the sieve generated by \(\{U_i\}\) is by definition the set of open sets \(U\) of \(X\) such that \(U\) is contained in one of the \(U_i\).

A property \(P(U)\), defined for every open set \(U\) of \(X\), is said to be local if, for every covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) of every open set \(U\) of \(X\), \(P(U)\) is true if and only if \(P(V)\) is true for every \(V\in \mathscr{U}\). For example, given \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{R}\), the property “\(f\) is continuous on \(U\)” is local.

1.2 Sheaves

Let us make precise the notion of a function given locally on \(X\).

1.2.1 The point of view of sieves

Let \(\mathscr{U}\) be a sieve of open sets of \(X\). By a function given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally on \(X\) one means the datum, for every \(U\in \mathscr{U}\), of a function \(f_U\) on \(U\) such that, if \(V\subset U\), one has \(f_V=f_U|V\).

1.2.2 The point of view of Čech

If the sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) is generated by a family of open sets \(U_i\) of \(X\), giving a function \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to giving a function \(f_i\) on each \(U_i\), such that \(f_i|{U_i\cap U_j} = f_j|{U_i\cap U_j}\).

In other words, if \(Z=\coprod U_i\), giving a function \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to giving a function on \(Z\) that is constant on the fibres of the natural projection \(Z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\).

1.2.3

The continuous functions form a sheaf; this means that for every covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) of an open set \(V\) of \(X\) and every function given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally \(\{f_U\}\) such that each \(f_U\) is continuous on \(U\), there exists a unique continuous function \(f\) on \(V\) such that \(f|U=f_U\) for every \(U\in \mathscr{U}\).

1.3 Stacks

Let us now make precise the notion of a vector bundle given locally on \(X\).

1.3.1 The point of view of sieves

Let \(\mathscr{U}\) be a sieve of open sets of \(X\). By a vector bundle given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally on \(X\) one means the data of

  1. a vector bundle \(E_U\) on each \(U\in \mathscr{U}\),

  2. if \(V\subset U\), an isomorphism \(\rho_{U,V} : E_V\xrightarrow{\sim} E_U|V\), satisfying

  3. if \(W\subset V\subset U\), the diagram

    \[ \xymatrix{ E_W \ar[r]^-{\rho_{U,W}} \ar[dr]_-{\rho_{V,W}} & E_U|W \\ & E_V|W \ar[u]_-{\rho_{U,V}|W} } \]

    commutes, that is, \(\rho_{U,V} = (\rho_{U,V} \mbox{ restricted to } W) \circ \rho_{V,W}\).

1.3.2 The point of view of Čech

If the sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) is generated by a family of open sets \(U_i\) of \(X\), giving a vector bundle \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to giving:

  1. a vector bundle \(E_i\) on each \(U_i\),

  2. if \(U_{ij} = U_i\cap U_j = U_i\times_X U_j\), an isomorphism \(\rho_{ji} : E_i|U_{ij} \xrightarrow{\sim} E_j|U_{ij}\), so that

  3. if \(U_{ijk} = U_i\times_X U_j\times_X U_k\), the diagram

    \[ \xymatrix{ E_i |U_{ijk} \ar[r]^-{\rho_{ki}|U_{ijk}} \ar[dr]_-{\rho_{ji}|U_{ijk}} & E_k|U_{ijk} \\ & E_j|U_{ijk} \ar[u]_-{\rho_{kj}|U_{ijk}} } \]

    commutes, that is, \(\rho_{ki} = \rho_{kj}\circ \rho_{ji}\) on \(U_{ijk}\).

In other words, if \(Z=\coprod U_i\) and if \(\pi:Z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is the natural projection, giving a vector bundle \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to giving:

  1. a vector bundle \(E\) on \(Z\),

  2. if \(x\) and \(y\) are two points of \(Z\) such that \(\pi(x) = \pi(y)\), an isomorphism \(\rho_{y x}:E_x\xrightarrow{\sim} E_y\) between the fibres of \(E\) at \(x\) and at \(y\), depending continuously on \((x,y)\) and such that,

  3. if \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) are three points of \(Z\) such that \(\pi(x)=\pi(y)=\pi(z)\), one has \(\rho_{zx} = \rho_{zy}\circ \rho_{yx}\).

1.3.3

A vector bundle \(E\) on \(X\) defines a vector bundle given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally \(E_\mathscr{U}\); the system of restrictions \(E_U\) of \(E\) to the objects of \(\mathscr{U}\). The fact that the notion of vector bundle is of local nature can be expressed as follows: for every covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) of \(X\), the functor \(E\mapsto E_\mathscr{U}\), from vector bundles on \(X\) to vector bundles given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally, is an equivalence of categories.

1.3.4

If in 1 one replaces “open set of \(X\)” by “subset of \(X\),” one obtains the notion of a sieve of subspaces of \(X\). In this framework too one has gluing theorems. For example: let \(X\) be a space and \(\mathscr{C}\) a sieve of subspaces of \(X\) generated by a locally finite closed covering of \(X\); then the functor \(E\mapsto E_\mathscr{C}\), from vector bundles on \(X\) to vector bundles given \(\mathscr{C}\)-locally, is an equivalence of categories.

In algebraic geometry, it is useful to consider also “sieves of spaces over \(X\)”; this is what we shall see in the following section.

1.4 Faithfully flat descent

1.4.1

In the framework of schemes, the Zariski topology is not fine enough for the study of non-linear problems, and one is led to replace, in the preceding definitions, the open immersions by more general morphisms. From this point of view, descent techniques appear as localization techniques. Thus the following descent statement can be expressed by saying that the properties considered are of local nature for the faithfully flat topology (a morphism of schemes is said to be faithfully flat if it is flat and surjective).

Proposition 1.4.2

Let \(A\) be a ring and \(B\) a faithfully flat \(A\)-algebra. Then:

  1. A sequence \(\Sigma=(M'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M'')\) of \(A\)-modules is exact as soon as the sequence \(\Sigma_{(B)}\) deduced from it by extension of scalars to \(B\) is exact.

  2. An \(A\)-module \(M\) is of finite type (resp. of finite presentation, flat, locally free of finite rank, invertible (i.e. locally free of rank one)) as soon as the \(B\)-module \(M_{(B)}\) is.

Proof▾

(i) Since the functor \(M\mapsto M_{(B)}\) is exact (flatness of \(B\)), it suffices to show that, if an \(A\)-module \(N\) is non-zero, then \(N_{(B)}\) is non-zero. If \(N\) is non-zero, \(N\) contains a non-zero monogenic submodule \(A/\mathfrak{a}\); then \(N_{(B)}\) contains a monogenic submodule \((A/\mathfrak{a})_{(B)} = B/\mathfrak{a} B\), non-zero by surjectivity of the structural morphism \(\varphi:\operatorname{Spec}(B)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) (if \(V(\mathfrak{a})\) is non-empty, \(\varphi^{-1}(V(\mathfrak{a}))=V(\mathfrak{a} B)\) is non-empty).

(ii) For every family \((x_i)\) of elements of \(M_{(B)}\), there exists a submodule \(M'\) of \(M\) of finite type such that \(M'_{(B)}\) contains the \(x_i\). If \(M_{(B)}\) is of finite type and if the \(x_i\) generate \(M_{(B)}\), then \(M'_{(B)}=M_{(B)}\), hence \(M'=M\) and \(M\) is of finite type.

Q.E.D.

If \(M_{(B)}\) is of finite presentation, one can, by what precedes, find a surjection \(A^n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\). If \(N\) is the kernel of this surjection, the \(B\)-module \(N_{(B)}\) is of finite type, hence so is \(N\), and \(M\) is of finite presentation. The assertion for “flat” follows immediately from (i); “locally free of finite rank” means “flat and of finite presentation,” and the rank is tested by extension of scalars to fields.

1.4.3

Let \(X\) be a scheme and \(\mathscr{S}\) a class of \(X\)-schemes stable under fibre product over \(X\). A class \(\mathscr{U}\subset \mathscr{S}\) is a sieve on \(X\) (relative to \(\mathscr{S}\)) if, for every morphism \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) of \(X\)-schemes, with \(U,V\in \mathscr{S}\) and \(U\in\mathscr{U}\), one has \(V\in \mathscr{U}\). The sieve generated by a family \(\{U_i\}\) of \(X\)-schemes in \(\mathscr{S}\) is the class of \(V\in\mathscr{S}\) such that there exists a morphism of \(X\)-schemes from \(V\) to one of the \(U_i\).

1.4.4

Let \(\mathscr{U}\) be a sieve on \(X\). By a quasi-coherent module given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally on \(X\) one means the datum of

  1. a quasi-coherent module \(E_U\) on each \(U\in\mathscr{U}\),

  2. for every \(U\in\mathscr{U}\) and for every morphism \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) of \(X\)-schemes in \(\mathscr{S}\), an isomorphism \(\rho_\varphi:E_V\xrightarrow{\sim} \varphi^* E_U\), these being such that

  3. if \(\psi:W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\) is a morphism of \(X\)-schemes in \(\mathscr{S}\), the diagram

    \[ \xymatrix{ E_W \ar[r]^-{\rho_{\varphi\circ\psi}} \ar[dr]_-{\rho_\psi} & \psi^*\varphi^* E_U \\ & \psi^* E_V \ar[u]_-{\psi^*\rho_\varphi} } \]

    commutes, that is, \(\rho_{\varphi\circ\psi}=(\psi^*\rho_\varphi)\circ \rho_\psi\).

If \(E\) is a quasi-coherent module on \(X\), one denotes by \(E_\mathscr{U}\) the module given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally equal to \(\varphi_U^* E\) on \(\varphi:U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) and such that, for every morphism \(\psi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) the restriction isomorphism \(\rho_\psi\) is the canonical isomorphism \(E_V=(\varphi_U\circ \psi)^* E\xrightarrow{\sim} \psi^* \varphi_U^* E = \psi^* E_U\).

Theorem 1.4.5

Let \(\{U_i\}\in\mathscr{S}\) be a finite family of \(X\)-schemes flat over \(X\) such that \(X\) is the union of the images of the \(U_i\), and let \(\mathscr{U}\) be the sieve generated by \(\{U_i\}\). Then the functor \(E\mapsto E_\mathscr{U}\) is an equivalence of the category of quasi-coherent modules on \(X\) with the category of modules quasi-coherent given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally.

Proof▾

We shall treat only the case where \(x\) is affine and where \(\mathscr{U}\) is generated by an affine \(X\)-scheme \(U\) faithfully flat over \(X\). The reduction to this case is formal. One sets \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(U=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\).

If the morphism \(U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) admits a section, then \(X\) belongs to the sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) and the assertion is obvious. We shall reduce to this case.

A quasi-coherent module given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally defines modules \(M'\), \(M''\), and \(M'''\) on \(U\), \(U\times_X U\), and \(U\times_X U\times_X U\), and isomorphisms \(\rho:p^* M^\bullet\simeq M^\bullet\) for every projection morphism \(p\) between these spaces; this is a cartesian diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ M^* : M' \ar@<2pt>[r] \ar@<-2pt>[r] & M'' \ar[r] \ar@<4pt>[r] \ar@<-4pt>[r] & M''' } \]

over

\[ \xymatrix{ U_* : U & U\times_X U \ar@<2pt>[l] \ar@<-2pt>[l] & U\times_X U\times_X U \ar[l] \ar@<4pt>[l] \ar@<-4pt>[l] . } \]

Conversely, \(M^*\) determines the module given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally: for \(V\in\mathscr{U}\), there exists \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) and one sets \(M_U=\varphi^* M'\); for \(\varphi_1,\varphi_2:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\), one has a natural identification \(\varphi_1^* M'\simeq (\varphi_1\times \varphi_2)^* M'' \simeq \varphi_2^* M'\), and one sees, using \(M'''\), that these identifications are compatible, so that the definition is legitimate. In short, giving a module \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to the same thing as giving a cartesian diagram \(M^*\) on \(U_*\).

Let us translate into algebraic terms: giving \(M^*\) amounts to giving a cartesian diagram of modules

\[ \xymatrix{ M' \ar@<3pt>[r]|-{\partial_0} \ar@<-3pt>[r]|-{\partial_1} & M'' \ar@<6pt>[r]|-{\partial_0} \ar[r]|-{\partial_1} \ar@<-6pt>[r]|-{\partial_2} & M''' } \]

over the diagram of rings

\[ \xymatrix{ B \ar@<3pt>[r]|-{\partial_0} \ar@<-3pt>[r]|-{\partial_1} & B\otimes_A B \ar@<6pt>[r]|-{\partial_0} \ar[r]|-{\partial_1} \ar@<-6pt>[r]|-{\partial_2} & B\otimes_A B\otimes_A B } \]

(let us be precise: one has \(\partial_i(b m)=\partial_i(b)\cdot\partial_i(m)\), the usual identities such as \(\partial_0\partial_1=\partial_0\partial_0\) hold, and “cartesian” means that the morphisms \(\partial_i:M'\otimes_{B,\partial_i}(B\otimes_A B)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M''\) and \(M''\otimes_{B\otimes_A B,\partial_i}(B\otimes_A B\otimes_A B)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M'''\) are isomorphisms).

The functor \(E\mapsto E_\mathscr{U}\) becomes the functor that, to an \(A\)-module \(M\), associates

\[ \xymatrix{ M^* = (M\otimes_A B \ar@<2pt>[r] \ar@<-2pt>[r] & M\otimes_A B\otimes_A B \ar@<-4pt>[r] \ar[r] \ar@<4pt>[r] & M\otimes_A B\otimes_A B\otimes_A B). } \]

It admits as right adjoint the functor

\[ \xymatrix{ (M' \ar@<2pt>[r] \ar@<-2pt>[r] & M'' \ar@<-4pt>[r] \ar[r] \ar@<4pt>[r] & M''') \ar@{|->}[r] & \ker(M' \ar@<2pt>[r] \ar@<-2pt>[r] & M'''). } \]

We must prove that the adjunction arrows

\[ M \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\ker(M\otimes_A B\rightrightarrows M\otimes_A B\otimes_A B) \]

and

\[ \ker(M'\rightrightarrows M'')\otimes_A B \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M' \]

are isomorphisms. By (1.4.2.i), it suffices to prove it after a faithfully flat base change \(A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} A'\) (\(B\) becoming \(B'=B\otimes_A A'\)). Taking \(A'=B\), this brings us back to the case where \(U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) admits a section.

Q.E.D.

1.5 A special case: Hilbert's Theorem 90

1.5.1

Let \(k\) be a field, \(k'\) a Galois extension of \(k\), and \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(k'/k)\). Then the homomorphism

\begin{align*} k'\otimes_k k' &\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \oplus_{\sigma\in G} k' \\ x\otimes y &\mapsto \{x\cdot \sigma(y)\}_{\sigma\in G} \end{align*}

is bijective.

One deduces that giving a module locally for the sieve generated by \(\operatorname{Spec}(k')\) on \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\) amounts to the same thing as giving a \(k'\)-vector space equipped with a semi-linear action of \(G\), that is:

  1. a \(k'\)-vector space \(V'\),

  2. for every \(\sigma\in G\), an endomorphism \(\varphi_\sigma\) of the group structure of \(V'\) such that \(\varphi_\sigma(\lambda v) = \sigma(\lambda) \varphi_\sigma(v)\), for every \(\lambda\in k'\) and \(v\in V'\), satisfying the condition

  3. for every \(\sigma,\tau\in G\), one has \(\varphi_{\tau\sigma} = \varphi_\tau\circ\varphi_\sigma\).

Let \(V={V'}^G\) be the group of invariants under this action of \(G\); it is a \(k\)-vector space and, by Theorem 1.4.5, one has:

Proposition 1.5.2

The inclusion of \(V\) in \(V'\) defines an isomorphism \(V\otimes_k k' \xrightarrow{\sim} V'\).

In particular, if \(V'\) is of dimension \(1\) and if \(v'\in V\) is non-zero, then \(\varphi_\sigma\) is determined by the constant \(c(\sigma)\in {k'}^\times\) such that \(\varphi_\sigma(v')=c(\sigma)v'\), and condition c) is written

\[ c(\tau\sigma) = c(\tau)\cdot \tau(c(\sigma))\text{.} \]

By the proposition, there exists a non-zero invariant vector \(v=\mu v'\), \(\mu\in {k'}^\times\). Hence for every \(\sigma\in G\), one has

\[ c(\sigma) = \mu\cdot \sigma(\mu^{-1})\text{.} \]

In other words, every \(1\)-cocycle of \(G\) with values in \({k'}^\times\) is a coboundary:

Corollary 1.5.3

One has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(G,{k'}^\times)=0\).

1.6 Grothendieck topologies

We now transcribe the definitions of the preceding sections in an abstract framework encompassing at once the case of topological spaces and that of schemes.

1.6.1

Let \(\mathscr{S}\) be a category and \(U\) an object of \(\mathscr{S}\). By a sieve on \(U\) one means a subset \(\mathscr{U}\) of \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathscr{S}/U)\) such that if \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belongs to \(\mathscr{U}\) and if \(\psi:W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\) is a morphism in \(\mathscr{S}\), then \(\varphi\circ\psi:W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belongs to \(\mathscr{U}\).

If \(\{\varphi_i:U_i\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\}\) is a family of morphisms, the sieve generated by the \(U_i\) is by definition the set of morphisms \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) that factor through one of the \(\varphi_i\).

If \(\mathscr{U}\) is a sieve on \(U\) and if \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) is a morphism, the restriction \(\mathscr{U}_V\) of \(\mathscr{U}\) to \(V\) is by definition the sieve on \(V\) consisting of the morphisms \(\psi:w\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\) such that \(\varphi\circ\psi:W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belongs to \(\mathscr{U}\).

1.6.2

The datum of a Grothendieck topology on \(\mathscr{S}\) consists of the datum, for every object \(U\) of \(\mathscr{S}\), of a set \(C(U)\) of sieves on \(U\), called covering sieves, such that the following axioms are satisfied:

  1. The sieve generated by the identity of \(U\) is covering.

  2. If \(\mathscr{U}\) is a covering sieve on \(U\) and if \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) is a morphism, then the sieve \(\mathscr{U}_V\) is covering.

  3. A locally covering sieve is covering. In other words, if \(\mathscr{U}\) is a covering sieve on \(U\) and if \(\mathscr{U}'\) is a sieve on \(U\) such that, for every \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belonging to \(\mathscr{U}\), the sieve \(\mathscr{U}_V'\) is covering, then \(\mathscr{U}'\) is covering.

By a site one means the datum of a category equipped with a Grothendieck topology.

1.6.3

Given a site \(\mathscr{S}\), by a presheaf on \(\mathscr{S}\) one means a contravariant functor \(\mathscr{F}\) from \(\mathscr{S}\) to the category of sets. For every object \(U\) of \(\mathscr{S}\), the elements of \(\mathscr{F}(U)\) are called sections of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(U\). For every morphism \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) and every \(s\in \mathscr{F}(U)\), one denotes by \(s|V\) (\(s\) restricted to \(V\)) the image of \(s\) in \(\mathscr{F}(V)\).

If \(\mathscr{U}\) is a sieve on \(U\), by a section given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally one means the datum, for every \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belonging to \(\mathscr{U}\), of a section \(s_V\in\mathscr{F}(V)\) such that, for every morphism \(W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\), one has \(s_V|W=s_W\). One says that \(\mathscr{F}\) is a sheaf if, for every object \(U\) of \(\mathscr{S}\), for every covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) on \(U\), and for every section given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally \(\{s_V\}\), there exists a unique section \(s\in\mathscr{F}(U)\) such that \(s|V=s_V\), for every \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belonging to \(\mathscr{U}\).

One defines in an analogous manner the abelian sheaves by replacing the category of sets by that of abelian groups. One shows that the category of abelian sheaves on \(\mathscr{S}\) is an abelian category possessing enough injectives. A sequence \(\mathscr{F}\xrightarrow f \mathscr{G}\xrightarrow g \mathscr{H}\) of sheaves is exact if, for every object \(U\) of \(\mathscr{S}\) and every \(s\in \mathscr{G}(U)\) such that \(g(s)=0\), there exists locally \(t\) such that \(f(t)=s\); i.e. if there exists a covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) on \(U\) and, for every \(V\in\mathscr{U}\), a section \(t_V\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(V\) such that \(f(t_V)=s|V\).

1.6.4 Examples

We have seen two of them above.

  1. Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(\mathscr{S}\) the category whose objects are the open sets of \(X\) and whose morphisms are the natural inclusions. The Grothendieck topology on \(\mathscr{S}\) corresponding to the usual topology of \(X\) is the one for which a sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) on an open set \(U\) of \(X\) is covering if the union of the open sets belonging to this sieve is equal to \(U\). It is clear that the category of sheaves on \(\mathscr{S}\) is equivalent to the category of sheaves on \(X\) in the usual sense.

  2. Let \(X\) be a scheme and \(\mathscr{S}\) the category of schemes over \(X\). By the fpqc topology (faithfully flat quasi-compact) on \(\mathscr{S}\) one means the Grothendieck topology for which a sieve on an \(X\)-scheme \(U\) is covering if it is generated by a finite family of flat morphisms whose images cover \(U\).

1.6.5 Cohomology

One will always assume that the category \(\mathscr{S}\) has a final object \(X\). Then the group \(\mathscr{F}(X)\) is called the group of global sections of an abelian sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\), and is denoted \(\Gamma\mathscr{F}\) or \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{F})\). The functor \(\mathscr{F}\mapsto\Gamma\mathscr{F}\) is a left exact functor from the category of abelian sheaves on \(\mathscr{S}\) to the category of abelian groups; one denotes by \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,-)\) its derived functors (or satellites). These cohomology groups represent the obstructions to passing from the local to the global. By definition, if \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{H}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) is an exact sequence of abelian sheaves, one has a long exact cohomology sequence:

\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{H}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \cdots \\ \ldots \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^n(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^n(X,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^n(X,\mathscr{H}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{n+1}(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \cdots } \]

1.6.6

Given an abelian sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(\mathscr{S}\), by an \(\mathscr{F}\)-torsor one means a sheaf \(\mathscr{G}\) equipped with an action \(\mathscr{F}\times\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) such that locally (after restriction to all the objects of a sieve covering the final object \(X\)) \(\mathscr{G}\), equipped with the action of \(\mathscr{F}\), is isomorphic to \(\mathscr{F}\) equipped with the canonical action \(\mathscr{F}\times \mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}\) by translations.

One can show that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) is interpreted as the set of isomorphism classes of \(\mathscr{F}\)-torsors.

blocks.html: 1 Grothendieck topologies

Originally, Grothendieck topologies appeared as underlying his theory of descent (cf. SGA 1 VI, VIII); the use of the corresponding cohomology theories came later. The same approach is followed here: by formalizing the classical notions of localization, local property, and gluing (1.1, 1.2, 1.3), one brings out the general concept of Grothendieck topology (1.6); to justify its introduction in algebraic geometry, one proves a faithfully flat descent theorem (1.4), a generalization of the classical theorem of Hilbert (1.5).

The reader will find a more complete, but concise, exposition of the formalism in Giraud [19]. M. Artin's notes: “Grothendieck topologies” [1] (Chapters I to III) also remain useful. The 866 pages of Exposés I to V of SGA 4 are valuable when one considers exotic topologies, such as the one giving rise to crystalline cohomology; to use the étale topology, so close to classical intuition, it is not indispensable to read them.

Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{R}\) a real-valued function on \(X\). The continuity of \(f\) is a property of local nature; in other words, if \(f\) is continuous on every sufficiently small open set of \(X\), then \(f\) is continuous on all of \(X\). To formalize the notion of “property of local nature,” we introduce a few definitions.

A set \(\mathscr{U}\) of open sets of \(X\) is called a sieve if for every \(U\in\mathscr{U}\) and \(V\subset U\), one has \(V\in\mathscr{U}\). A sieve is said to be covering if the union of all the open sets belonging to this sieve is equal to \(X\).
Given a family \(\{U_i\}\) of open sets of \(X\), the sieve generated by \(\{U_i\}\) is by definition the set of open sets \(U\) of \(X\) such that \(U\) is contained in one of the \(U_i\).

A property \(P(U)\), defined for every open set \(U\) of \(X\), is said to be local if, for every covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) of every open set \(U\) of \(X\), \(P(U)\) is true if and only if \(P(V)\) is true for every \(V\in \mathscr{U}\). For example, given \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{R}\), the property “\(f\) is continuous on \(U\)” is local.
1.2 Sheaves
Let us make precise the notion of a function given locally on \(X\).
1.2.1 The point of view of sieves

Let \(\mathscr{U}\) be a sieve of open sets of \(X\). By a function given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally on \(X\) one means the datum, for every \(U\in \mathscr{U}\), of a function \(f_U\) on \(U\) such that, if \(V\subset U\), one has \(f_V=f_U|V\).
1.2.2 The point of view of Čech

If the sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) is generated by a family of open sets \(U_i\) of \(X\), giving a function \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to giving a function \(f_i\) on each \(U_i\), such that \(f_i|{U_i\cap U_j} = f_j|{U_i\cap U_j}\).

In other words, if \(Z=\coprod U_i\), giving a function \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to giving a function on \(Z\) that is constant on the fibres of the natural projection \(Z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\).

The continuous functions form a sheaf; this means that for every covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) of an open set \(V\) of \(X\) and every function given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally \(\{f_U\}\) such that each \(f_U\) is continuous on \(U\), there exists a unique continuous function \(f\) on \(V\) such that \(f|U=f_U\) for every \(U\in \mathscr{U}\).
Let us now make precise the notion of a vector bundle given locally on \(X\).
1.3.1 The point of view of sieves
Let \(\mathscr{U}\) be a sieve of open sets of \(X\). By a vector bundle given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally on \(X\) one means the data of

1. a vector bundle \(E_U\) on each \(U\in \mathscr{U}\),

  2. if \(V\subset U\), an isomorphism \(\rho_{U,V} : E_V\xrightarrow{\sim} E_U|V\), satisfying

  3. if \(W\subset V\subset U\), the diagram

    \[ \xymatrix{ E_W \ar[r]^-{\rho_{U,W}} \ar[dr]_-{\rho_{V,W}} & E_U|W \\ & E_V|W \ar[u]_-{\rho_{U,V}|W} } \]

    commutes, that is, \(\rho_{U,V} = (\rho_{U,V} \mbox{ restricted to } W) \circ \rho_{V,W}\).
1.3.2 The point of view of Čech
If the sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) is generated by a family of open sets \(U_i\) of \(X\), giving a vector bundle \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to giving:

1. a vector bundle \(E_i\) on each \(U_i\),

  2. if \(U_{ij} = U_i\cap U_j = U_i\times_X U_j\), an isomorphism \(\rho_{ji} : E_i|U_{ij} \xrightarrow{\sim} E_j|U_{ij}\), so that

  3. if \(U_{ijk} = U_i\times_X U_j\times_X U_k\), the diagram

    \[ \xymatrix{ E_i |U_{ijk} \ar[r]^-{\rho_{ki}|U_{ijk}} \ar[dr]_-{\rho_{ji}|U_{ijk}} & E_k|U_{ijk} \\ & E_j|U_{ijk} \ar[u]_-{\rho_{kj}|U_{ijk}} } \]

    commutes, that is, \(\rho_{ki} = \rho_{kj}\circ \rho_{ji}\) on \(U_{ijk}\).

In other words, if \(Z=\coprod U_i\) and if \(\pi:Z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is the natural projection, giving a vector bundle \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to giving:

1. a vector bundle \(E\) on \(Z\),

  2. if \(x\) and \(y\) are two points of \(Z\) such that \(\pi(x) = \pi(y)\), an isomorphism \(\rho_{y x}:E_x\xrightarrow{\sim} E_y\) between the fibres of \(E\) at \(x\) and at \(y\), depending continuously on \((x,y)\) and such that,

  3. if \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) are three points of \(Z\) such that \(\pi(x)=\pi(y)=\pi(z)\), one has \(\rho_{zx} = \rho_{zy}\circ \rho_{yx}\).

A vector bundle \(E\) on \(X\) defines a vector bundle given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally \(E_\mathscr{U}\); the system of restrictions \(E_U\) of \(E\) to the objects of \(\mathscr{U}\). The fact that the notion of vector bundle is of local nature can be expressed as follows: for every covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) of \(X\), the functor \(E\mapsto E_\mathscr{U}\), from vector bundles on \(X\) to vector bundles given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally, is an equivalence of categories.

If in 1 one replaces “open set of \(X\)” by “subset of \(X\),” one obtains the notion of a sieve of subspaces of \(X\). In this framework too one has gluing theorems. For example: let \(X\) be a space and \(\mathscr{C}\) a sieve of subspaces of \(X\) generated by a locally finite closed covering of \(X\); then the functor \(E\mapsto E_\mathscr{C}\), from vector bundles on \(X\) to vector bundles given \(\mathscr{C}\)-locally, is an equivalence of categories.
In algebraic geometry, it is useful to consider also “sieves of spaces over \(X\)”; this is what we shall see in the following section.
1.4 Faithfully flat descent

In the framework of schemes, the Zariski topology is not fine enough for the study of non-linear problems, and one is led to replace, in the preceding definitions, the open immersions by more general morphisms. From this point of view, descent techniques appear as localization techniques. Thus the following descent statement can be expressed by saying that the properties considered are of local nature for the faithfully flat topology (a morphism of schemes is said to be faithfully flat if it is flat and surjective).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.4.2

Let \(A\) be a ring and \(B\) a faithfully flat \(A\)-algebra. Then:

  1. A sequence \(\Sigma=(M'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M'')\) of \(A\)-modules is exact as soon as the sequence \(\Sigma_{(B)}\) deduced from it by extension of scalars to \(B\) is exact.

  2. An \(A\)-module \(M\) is of finite type (resp. of finite presentation, flat, locally free of finite rank, invertible (i.e. locally free of rank one)) as soon as the \(B\)-module \(M_{(B)}\) is.

blocks.title: Démonstration
blocks.html:
Proof▾

(i) Since the functor \(M\mapsto M_{(B)}\) is exact (flatness of \(B\)), it suffices to show that, if an \(A\)-module \(N\) is non-zero, then \(N_{(B)}\) is non-zero. If \(N\) is non-zero, \(N\) contains a non-zero monogenic submodule \(A/\mathfrak{a}\); then \(N_{(B)}\) contains a monogenic submodule \((A/\mathfrak{a})_{(B)} = B/\mathfrak{a} B\), non-zero by surjectivity of the structural morphism \(\varphi:\operatorname{Spec}(B)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) (if \(V(\mathfrak{a})\) is non-empty, \(\varphi^{-1}(V(\mathfrak{a}))=V(\mathfrak{a} B)\) is non-empty).

(ii) For every family \((x_i)\) of elements of \(M_{(B)}\), there exists a submodule \(M'\) of \(M\) of finite type such that \(M'_{(B)}\) contains the \(x_i\). If \(M_{(B)}\) is of finite type and if the \(x_i\) generate \(M_{(B)}\), then \(M'_{(B)}=M_{(B)}\), hence \(M'=M\) and \(M\) is of finite type.

Q.E.D.

If \(M_{(B)}\) is of finite presentation, one can, by what precedes, find a surjection \(A^n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\). If \(N\) is the kernel of this surjection, the \(B\)-module \(N_{(B)}\) is of finite type, hence so is \(N\), and \(M\) is of finite presentation. The assertion for “flat” follows immediately from (i); “locally free of finite rank” means “flat and of finite presentation,” and the rank is tested by extension of scalars to fields.

Let \(X\) be a scheme and \(\mathscr{S}\) a class of \(X\)-schemes stable under fibre product over \(X\). A class \(\mathscr{U}\subset \mathscr{S}\) is a sieve on \(X\) (relative to \(\mathscr{S}\)) if, for every morphism \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) of \(X\)-schemes, with \(U,V\in \mathscr{S}\) and \(U\in\mathscr{U}\), one has \(V\in \mathscr{U}\). The sieve generated by a family \(\{U_i\}\) of \(X\)-schemes in \(\mathscr{S}\) is the class of \(V\in\mathscr{S}\) such that there exists a morphism of \(X\)-schemes from \(V\) to one of the \(U_i\).
Let \(\mathscr{U}\) be a sieve on \(X\). By a quasi-coherent module given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally on \(X\) one means the datum of

1. a quasi-coherent module \(E_U\) on each \(U\in\mathscr{U}\),

  2. for every \(U\in\mathscr{U}\) and for every morphism \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) of \(X\)-schemes in \(\mathscr{S}\), an isomorphism \(\rho_\varphi:E_V\xrightarrow{\sim} \varphi^* E_U\), these being such that

  3. if \(\psi:W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\) is a morphism of \(X\)-schemes in \(\mathscr{S}\), the diagram

    \[ \xymatrix{ E_W \ar[r]^-{\rho_{\varphi\circ\psi}} \ar[dr]_-{\rho_\psi} & \psi^*\varphi^* E_U \\ & \psi^* E_V \ar[u]_-{\psi^*\rho_\varphi} } \]

    commutes, that is, \(\rho_{\varphi\circ\psi}=(\psi^*\rho_\varphi)\circ \rho_\psi\).

If \(E\) is a quasi-coherent module on \(X\), one denotes by \(E_\mathscr{U}\) the module given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally equal to \(\varphi_U^* E\) on \(\varphi:U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) and such that, for every morphism \(\psi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) the restriction isomorphism \(\rho_\psi\) is the canonical isomorphism \(E_V=(\varphi_U\circ \psi)^* E\xrightarrow{\sim} \psi^* \varphi_U^* E = \psi^* E_U\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.4.5

Let \(\{U_i\}\in\mathscr{S}\) be a finite family of \(X\)-schemes flat over \(X\) such that \(X\) is the union of the images of the \(U_i\), and let \(\mathscr{U}\) be the sieve generated by \(\{U_i\}\). Then the functor \(E\mapsto E_\mathscr{U}\) is an equivalence of the category of quasi-coherent modules on \(X\) with the category of modules quasi-coherent given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally.

blocks.title: Démonstration
blocks.html:
Proof▾

We shall treat only the case where \(x\) is affine and where \(\mathscr{U}\) is generated by an affine \(X\)-scheme \(U\) faithfully flat over \(X\). The reduction to this case is formal. One sets \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(U=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\).

If the morphism \(U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) admits a section, then \(X\) belongs to the sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) and the assertion is obvious. We shall reduce to this case.

A quasi-coherent module given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally defines modules \(M'\), \(M''\), and \(M'''\) on \(U\), \(U\times_X U\), and \(U\times_X U\times_X U\), and isomorphisms \(\rho:p^* M^\bullet\simeq M^\bullet\) for every projection morphism \(p\) between these spaces; this is a cartesian diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ M^* : M' \ar@<2pt>[r] \ar@<-2pt>[r] & M'' \ar[r] \ar@<4pt>[r] \ar@<-4pt>[r] & M''' } \]

over

\[ \xymatrix{ U_* : U & U\times_X U \ar@<2pt>[l] \ar@<-2pt>[l] & U\times_X U\times_X U \ar[l] \ar@<4pt>[l] \ar@<-4pt>[l] . } \]

Conversely, \(M^*\) determines the module given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally: for \(V\in\mathscr{U}\), there exists \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) and one sets \(M_U=\varphi^* M'\); for \(\varphi_1,\varphi_2:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\), one has a natural identification \(\varphi_1^* M'\simeq (\varphi_1\times \varphi_2)^* M'' \simeq \varphi_2^* M'\), and one sees, using \(M'''\), that these identifications are compatible, so that the definition is legitimate. In short, giving a module \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally amounts to the same thing as giving a cartesian diagram \(M^*\) on \(U_*\).

Let us translate into algebraic terms: giving \(M^*\) amounts to giving a cartesian diagram of modules

\[ \xymatrix{ M' \ar@<3pt>[r]|-{\partial_0} \ar@<-3pt>[r]|-{\partial_1} & M'' \ar@<6pt>[r]|-{\partial_0} \ar[r]|-{\partial_1} \ar@<-6pt>[r]|-{\partial_2} & M''' } \]

over the diagram of rings

\[ \xymatrix{ B \ar@<3pt>[r]|-{\partial_0} \ar@<-3pt>[r]|-{\partial_1} & B\otimes_A B \ar@<6pt>[r]|-{\partial_0} \ar[r]|-{\partial_1} \ar@<-6pt>[r]|-{\partial_2} & B\otimes_A B\otimes_A B } \]

(let us be precise: one has \(\partial_i(b m)=\partial_i(b)\cdot\partial_i(m)\), the usual identities such as \(\partial_0\partial_1=\partial_0\partial_0\) hold, and “cartesian” means that the morphisms \(\partial_i:M'\otimes_{B,\partial_i}(B\otimes_A B)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M''\) and \(M''\otimes_{B\otimes_A B,\partial_i}(B\otimes_A B\otimes_A B)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M'''\) are isomorphisms).

The functor \(E\mapsto E_\mathscr{U}\) becomes the functor that, to an \(A\)-module \(M\), associates

\[ \xymatrix{ M^* = (M\otimes_A B \ar@<2pt>[r] \ar@<-2pt>[r] & M\otimes_A B\otimes_A B \ar@<-4pt>[r] \ar[r] \ar@<4pt>[r] & M\otimes_A B\otimes_A B\otimes_A B). } \]

It admits as right adjoint the functor

\[ \xymatrix{ (M' \ar@<2pt>[r] \ar@<-2pt>[r] & M'' \ar@<-4pt>[r] \ar[r] \ar@<4pt>[r] & M''') \ar@{|->}[r] & \ker(M' \ar@<2pt>[r] \ar@<-2pt>[r] & M'''). } \]

We must prove that the adjunction arrows

\[ M \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\ker(M\otimes_A B\rightrightarrows M\otimes_A B\otimes_A B) \]

and

\[ \ker(M'\rightrightarrows M'')\otimes_A B \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M' \]

are isomorphisms. By (1.4.2.i), it suffices to prove it after a faithfully flat base change \(A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} A'\) (\(B\) becoming \(B'=B\otimes_A A'\)). Taking \(A'=B\), this brings us back to the case where \(U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) admits a section.

Q.E.D.
1.5 A special case: Hilbert's Theorem 90
Let \(k\) be a field, \(k'\) a Galois extension of \(k\), and \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(k'/k)\). Then the homomorphism
\begin{align*} k'\otimes_k k' &\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \oplus_{\sigma\in G} k' \\ x\otimes y &\mapsto \{x\cdot \sigma(y)\}_{\sigma\in G} \end{align*}
is bijective.

One deduces that giving a module locally for the sieve generated by \(\operatorname{Spec}(k')\) on \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\) amounts to the same thing as giving a \(k'\)-vector space equipped with a semi-linear action of \(G\), that is:

1. a \(k'\)-vector space \(V'\),

  2. for every \(\sigma\in G\), an endomorphism \(\varphi_\sigma\) of the group structure of \(V'\) such that \(\varphi_\sigma(\lambda v) = \sigma(\lambda) \varphi_\sigma(v)\), for every \(\lambda\in k'\) and \(v\in V'\), satisfying the condition

  3. for every \(\sigma,\tau\in G\), one has \(\varphi_{\tau\sigma} = \varphi_\tau\circ\varphi_\sigma\).
Let \(V={V'}^G\) be the group of invariants under this action of \(G\); it is a \(k\)-vector space and, by Theorem 1.4.5, one has:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.5.2

The inclusion of \(V\) in \(V'\) defines an isomorphism \(V\otimes_k k' \xrightarrow{\sim} V'\).

In particular, if \(V'\) is of dimension \(1\) and if \(v'\in V\) is non-zero, then \(\varphi_\sigma\) is determined by the constant \(c(\sigma)\in {k'}^\times\) such that \(\varphi_\sigma(v')=c(\sigma)v'\), and condition c) is written
\[ c(\tau\sigma) = c(\tau)\cdot \tau(c(\sigma))\text{.} \]
By the proposition, there exists a non-zero invariant vector \(v=\mu v'\), \(\mu\in {k'}^\times\). Hence for every \(\sigma\in G\), one has
\[ c(\sigma) = \mu\cdot \sigma(\mu^{-1})\text{.} \]
In other words, every \(1\)-cocycle of \(G\) with values in \({k'}^\times\) is a coboundary:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.5.3

One has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(G,{k'}^\times)=0\).
1.6 Grothendieck topologies
We now transcribe the definitions of the preceding sections in an abstract framework encompassing at once the case of topological spaces and that of schemes.

Let \(\mathscr{S}\) be a category and \(U\) an object of \(\mathscr{S}\). By a sieve on \(U\) one means a subset \(\mathscr{U}\) of \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathscr{S}/U)\) such that if \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belongs to \(\mathscr{U}\) and if \(\psi:W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\) is a morphism in \(\mathscr{S}\), then \(\varphi\circ\psi:W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belongs to \(\mathscr{U}\).

If \(\{\varphi_i:U_i\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\}\) is a family of morphisms, the sieve generated by the \(U_i\) is by definition the set of morphisms \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) that factor through one of the \(\varphi_i\).

If \(\mathscr{U}\) is a sieve on \(U\) and if \(\varphi:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) is a morphism, the restriction \(\mathscr{U}_V\) of \(\mathscr{U}\) to \(V\) is by definition the sieve on \(V\) consisting of the morphisms \(\psi:w\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\) such that \(\varphi\circ\psi:W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belongs to \(\mathscr{U}\).

The datum of a Grothendieck topology on \(\mathscr{S}\) consists of the datum, for every object \(U\) of \(\mathscr{S}\), of a set \(C(U)\) of sieves on \(U\), called covering sieves, such that the following axioms are satisfied:

1. The sieve generated by the identity of \(U\) is covering.

  2. If \(\mathscr{U}\) is a covering sieve on \(U\) and if \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) is a morphism, then the sieve \(\mathscr{U}_V\) is covering.

  3. A locally covering sieve is covering. In other words, if \(\mathscr{U}\) is a covering sieve on \(U\) and if \(\mathscr{U}'\) is a sieve on \(U\) such that, for every \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belonging to \(\mathscr{U}\), the sieve \(\mathscr{U}_V'\) is covering, then \(\mathscr{U}'\) is covering.
By a site one means the datum of a category equipped with a Grothendieck topology.

Given a site \(\mathscr{S}\), by a presheaf on \(\mathscr{S}\) one means a contravariant functor \(\mathscr{F}\) from \(\mathscr{S}\) to the category of sets. For every object \(U\) of \(\mathscr{S}\), the elements of \(\mathscr{F}(U)\) are called sections of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(U\). For every morphism \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) and every \(s\in \mathscr{F}(U)\), one denotes by \(s|V\) (\(s\) restricted to \(V\)) the image of \(s\) in \(\mathscr{F}(V)\).

If \(\mathscr{U}\) is a sieve on \(U\), by a section given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally one means the datum, for every \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belonging to \(\mathscr{U}\), of a section \(s_V\in\mathscr{F}(V)\) such that, for every morphism \(W\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V\), one has \(s_V|W=s_W\). One says that \(\mathscr{F}\) is a sheaf if, for every object \(U\) of \(\mathscr{S}\), for every covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) on \(U\), and for every section given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally \(\{s_V\}\), there exists a unique section \(s\in\mathscr{F}(U)\) such that \(s|V=s_V\), for every \(V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) belonging to \(\mathscr{U}\).

One defines in an analogous manner the abelian sheaves by replacing the category of sets by that of abelian groups. One shows that the category of abelian sheaves on \(\mathscr{S}\) is an abelian category possessing enough injectives. A sequence \(\mathscr{F}\xrightarrow f \mathscr{G}\xrightarrow g \mathscr{H}\) of sheaves is exact if, for every object \(U\) of \(\mathscr{S}\) and every \(s\in \mathscr{G}(U)\) such that \(g(s)=0\), there exists locally \(t\) such that \(f(t)=s\); i.e. if there exists a covering sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) on \(U\) and, for every \(V\in\mathscr{U}\), a section \(t_V\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(V\) such that \(f(t_V)=s|V\).
We have seen two of them above.

1. Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(\mathscr{S}\) the category whose objects are the open sets of \(X\) and whose morphisms are the natural inclusions. The Grothendieck topology on \(\mathscr{S}\) corresponding to the usual topology of \(X\) is the one for which a sieve \(\mathscr{U}\) on an open set \(U\) of \(X\) is covering if the union of the open sets belonging to this sieve is equal to \(U\). It is clear that the category of sheaves on \(\mathscr{S}\) is equivalent to the category of sheaves on \(X\) in the usual sense.

  2. Let \(X\) be a scheme and \(\mathscr{S}\) the category of schemes over \(X\). By the fpqc topology (faithfully flat quasi-compact) on \(\mathscr{S}\) one means the Grothendieck topology for which a sieve on an \(X\)-scheme \(U\) is covering if it is generated by a finite family of flat morphisms whose images cover \(U\).
1.6.5 Cohomology

One will always assume that the category \(\mathscr{S}\) has a final object \(X\). Then the group \(\mathscr{F}(X)\) is called the group of global sections of an abelian sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\), and is denoted \(\Gamma\mathscr{F}\) or \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{F})\). The functor \(\mathscr{F}\mapsto\Gamma\mathscr{F}\) is a left exact functor from the category of abelian sheaves on \(\mathscr{S}\) to the category of abelian groups; one denotes by \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,-)\) its derived functors (or satellites). These cohomology groups represent the obstructions to passing from the local to the global. By definition, if \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{H}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) is an exact sequence of abelian sheaves, one has a long exact cohomology sequence:

\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{H}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \cdots \\ \ldots \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^n(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^n(X,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^n(X,\mathscr{H}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{n+1}(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \cdots } \]

Given an abelian sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(\mathscr{S}\), by an \(\mathscr{F}\)-torsor one means a sheaf \(\mathscr{G}\) equipped with an action \(\mathscr{F}\times\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) such that locally (after restriction to all the objects of a sieve covering the final object \(X\)) \(\mathscr{G}\), equipped with the action of \(\mathscr{F}\), is isomorphic to \(\mathscr{F}\) equipped with the canonical action \(\mathscr{F}\times \mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}\) by translations.
One can show that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) is interpreted as the set of isomorphism classes of \(\mathscr{F}\)-torsors.

pages.title: Étale topology
pages.html:
2 Étale topology

One specializes the definitions of the preceding chapter to the case of the étale topology of a scheme \(X\) (2.1, 2.2, 2.3). In the case where \(X\) is the spectrum of a field \(K\), the corresponding cohomology coincides with the Galois cohomology of \(K\) (2.4).

2.1 Étale topology

We shall begin with some reminders on the notion of étale morphism.

Definition 2.1.1

Let \(A\) be a (commutative) ring. One says that an \(A\)-algebra \(B\) is étale if \(B\) is an \(A\)-algebra of finite presentation and if the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:

  1. For every \(A\)-algebra \(C\) and every ideal \(J\) of \(C\) of square zero, the canonical map

    \[ \hom_{A\textnormal{-alg}}(B,C) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \hom_{A\textnormal{-alg}}(B,C/J) \]

    is a bijection.

  2. \(B\) is a flat \(A\)-module and \(\Omega_{B/A}=0\) (one denotes by \(\Omega_{B/A}\) the module of relative differentials).

  3. Let \(B=A[X_1,\dotsc,X_n]/I\) be a presentation of \(B\). Then for every prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\) of \(A[X_1,\dotsc,X_n]\) containing \(I\), there exist polynomials \(P_1,\dotsc,P_n\in I\) such that \(I_\mathfrak{p}\) is generated by the images of \(P_1,\dotsc,P_n\) and \(\det(\partial P_i/\partial X_j)\notin \mathfrak{p}\).

(cf. [23] or [30])

One says that a morphism of schemes \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is étale if for every \(x\in X\) there exist an affine open neighbourhood \(U=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) of \(f(x)\) and an affine open neighbourhood \(V=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\) of \(x\) in \(X\times_S U\) such that \(B\) is an étale \(A\)-algebra.

2.1.2 Examples

  1. If \(A\) is a field, an \(A\)-algebra \(B\) is étale if and only if it is a finite product of separable extensions of \(A\).

  2. If \(X\) and \(S\) are schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\), a morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is étale if and only if its analytification \(f^{\text{an}}:X^{\text{an}}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^{\text{an}}\) is a local isomorphism.

2.1.3 Sorite

  1. (base change) If \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is an étale morphism, then so is \(f_{S'}:X\times_S S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S'\) for every morphism \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\).

  2. If \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and \(g:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) are two étale morphisms, then every \(S\)-morphism from \(X\) to \(Y\) is étale.

  3. (descent) Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a morphism. If there exists a faithfully flat morphism \(S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) such that \(f_{S'}:X\times_S S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S'\) is étale, then \(f\) is étale.

2.1.4

Let \(X\) be a scheme. Let \(\mathscr{S}\) be the category of étale \(X\)-schemes; by (2.1.3.c), every morphism of \(\mathscr{S}\) is an étale morphism. By the étale topology on \(\mathscr{S}\) one means the topology for which a sieve on \(U\) is covering if it is generated by a finite family of morphisms \(\varphi_i:U_i\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) such that the union of the images of the \(\varphi_i\) covers \(U\). By the étale site of \(X\), denoted \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\), one means the site defined by \(\mathscr{S}\) with the étale topology.

2.2 Examples of sheaves

2.2.1 Constant sheaf

Let \(C\) be an abelian group, and suppose for simplicity that \(X\) is noetherian. One denotes by \(\underline{C}_X\) (or even \(C\) if there is no ambiguity) the sheaf defined by \(U\mapsto C^{\pi_0(U)}\), where \(\pi_0(U)\) is the (finite) set of connected components of \(U\). The most important case will be \(C=\mathbb{Z}/n\). One thus has by definition

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)=\left(\mathbb{Z}/n\right)^{\pi_0(X)}\text{.} \]

Moreover, \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) is the set of isomorphism classes of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-torsors (1.6.6), in other words of Galois étale coverings of \(X\) with group \(\mathbb{Z}/n\). In particular, if \(X\) is connected and if \(\pi_1(X)\) is its fundamental group for a chosen base point, one has

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \hom(\pi_1(X),\mathbb{Z}/n)\text{.} \]

2.2.2 Multiplicative group

One denotes by \(\mathbb{G}_{m,X}\) (or \(\mathbb{G}_m\) if there is no ambiguity) the sheaf defined by \(U\mapsto \Gamma(U,\mathscr{O}_U^\times)\); this is indeed a sheaf thanks to the faithfully flat descent theorem (1.4.5). One has by definition

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathbb{G}_m) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{O}_X)^\times\text{;} \]

in particular, if \(X\) is reduced, connected, and proper over an algebraically closed field \(k\), one has:

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathbb{G}_m) = k^\times\text{.} \]
Proposition 2.2.3

One has an isomorphism:

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{G}_m) = \operatorname{Pic}(X)\text{,} \]

where \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)\) is the group of classes of invertible sheaves on \(X\).

Proof▾

Let \(*\) be the functor that, to an invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{L}\) on \(X\), associates the following presheaf \(\mathscr{L}^*\) on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\): for \(\varphi:U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) étale,

\[ \mathscr{L}^*(U)=\operatorname{Isom}_U(\mathscr{O}_U,\varphi^*\mathscr{L})\text{.} \]

By (1.4.2.i) and (1.4.5) (full faithfulness), this presheaf is a sheaf; it is even a \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsor. One verifies immediately that

  1. the functor \(*\) is compatible with (étale) localization;

  2. it induces an equivalence of the category of trivial invertible sheaves (i.e. isomorphic to \(\mathscr{O}_X\)) with the category of trivial \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsors: \(\mathscr{L}\) is trivial if and only if \(\mathscr{L}^*\) is.

Moreover, by (1.4.2.ii) and (1.4.5),

  1. the notion of invertible sheaf is local for the étale topology.

It follows formally from a), b), c) that \(*\) is an equivalence between the category of invertible sheaves on \(X\) and that of \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsors on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\); it induces the desired isomorphism. One constructs as follows the inverse equivalence: if \(\mathscr{T}\) is a \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsor, there exists a finite étale covering \(\{U_i\}\) of \(X\) such that the torsors \(\mathscr{T}/U_i\) are trivial; \(\mathscr{T}\) is then trivial on each \(V\) étale over \(X\) belonging to the sieve \(\mathscr{U}\subset {X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\) generated by \(\{U_i\}\). On each \(V\in\mathscr{U}\), \(\mathscr{T}|V\) corresponds to an invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{L}_V\) (by b)), and the \(\mathscr{L}_V\) constitute an invertible sheaf given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally \(\mathscr{L}_\mathscr{U}\) (by a)). By c), the latter comes from an invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{L}(\mathscr{T})\) on \(X\), and \(\mathscr{T}\mapsto \mathscr{L}(\mathscr{T})\) is the desired inverse of \(*\).

Q.E.D.

2.2.4 Roots of unity

For every integer \(n>0\), the kernel of raising to the \(n\)-th power in \(\mathbb{G}_m\) is called the sheaf of \(n\)-th roots of unity, denoted \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\). If \(X\) is a scheme over a separably closed field \(k\) and if \(n\) is invertible in \(k\), the choice of a primitive \(n\)-th root of unity \(\zeta\in k\) defines an isomorphism \(i\mapsto \zeta^i\) from \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) to \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\).

The relation between cohomology with coefficients in \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_m\) and cohomology with coefficients in \(\mathbb{G}_m\) is given by the exact cohomology sequence deduced from the

Theorem 2.2.5 (Kummer theory)

If \(n\) is invertible on \(X\), the raising to the \(n\)-th power in \(\mathbb{G}_m\) is an epimorphism of sheaves. One thus has an exact sequence

\[ 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\text{.} \]
Proof▾

Let \(U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) be an étale morphism and \(a\in \mathbb{G}_m(U) =\Gamma(U,\mathscr{O}_U^\times)\). Since \(n\) is invertible on \(U\), the equation \(T^n-a = 0\) is separable; in other words, \(U'=\operatorname{Spec}\left(\mathscr{O}_U[T]/(T^n-a)\right)\) is étale over \(U\). Moreover, \(U'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) is surjective and a admits an \(n\)-th root on \(U'\), whence the result.

Q.E.D.

2.3 Fibres, direct images

2.3.1

We call a geometric point of \(X\) a morphism \(\overline{x}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), where \(\overline{x}\) is the spectrum of a separably closed field \(k(\overline{x})\). We shall denote it, by abuse of notation, \(\overline{x}\), leaving the morphism \(\overline{x}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) understood. If \(x\) is the image of \(\overline{x}\) in \(X\), we say that \(\overline{x}\) is centered at \(x\). If the field \(k(\overline{x})\) is an algebraic extension of the residue field \(k(x)\), we say that \(\overline{x}\) is an algebraic geometric point of \(X\).

We call an étale neighbourhood of \(\overline{x}\) a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ & U \ar[d] \\ \overline{x} \ar[ur] \ar[r] & X, } \]

where \(U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is an étale morphism.

The strict localization of \(X\) at \(\overline{x}\) is the ring \(\mathscr{O}_{X,\overline{x}} = \varinjlim \Gamma(U,\mathscr{O}_U)\), the inductive limit being taken over the étale neighbourhoods of \(\overline{x}\). It is a strictly henselian local ring whose residue field is the separable closure of the residue field \(k(x)\) of \(X\) at \(x\) in \(k(\overline{x})\). It plays the role of local ring for the étale topology.

2.3.2

Given a sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\), the stalk of \(\mathscr{F}\) at \(\overline{x}\) is the set (resp. the group, …) \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{x}}=\varinjlim \mathscr{F}(U)\), the inductive limit again being taken over the étale neighbourhoods of \(X\).

For a homomorphism of sheaves \(\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{G}\) to be a mono-/epi-/isomorphism it is necessary and sufficient that the same hold for the morphisms \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{x}}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{G}_{\overline{x}}\) induced on the stalks at every geometric point of \(X\). If \(X\) is of finite type over an algebraically closed field, it suffices that this hold at the rational points of \(X\).

2.3.3

If \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) is a morphism of schemes and \(\mathscr{F}\) a sheaf on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\), the direct image \(f_* \mathscr{F}\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) under \(f\) is the sheaf on \({Y}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\) defined by \(f_* \mathscr{F}(V) = \mathscr{F}(X\times_Y V)\) for every \(V\) étale over \(Y\). The functor \(f_*:\operatorname{Sh}({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Sh}({Y}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}})\) is left exact. Its right derived functors \(\mathsf{R}^q f_*\) are called higher direct images. If \(\overline{y}\) is a geometric point of \(Y\), one has

\[ (\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F})_{\overline{y}} = \varinjlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(V\times_Y X,\mathscr{F})\text{,} \]

the inductive limit being taken over the étale neighbourhoods \(V\) of \(\overline{y}\).

Let \(\mathscr{O}_{Y,\overline{y}}\) be the strict localization of \(Y\) at \(\overline{y}\), \(\widetilde Y=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathscr{O}_{Y,\overline{y}})\) and \(\widetilde X=X\times_Y \widetilde Y\). One can extend \(\mathscr{F}\) to \({\widetilde X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\) (this is a special case of the general notion of inverse image) in the following way: let \(\widetilde U\) be a scheme étale over \(\widetilde X\); then there exist an étale neighbourhood \(V\) of \(\overline{y}\) and a scheme \(U\) étale over \(X\times_Y V\) such that \(\widetilde U=U\times_V \widetilde Y\); we shall set

\[ \mathscr{F}(\widetilde U)=\varinjlim \mathscr{F}\left(U\times_V V'\right)\text{,} \]

the inductive limit being taken over the étale neighbourhoods \(V'\) of \(\overline{y}\) that dominate \(V\). With this definition, one has

\[ \left(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\right)_{\overline{y}} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\widetilde X,\mathscr{F})\text{.} \]

The functor \(f_*\) has a left adjoint \(f^*\), the “inverse image” functor. If \(\overline{x}\) is a geometric point of \(X\) and \(f(\overline{x})\) its image in \(Y\), one has \((f^* \mathscr{F})_{\overline{x}} = \mathscr{F}_{f(\overline{x})}\). This formula shows that \(f^*\) is an exact functor. The functor \(f_*\) therefore takes injective sheaves to injective sheaves, and the spectral sequence of the composite functor \(\Gamma\circ f_*\) (resp. \(g_* f_*\)) yields the

Theorem 2.3.4 (Leray spectral sequence)

Let \(\mathscr{F}\) be an abelian sheaf on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\) and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) a morphism of schemes (resp. let \(X\xrightarrow f Y \xrightarrow g Z\) be morphisms of schemes). One has a spectral sequence

\begin{align*} E_2^{pq} &= \underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(Y,\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}) \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{F}) \\ \text{(resp.}\qquad E_2^{pq} &= \mathsf{R}^p g_* \mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F} \Rightarrow \mathsf{R}^{p+q}(gf)_* \mathscr{F}\text{).} \end{align*}
Corollary 2.3.5

If \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}=0\) for every \(q>0\), then \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(Y,f_* \mathscr{F})=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(X,\mathscr{F})\) (resp. \(\mathsf{R}^p g_*(\mathscr{F}_* \mathscr{F}) = \mathsf{R}^p(g f)_* \mathscr{F}\)) for every \(p\geqslant 0\).

This applies in particular in the following case:

Proposition 2.3.6

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be a finite morphism (or even, by passage to the limit, an integral morphism) and \(\mathscr{F}\) an abelian sheaf on \(X\). Then \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}=0\), for every \(q>0\).

Indeed, let \(\overline{y}\) be a geometric point of \(Y\), \(\widetilde Y\) the spectrum of the strict localization of \(Y\) at \(y\) and \(\widetilde X=X\times_Y \widetilde Y\); by what precedes, it suffices to show that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\widetilde X,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for every \(q>0\). Now \(\widetilde X\) is the spectrum of a product of strictly henselian local rings (cf. [30]), the functor \(\Gamma(\widetilde X,-)\) is exact because every étale surjective \(\widetilde X\)-scheme admits a section, whence the assertion.

2.4 Galois cohomology

For \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(K)\) the spectrum of a field, we shall see that étale cohomology is identified with Galois cohomology.

2.4.1

Let us begin with a topological analogy. If \(K\) is the function field of an integral affine algebraic variety \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) over \(\mathbb{C}\), one has \(K=\varinjlim_{f\in A} A[1/f]\).

In other words \(X=\varprojlim U\), where \(U\) runs over the set of open subsets of \(Y\). It is known that there exist arbitrarily small Zariski opens which, for the classical topology, are \(K(\pi,1)\)'s. One will therefore not be surprised to regard \(\operatorname{Spec}(K)\) itself as a \(K(\pi,1)\), \(\pi\) being the fundamental group (in the algebraic sense) of \(X\), in other words the Galois group of \(\overline{K}/K\), where \(\overline{K}\) is a separable closure of \(K\).

2.4.2

More precisely, let \(K\) be a field, \(\overline{K}\) a separable closure of \(K\) and \(G = \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)\) the topological Galois group. To every finite étale \(K\)-algebra \(A\) (a finite product of separable extensions of \(K\)), let us associate the finite set \(\hom_K(A,\overline{K})\). The Galois group \(G\) acts on this set through a discrete (hence finite) quotient. If \(A=K[T]/(F)\), it is identified with the set of roots in \(\overline{K}\) of the polynomial \(F\). Galois theory, in the form given to it by Grothendieck, states that:

Proposition 2.4.3

The functor

\[ \left\{\begin{array}{c} K \textnormal{-algebras} \\ \textnormal{finite étale} \end{array}\right\} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \left\{\begin{array}{c} \textnormal{finite sets on which} \\ G \textnormal{ acts continuously} \end{array}\right\} \]

which to an étale algebra \(A\) associates \(\hom_K(A,\overline{K})\) is an anti-equivalence of categories.

From this one deduces an analogous description of sheaves for the étale topology on \(\operatorname{Spec}(K)\):

Proposition 2.4.4

The functor

\[ \left\{\begin{array}{c} \textnormal{étale sheaves} \\ \textnormal{on } \operatorname{Spec}(K) \end{array}\right\} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \left\{\begin{array}{c} \textnormal{sets on which} \\ G \textnormal{ acts continuously} \end{array}\right\} \]

which to a sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) associates its stalk \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{K}}\) at the geometric point \(\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{K})\) is an equivalence of categories.

One says that \(G\) acts continuously on a set \(E\) if the stabilizer of every element of \(E\) is an open subgroup of \(G\). The functor in the reverse direction is described in the obvious way: let \(A\) be a finite étale \(K\)-algebra, \(U=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(U(\overline{K})=\hom_K(A,\overline{K})\) the corresponding \(G\)-set; then one has \(\mathscr{F}(U)= \hom_{G\text{-ens}}(U(\overline{K}),\mathscr{F}_{\overline{K}})\).

In particular, if \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(K)\), one has \(\mathscr{F}(X) = \mathscr{F}_{\overline{K}}^G\). If one restricts to abelian sheaves, one obtains, on passing to the derived functors, canonical isomorphisms

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}},\mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(G,\mathscr{F}_{\overline{K}}) \]

2.4.5 Examples

  1. To the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) corresponds \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) with the trivial action of \(G\).

  2. To the sheaf of \(n\)-th roots of unity \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\) corresponds the group \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n(\overline{K})\) of \(n\)-th roots of unity in \(\overline{K}\), with the natural action of \(G\).

  3. To the sheaf \(\mathbb{G}_m\) corresponds the group \(\overline{K}^\times\) with the natural action of \(G\).

blocks.html: 2 Étale topology

One specializes the definitions of the preceding chapter to the case of the étale topology of a scheme \(X\) (2.1, 2.2, 2.3). In the case where \(X\) is the spectrum of a field \(K\), the corresponding cohomology coincides with the Galois cohomology of \(K\) (2.4).
2.1 Étale topology
We shall begin with some reminders on the notion of étale morphism.

One constructs as follows the inverse equivalence: if \(\mathscr{T}\) is a \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsor, there exists a finite étale covering \(\{U_i\}\) of \(X\) such that the torsors \(\mathscr{T}/U_i\) are trivial; \(\mathscr{T}\) is then trivial on each \(V\) étale over \(X\) belonging to the sieve \(\mathscr{U}\subset {X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\) generated by \(\{U_i\}\). On each \(V\in\mathscr{U}\), \(\mathscr{T}|V\) corresponds to an invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{L}_V\) (by b)), and the \(\mathscr{L}_V\) constitute an invertible sheaf given \(\mathscr{U}\)-locally \(\mathscr{L}_\mathscr{U}\) (by a)). By c), the latter comes from an invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{L}(\mathscr{T})\) on \(X\), and \(\mathscr{T}\mapsto \mathscr{L}(\mathscr{T})\) is the desired inverse of \(*\).

Q.E.D.
2.2.4 Roots of unity

For every integer \(n>0\), the kernel of raising to the \(n\)-th power in \(\mathbb{G}_m\) is called the sheaf of \(n\)-th roots of unity, denoted \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\). If \(X\) is a scheme over a separably closed field \(k\) and if \(n\) is invertible in \(k\), the choice of a primitive \(n\)-th root of unity \(\zeta\in k\) defines an isomorphism \(i\mapsto \zeta^i\) from \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) to \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\).
The relation between cohomology with coefficients in \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_m\) and cohomology with coefficients in \(\mathbb{G}_m\) is given by the exact cohomology sequence deduced from the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.2.5 (Kummer theory)

If \(n\) is invertible on \(X\), the raising to the \(n\)-th power in \(\mathbb{G}_m\) is an epimorphism of sheaves. One thus has an exact sequence

\[ 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\text{.} \]

blocks.title: Démonstration
blocks.html:
Proof▾

Let \(U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) be an étale morphism and \(a\in \mathbb{G}_m(U) =\Gamma(U,\mathscr{O}_U^\times)\). Since \(n\) is invertible on \(U\), the equation \(T^n-a = 0\) is separable; in other words, \(U'=\operatorname{Spec}\left(\mathscr{O}_U[T]/(T^n-a)\right)\) is étale over \(U\). Moreover, \(U'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U\) is surjective and a admits an \(n\)-th root on \(U'\), whence the result.

Q.E.D.
2.3 Fibres, direct images

We call a geometric point of \(X\) a morphism \(\overline{x}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), where \(\overline{x}\) is the spectrum of a separably closed field \(k(\overline{x})\). We shall denote it, by abuse of notation, \(\overline{x}\), leaving the morphism \(\overline{x}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) understood. If \(x\) is the image of \(\overline{x}\) in \(X\), we say that \(\overline{x}\) is centered at \(x\). If the field \(k(\overline{x})\) is an algebraic extension of the residue field \(k(x)\), we say that \(\overline{x}\) is an algebraic geometric point of \(X\).
We call an étale neighbourhood of \(\overline{x}\) a commutative diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ & U \ar[d] \\ \overline{x} \ar[ur] \ar[r] & X, } \]
where \(U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is an étale morphism.

The strict localization of \(X\) at \(\overline{x}\) is the ring \(\mathscr{O}_{X,\overline{x}} = \varinjlim \Gamma(U,\mathscr{O}_U)\), the inductive limit being taken over the étale neighbourhoods of \(\overline{x}\). It is a strictly henselian local ring whose residue field is the separable closure of the residue field \(k(x)\) of \(X\) at \(x\) in \(k(\overline{x})\). It plays the role of local ring for the étale topology.

Given a sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\), the stalk of \(\mathscr{F}\) at \(\overline{x}\) is the set (resp. the group, …) \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{x}}=\varinjlim \mathscr{F}(U)\), the inductive limit again being taken over the étale neighbourhoods of \(X\).

For a homomorphism of sheaves \(\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{G}\) to be a mono-/epi-/isomorphism it is necessary and sufficient that the same hold for the morphisms \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{x}}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{G}_{\overline{x}}\) induced on the stalks at every geometric point of \(X\). If \(X\) is of finite type over an algebraically closed field, it suffices that this hold at the rational points of \(X\).

If \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) is a morphism of schemes and \(\mathscr{F}\) a sheaf on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\), the direct image \(f_* \mathscr{F}\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) under \(f\) is the sheaf on \({Y}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\) defined by \(f_* \mathscr{F}(V) = \mathscr{F}(X\times_Y V)\) for every \(V\) étale over \(Y\). The functor \(f_*:\operatorname{Sh}({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Sh}({Y}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}})\) is left exact. Its right derived functors \(\mathsf{R}^q f_*\) are called higher direct images. If \(\overline{y}\) is a geometric point of \(Y\), one has
\[ (\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F})_{\overline{y}} = \varinjlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(V\times_Y X,\mathscr{F})\text{,} \]
the inductive limit being taken over the étale neighbourhoods \(V\) of \(\overline{y}\).

Let \(\mathscr{O}_{Y,\overline{y}}\) be the strict localization of \(Y\) at \(\overline{y}\), \(\widetilde Y=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathscr{O}_{Y,\overline{y}})\) and \(\widetilde X=X\times_Y \widetilde Y\). One can extend \(\mathscr{F}\) to \({\widetilde X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\) (this is a special case of the general notion of inverse image) in the following way: let \(\widetilde U\) be a scheme étale over \(\widetilde X\); then there exist an étale neighbourhood \(V\) of \(\overline{y}\) and a scheme \(U\) étale over \(X\times_Y V\) such that \(\widetilde U=U\times_V \widetilde Y\); we shall set
\[ \mathscr{F}(\widetilde U)=\varinjlim \mathscr{F}\left(U\times_V V'\right)\text{,} \]
the inductive limit being taken over the étale neighbourhoods \(V'\) of \(\overline{y}\) that dominate \(V\). With this definition, one has
\[ \left(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\right)_{\overline{y}} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\widetilde X,\mathscr{F})\text{.} \]

The functor \(f_*\) has a left adjoint \(f^*\), the “inverse image” functor. If \(\overline{x}\) is a geometric point of \(X\) and \(f(\overline{x})\) its image in \(Y\), one has \((f^* \mathscr{F})_{\overline{x}} = \mathscr{F}_{f(\overline{x})}\). This formula shows that \(f^*\) is an exact functor. The functor \(f_*\) therefore takes injective sheaves to injective sheaves, and the spectral sequence of the composite functor \(\Gamma\circ f_*\) (resp. \(g_* f_*\)) yields the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.3.4 (Leray spectral sequence)

Let \(\mathscr{F}\) be an abelian sheaf on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\) and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) a morphism of schemes (resp. let \(X\xrightarrow f Y \xrightarrow g Z\) be morphisms of schemes). One has a spectral sequence

\begin{align*} E_2^{pq} &= \underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(Y,\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}) \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{F}) \\ \text{(resp.}\qquad E_2^{pq} &= \mathsf{R}^p g_* \mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F} \Rightarrow \mathsf{R}^{p+q}(gf)_* \mathscr{F}\text{).} \end{align*}

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3.5

If \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}=0\) for every \(q>0\), then \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(Y,f_* \mathscr{F})=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(X,\mathscr{F})\) (resp. \(\mathsf{R}^p g_*(\mathscr{F}_* \mathscr{F}) = \mathsf{R}^p(g f)_* \mathscr{F}\)) for every \(p\geqslant 0\).
This applies in particular in the following case:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.3.6

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be a finite morphism (or even, by passage to the limit, an integral morphism) and \(\mathscr{F}\) an abelian sheaf on \(X\). Then \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}=0\), for every \(q>0\).

Indeed, let \(\overline{y}\) be a geometric point of \(Y\), \(\widetilde Y\) the spectrum of the strict localization of \(Y\) at \(y\) and \(\widetilde X=X\times_Y \widetilde Y\); by what precedes, it suffices to show that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\widetilde X,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for every \(q>0\). Now \(\widetilde X\) is the spectrum of a product of strictly henselian local rings (cf. [30]), the functor \(\Gamma(\widetilde X,-)\) is exact because every étale surjective \(\widetilde X\)-scheme admits a section, whence the assertion.
2.4 Galois cohomology
For \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(K)\) the spectrum of a field, we shall see that étale cohomology is identified with Galois cohomology.

Let us begin with a topological analogy. If \(K\) is the function field of an integral affine algebraic variety \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) over \(\mathbb{C}\), one has \(K=\varinjlim_{f\in A} A[1/f]\).

In other words \(X=\varprojlim U\), where \(U\) runs over the set of open subsets of \(Y\). It is known that there exist arbitrarily small Zariski opens which, for the classical topology, are \(K(\pi,1)\)'s. One will therefore not be surprised to regard \(\operatorname{Spec}(K)\) itself as a \(K(\pi,1)\), \(\pi\) being the fundamental group (in the algebraic sense) of \(X\), in other words the Galois group of \(\overline{K}/K\), where \(\overline{K}\) is a separable closure of \(K\).

More precisely, let \(K\) be a field, \(\overline{K}\) a separable closure of \(K\) and \(G = \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)\) the topological Galois group. To every finite étale \(K\)-algebra \(A\) (a finite product of separable extensions of \(K\)), let us associate the finite set \(\hom_K(A,\overline{K})\).
