The Galois group \(G\) acts on this set through a discrete (hence finite) quotient. If \(A=K[T]/(F)\), it is identified with the set of roots in \(\overline{K}\) of the polynomial \(F\). Galois theory, in the form given to it by Grothendieck, states that:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.4.3

The functor

\[ \left\{\begin{array}{c} K \textnormal{-algebras} \\ \textnormal{finite étale} \end{array}\right\} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \left\{\begin{array}{c} \textnormal{finite sets on which} \\ G \textnormal{ acts continuously} \end{array}\right\} \]

which to an étale algebra \(A\) associates \(\hom_K(A,\overline{K})\) is an anti-equivalence of categories.
From this one deduces an analogous description of sheaves for the étale topology on \(\operatorname{Spec}(K)\):

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.4.4

The functor

\[ \left\{\begin{array}{c} \textnormal{étale sheaves} \\ \textnormal{on } \operatorname{Spec}(K) \end{array}\right\} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \left\{\begin{array}{c} \textnormal{sets on which} \\ G \textnormal{ acts continuously} \end{array}\right\} \]

which to a sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) associates its stalk \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{K}}\) at the geometric point \(\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{K})\) is an equivalence of categories.

One says that \(G\) acts continuously on a set \(E\) if the stabilizer of every element of \(E\) is an open subgroup of \(G\). The functor in the reverse direction is described in the obvious way: let \(A\) be a finite étale \(K\)-algebra, \(U=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(U(\overline{K})=\hom_K(A,\overline{K})\) the corresponding \(G\)-set; then one has \(\mathscr{F}(U)= \hom_{G\text{-ens}}(U(\overline{K}),\mathscr{F}_{\overline{K}})\).

In particular, if \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(K)\), one has \(\mathscr{F}(X) = \mathscr{F}_{\overline{K}}^G\). If one restricts to abelian sheaves, one obtains, on passing to the derived functors, canonical isomorphisms
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}},\mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(G,\mathscr{F}_{\overline{K}}) \]

1. To the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) corresponds \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) with the trivial action of \(G\).

  2. To the sheaf of \(n\)-th roots of unity \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\) corresponds the group \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n(\overline{K})\) of \(n\)-th roots of unity in \(\overline{K}\), with the natural action of \(G\).

  3. To the sheaf \(\mathbb{G}_m\) corresponds the group \(\overline{K}^\times\) with the natural action of \(G\).

pages.title: Cohomology of curves
pages.html:
3 Cohomology of curves

In the case of topological spaces, dévissages using the Künneth formula and simplicial decompositions allow one, in order to compute the cohomology, to reduce to the interval \(I=[0,1]\), for which one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(I,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(I,\mathbb{Z})=0\) for \(q>0\).

In our case, the dévissages will lead to more complicated objects, namely curves over an algebraically closed field; we shall compute their cohomology in this chapter. The situation is more complex than in the topological case, since the cohomology groups vanish only for \(q>2\). The essential ingredient of the computations is the vanishing of the Brauer group of the function field of such a curve (Tsen's theorem, 3.2).

3.1 The Brauer group

Let us first recall its classical definition:

Definition 3.1.1

Let \(K\) be a field and \(A\) a \(K\)-algebra of finite dimension. One says that \(A\) is a central simple algebra over \(K\) if the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:

  1. \(A\) has no nontrivial two-sided ideal and its centre is \(K\).

  2. There exists a finite Galois extension \(K'/K\) such that \(A_{K'} = A\otimes_K K'\) is isomorphic to an algebra of square matrices over \(K'\).

  3. \(A\) is \(K\)-isomorphic to an algebra of square matrices over a skew field with centre \(K\).

Two such algebras are said to be equivalent if the skew fields that are associated with them by c) are \(K\)-isomorphic. If these algebras have the same dimension, this amounts to saying that they are \(K\)-isomorphic. The tensor product defines, by passage to the quotient, an abelian group structure on the set of equivalence classes. It is this group that one classically calls the Brauer group of \(K\) and denotes \(\operatorname{Br}(K)\).

3.1.2

We shall denote by \(\operatorname{Br}(n,K)\) the set of \(K\)-isomorphism classes of \(K\)-algebras \(A\) such that there exists a finite Galois extension \(K'\) of \(K\) for which \(A_{K'}\) is isomorphic to the algebra \(M_n(K')\) of \(n\times n\) square matrices over \(K'\). By definition \(\operatorname{Br}(K)\) is the union of the subsets \(\operatorname{Br}(n,K)\) for \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Let \(\overline{K}\) be an algebraic closure of \(K\) and \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)\). The set \(\operatorname{Br}(n,K)\) is the set of “forms” of \(M_n(\overline{K})\); it is therefore canonically isomorphic to \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{Aut}(M_n(\overline{K}))\right)\).

It is known that every automorphism of \(M_n(\overline{K})\) is inner. Consequently the group \(\operatorname{Aut}(M_n(\overline{K}))\) is identified with the projective linear group \(\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\), and one has a canonical bijection:

\[ \theta_n : \operatorname{Br}(n,K) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right)\text{.} \]

On the other hand, the exact sequence:

\[ \tag{3.1.2.1} 1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{K}^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{gl}(n,\overline{K}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 1\text{,} \]

allows one to define a coboundary operator:

\[ \Delta_n : \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\text{.} \]

By composing \(\theta_n\) and \(\Delta_n\), one obtains a map:

\[ \delta_n : \operatorname{Br}(n,K) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\text{.} \]

One easily checks that the maps \(\delta_n\) are compatible with one another and define a homomorphism of groups:

\[ \delta : \operatorname{Br}(K) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\text{.} \]
Proposition 3.1.3

The homomorphism \(\delta:\operatorname{Br}(K)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\) is bijective.

This results from the two following lemmas:

Lemma 3.1.4

The map \(\Delta_n:\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\) is injective.

By [36], Cor. to Prop. I-44, it suffices to check that each time one twists the exact sequence (3.1.2.1) by an element of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right)\), the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\) of the middle group is trivial. This middle group is the group of \(\overline{K}\)-points of the multiplicative group of a central simple algebra \(A\) of rank \(n^2\) over \(K\). To prove that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(G,A_{\overline{K}}^\times) = 0\), one interprets \(A^\times\) as the group of automorphisms of the free \(A\)-module \(L\) of rank \(1\), and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\) as the set of “forms” of \(L\) – the \(A\)-modules of rank \(n^2\) over \(K\), which are automatically free.

Lemma 3.1.5

Let \(\alpha\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\), \(K'\) a finite extension of \(K\) contained in \(\overline{K}\), \(n=[K':K]\), and \(G'=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K')\). If the image of \(\alpha\) in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G',\overline{K}^\times)\) is zero, then \(\alpha\) belongs to the image of \(\Delta_n\).

Let us first note that one has:

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G',\overline{K}^\times) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2\left(G,(\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times\right)\text{.} \]

(From a geometric point of view, if one denotes \(x=\operatorname{Spec}(K)\), \(x'=\operatorname{Spec}(K')\) and \(\pi:x'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} x\) the canonical morphism, one has \(\mathsf{R}^q \pi_*(\mathbb{G}_{m,x'}) = 0\) for \(q>0\), and consequently \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(x',\mathbb{G}_{m,X'})\simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(x,\pi_*\mathbb{G}_{m,X'})\) for \(q\geqslant 0\)).

Moreover, the choice of a basis of \(K'\) as a vector space over \(K\) allows one to define a homomorphism

\[ (\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{gl}(n,\overline{K}) \]

which, to an element \(x\), associates the endomorphism of multiplication by \(x\) of \(\overline{K}\otimes_K K'\). One then has a commutative diagram with exact rows:

\[ \xymatrix{ 1 \ar[r] & \overline{K}^\times \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & (\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times \ar[r] \ar[d] & (\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times / \overline{K}^\times \ar[r] \ar[d] & 1 \\ 1 \ar[r] & \overline{K}^\times \ar[r] & \operatorname{gl}(n,\overline{K}) \ar[r] & \operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K}) \ar[r] & 1 } \]

The lemma results from the commutative diagram deduced from it by passing to cohomology:

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,(\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times/\overline{K}^\times\right) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2\left(G,(\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times\right) \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right) \ar[r]^-{\Delta_n} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times) . } \]
Proposition 3.1.6

Let \(K\) be a field, \(\overline{K}\) an algebraic closure of \(K\) and \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)\). Suppose that, for every finite extension \(K'\) of \(K\), one has \(\operatorname{Br}(K')=0\). Then one has:

  1. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(G,\overline{K}^\times) = 0\) for every \(q>0\).

  2. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(G,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for every torsion \(G\)-module \(\mathscr{F}\) and for every \(q\geqslant 2\).

(For the proof, cf. [36]).

3.2 Tsen's theorem

Definition 3.2.1

One says that a field \(K\) is \(C_1\) if every non-constant homogeneous polynomial \(f(x_1,\dotsc,x_n)\) of degree \(d<n\) has a nontrivial zero.

Proposition 3.2.2

If a field \(K\) is \(C_1\), one has \(\operatorname{Br}(K)=0\).

It is a matter of showing that every skew field \(D\) with centre \(K\) and finite over \(K\) is equal to \(K\). Let \(r^2\) be the degree of \(D\) over \(K\) and \(\operatorname{Nrd}:D\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K\) the reduced norm.

(Locally for the étale topology on \(K\), \(D\) is isomorphic – not canonically – to a matrix algebra \(M_r\), and the reduced norm coincides with the determinant map. The latter is well defined, independently of the isomorphism chosen between \(D\) and \(M_r\), since every automorphism of \(M_r\) is inner and two similar matrices have the same determinant. This map, defined locally for the étale topology, descends, because of its local uniqueness, to a map \(\operatorname{Nrd}:D\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K\)).

The only zero of \(\operatorname{Nrd}\) is the zero element of \(D\), since, if \(x\ne 0\), one has \(\operatorname{Nrd}(x)\cdot \operatorname{Nrd}(x^{-1}) = 1\). On the other hand, if \(\{e_1,\dotsc,e_{r^2}\}\) is a basis of \(D\) over \(K\) and if \(x=\sum x_i e_i\), the function \(\operatorname{Nrd}(x)\) is written as a homogeneous polynomial \(\operatorname{Nrd}(x_1,\dotsc,x_{r^2})\) of degree \(r\) (this is clear locally for the étale topology). Since \(K\) is \(C_1\), one has \(r^2\leqslant r\), that is, \(r=1\) and \(D=K\).

Theorem 3.2.3 (Tsen)

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(K\) an extension of transcendence degree \(1\) of \(k\). Then \(K\) is \(C_1\).

Let us first suppose that \(K=k(X)\). Let

\[ f(T) = \sum a_{i_1,\dotsc i_n} T_1^{i_1} \dotsm T_n^{i_n} \]

be a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(d<n\) with coefficients in \(k(X)\). After multiplying the coefficients by a common denominator if necessary, one may assume that they lie in \(k[X]\). Let then \(\delta=\sup\deg(a_{i_1\dotsc i_n})\). One seeks a nontrivial zero in \(k[X]\) by the method of undetermined coefficients, writing each \(T_i\) (\(i=1,\dotsc,n\)) as a polynomial of degree \(N\) in \(X\). Then the equation \(f(T)=0\) becomes a system of homogeneous equations in the \(n\times (N+1)\) coefficients of the polynomials \(T_i(X)\), expressing the vanishing of the coefficients of the polynomial in \(X\) obtained by replacing \(T_i\) by \(T_i(X)\). This polynomial is of degree at most \(\delta+N D\), so there are \(\delta+N d+1\) equations in \(n\times (N+1)\) variables. Since \(k\) is algebraically closed, this system has a nontrivial solution if \(n(N+1)>N d+\delta+1\), which will be the case for \(N\) large enough if \(d<n\).

It is clear that, to prove the theorem in the general case, it suffices to prove it when \(K\) is a finite extension of a purely transcendental extension \(k(X)\) of \(k\). Let \(f(T)=f(T_1,\dotsc,T_n)\) be a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(d<n\) with coefficients in \(K\). Let \(a=[K:k(X)]\) and \(e_1,\dotsc,e_s\) a basis of \(K\) over \(k(X)\). Let us introduce new variables \(U_{i j}\), \(s n\) in number, such that \(T_i=\sum U_{i j}e_j\). For the polynomial \(f(T)\) to have a nontrivial zero in \(K\), it suffices that the polynomial \(g(X_{i j}) = N_{K/k}(f( T))\) have a nontrivial zero in \(k(X)\). Now \(g\) is a polynomial of degree \(s d\) in \(s n\) variables, whence the result.

Corollary 3.2.4

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(K\) an extension of transcendence degree \(1\) of \(k\). Then the étale cohomology groups \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\operatorname{Spec}(K),\mathbb{G}_m)\) are zero for every \(q>0\).

Cohomology of smooth curves

Henceforth, and unless expressly stated otherwise, the groups of cohomology considered are the étale cohomology groups.

Proposition 3.3.1

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(X\) a connected non-singular projective curve over \(k\). Then one has:

\begin{align*} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathbb{G}_m) &= k^\times \text{,} \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{G}_m) &= \operatorname{Pic}(X) \text{,} \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{G}_m) &= 0 \text{ for } q\geqslant 2 \text{.} \end{align*}

Let \(\eta\) be the generic point of \(X\), \(j:\eta\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) the canonical morphism and \(\mathbb{G}_{m,X}\) the multiplicative group of the field of fractions \(K(X)\). For every closed point \(x\) of \(X\), let \(i_x:x\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) be the canonical immersion and \(\mathbb{Z}_x\) the constant sheaf with value \(\mathbb{Z}\) on \(x\). Thus \(j_*\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}\) is the sheaf of nonzero meromorphic functions on \(X\) and \(\oplus_{x\in X} i_{x_I}\mathbb{Z}_x\) the sheaf of divisors; one therefore has an exact sequence of sheaves:

\[ \tag{3.3.1.1} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r] & j_* \mathbb{G}_{m,\eta} \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{div}} \ar[r] & \displaystyle\bigoplus_{x\in X} i_{x*} \mathbb{Z}_x \ar[r] & 0. } \]
Lemma 3.3.2

One has \(\mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{G}_{m,\eta} = 0\) for every \(q>0\).

It suffices to show that the stalk of this sheaf at every closed point \(x\) of \(X\) is zero. If \(\widetilde{\mathscr{O}}_{X,x}\) is the henselization of \(X\) at \(x\) and \(K\) the field of fractions of \(\widetilde{\mathscr{O}}_{X,x}\), one has

\[ \operatorname{Spec}(K) = \eta\times_X \operatorname{Spec}(\widetilde{\mathscr{O}}_{X,x})\text{,} \]

hence \((\mathsf{R}^qj_*\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta})_x = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\operatorname{Spec}(K),\mathbb{G}_m)\).

Now \(K\) is an algebraic extension of \(k(X)\), hence an extension of transcendence degree \(1\) of \(k\): the lemma results from (3.2.4).

Lemma 3.3.3

One has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X, j_*\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}) = 0\) for every \(q>0\).

Indeed, from (3.3.2) and the Leray spectral sequence for \(j\), one deduces:

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X, j_* \mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\eta,\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}) \]

for every \(q\geqslant 0\), and the right-hand side is zero for \(q>0\) by (3.2.4).

Lemma 3.3.4

One has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q\left(X,\bigoplus_{x\in X} i_{x*} \mathbb{Z}_x\right) = 0\) for every \(q>0\).

Indeed, for every closed point of \(X\), one has \(\mathsf{R}^q i_{x*}\mathbb{Z}_x 0\) for \(q>0\), since \(i_x\) is a finite morphism (2.3.6), and

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,i_{x*}\mathbb{Z}_x) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(x,\mathbb{Z}_x)\text{.} \]

The right-hand side is zero for every \(q>0\), since \(x\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field (One sees that the lemma is true more generally for every “skyscraper” sheaf on \(X\)).

From the preceding lemmas and the exact sequence (3.3.1.1) one deduces the equalities:

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{G}_m) = 0 \text{ for } q\geqslant 2 \text{,} \]

and an exact cohomology sequence in low degree:

\[ 1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathbb{G}_m) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X, j_*\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\left(X,\bigoplus_{x\in X} i_{x*}\mathbb{Z}_x\right) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{G}_m) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 1 \]

which is none other than the exact sequence:

\[ 1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k(X)^\times\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Div}(X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}(X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 1\text{.} \]

From proposition 3.3.1 one deduces that the cohomology groups of \(X\) with values in \(\mathbb{Z}/n\), \(n\) prime to the characteristic of \(k\), have a reasonable value:

Corollary 3.3.5

If \(X\) is of genus \(g\) and if \(n\) is invertible in \(k\), the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) are zero for \(q>2\), and free over \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) of rank \(1,2 g,1\) for \(q=0,1,2\). Replacing \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) by the isomorphic group \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\), one has canonical isomorphisms

\begin{align*} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) &= \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) &= \operatorname{Pic}^0(X)_n \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) &= \mathbb{Z}/n \text{.} \end{align*}

Since the field \(k\) is algebraically closed, \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) is isomorphic (not canonically) to \(\mu_n\). From the Kummer exact sequence:

\[ 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mu_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\text{,} \]

and from proposition 3.3.1, one deduces the equalities:

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0 \text{ for } q>2 \text{,} \]

and, in low degree, exact sequences:

\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r] & k^\times \ar[r]^-n & k^\times \ar[r] & 0 } \]
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}(X) \ar[r]^-n & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r] & 0. } \]

Moreover, one has an exact sequence:

\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}^0(X) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}(X) \ar[r]^-{\deg} & \mathbb{Z} \ar[r] & 0 , } \]

and \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\) is identified with the group of rational points over \(k\) of an abelian variety of dimension \(g\), the Jacobian of \(X\). In such a group, multiplication by \(n\) is surjective and its kernel is a free \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-module of rank \(2 g\) (since \(n\) is invertible in \(k\)); whence the corollary.

A clever dévissage, using the “trace method,” allows one to obtain as a corollary the

Proposition 3.3.6 ([2])

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, \(X\) an algebraic curve over \(k\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then:

  1. One has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for \(q>2\).

  2. If \(X\) is affine, one even has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for \(q>1\).

For the proof, as well as for the exposition of the “trace method,” we refer to [2].

3.4 Dévissages

To compute the cohomology of varieties of dimension \(>1\), one uses fibrations by curves, which allows one to reduce to studying the morphisms whose fibres are of dimension \(\leqslant 1\). This principle has several variants; let us indicate a few of them.

3.4.1

Let \(A\) be a \(k\)-algebra of finite type and \(a_1,\dotsc,a_n\) generators of \(A\). If one sets \(X_0=\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(X_i=\operatorname{Spec}(k[a_1,\dotsc,a_i])\), \(X_n=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\), the canonical inclusions \(k[a_1,\dotsc,a_i]\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k[a_1,\dotsc,a_i,a_{i+1}]\) define morphisms \(X_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_{n-1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_0\) whose fibres are of dimension \(\leqslant 1\).

3.4.2

In the case of a smooth morphism, one can be more precise. We call an elementary fibration a morphism of schemes \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) that can be embedded in a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-j \ar[dr]_-f & \overline{X} \ar[d]^-{\overline{f}} & Y \ar@{_{(}->}[l]_-i \ar[dl]^-g\\ & S } \]

satisfying the following conditions:

  1. \(j\) is an open immersion dense in each fibre and \(X=\overline{X} \setminus Y\).

  2. \(\overline{f}\) is smooth and projective, with irreducible geometric fibres of dimension \(1\).

  3. \(g\) is an étale covering and no fibre of \(g\) is empty.

A \(S\)-scheme \(X\) is called a good neighbourhood relative to \(S\) if there exist \(S\)-schemes \(X=X_n,\dotsc,X_0=S\) and elementary fibrations \(f_i:X_i\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_{i-1}\), \(i=1,\dotsc,n\). One can show [2] that if \(X\) is a smooth scheme over an algebraically closed field \(k\) every rational point of \(X\) has an open neighbourhood which is a good neighbourhood (relative to \(\operatorname{Spec}(K)\)).

3.4.3

One can carry out a dévissage of a proper morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) as follows. By Chow's lemma, there exists a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[dr]_-f & \overline{X} \ar[l]_-\pi \ar[d]^-{\overline{f}}\\ & S } \]

where \(\pi\) and \(\overline{f}\) are projective morphisms, \(\pi\) being moreover an isomorphism above a dense open subset of \(X\). Locally on \(S\), \(\overline{X}\) is a closed subscheme of a standard projective space \(\mathbb{P}_S^n\).

One carries out a dévissage of the latter by considering the projection \(\varphi:\mathbb{P}_S^n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{P}_S^1\) which sends the point with homogeneous coordinates \((x_0,x_1,\dotsc,x_n)\) to \((x_0,x_1)\). This is a rational map defined outside the closed subset \(Y\simeq \mathbb{P}_S^{n-2}\) of \(\mathbb{P}_S^n\) with homogeneous equations \(x_0=x_1=0\). Let \(u:P\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{P}_S^n\) be the blow-up with centre \(Y\); the fibres of \(u\) are of dimension \(\leqslant 1\). Moreover there exists a natural morphism \(v:P\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{P}_S^1\) which extends the rational map \(\varphi\) and \(v\) makes \(P\) into a \(\mathbb{P}_S^1\)-scheme locally isomorphic to the standard projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{n-1}\) which can in turn be projected onto a \(\mathbb{P}^1\), etc.

3.4.4

One can sweep out a smooth projective variety \(X\) by a Lefschetz pencil. The blow-up \(\widetilde X\) of the intersection of the axis of the pencil with \(X\) projects onto \(\mathbb{P}^1\) and the fibres of this projection are the hyperplane sections of \(X\) by the hyperplanes of the pencil.

blocks.html: 3 Cohomology of curves

In the case of topological spaces, dévissages using the Künneth formula and simplicial decompositions allow one, in order to compute the cohomology, to reduce to the interval \(I=[0,1]\), for which one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(I,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(I,\mathbb{Z})=0\) for \(q>0\).

In our case, the dévissages will lead to more complicated objects, namely curves over an algebraically closed field; we shall compute their cohomology in this chapter. The situation is more complex than in the topological case, since the cohomology groups vanish only for \(q>2\). The essential ingredient of the computations is the vanishing of the Brauer group of the function field of such a curve (Tsen's theorem, 3.2).
3.1 The Brauer group
Let us first recall its classical definition:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1.1

Let \(K\) be a field and \(A\) a \(K\)-algebra of finite dimension. One says that \(A\) is a central simple algebra over \(K\) if the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:

  1. \(A\) has no nontrivial two-sided ideal and its centre is \(K\).

  2. There exists a finite Galois extension \(K'/K\) such that \(A_{K'} = A\otimes_K K'\) is isomorphic to an algebra of square matrices over \(K'\).

  3. \(A\) is \(K\)-isomorphic to an algebra of square matrices over a skew field with centre \(K\).

Two such algebras are said to be equivalent if the skew fields that are associated with them by c) are \(K\)-isomorphic. If these algebras have the same dimension, this amounts to saying that they are \(K\)-isomorphic. The tensor product defines, by passage to the quotient, an abelian group structure on the set of equivalence classes. It is this group that one classically calls the Brauer group of \(K\) and denotes \(\operatorname{Br}(K)\).

We shall denote by \(\operatorname{Br}(n,K)\) the set of \(K\)-isomorphism classes of \(K\)-algebras \(A\) such that there exists a finite Galois extension \(K'\) of \(K\) for which \(A_{K'}\) is isomorphic to the algebra \(M_n(K')\) of \(n\times n\) square matrices over \(K'\). By definition \(\operatorname{Br}(K)\) is the union of the subsets \(\operatorname{Br}(n,K)\) for \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Let \(\overline{K}\) be an algebraic closure of \(K\) and \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)\). The set \(\operatorname{Br}(n,K)\) is the set of “forms” of \(M_n(\overline{K})\); it is therefore canonically isomorphic to \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{Aut}(M_n(\overline{K}))\right)\).

It is known that every automorphism of \(M_n(\overline{K})\) is inner. Consequently the group \(\operatorname{Aut}(M_n(\overline{K}))\) is identified with the projective linear group \(\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\), and one has a canonical bijection:
\[ \theta_n : \operatorname{Br}(n,K) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right)\text{.} \]
On the other hand, the exact sequence:

\[ \tag{3.1.2.1} 1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{K}^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{gl}(n,\overline{K}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 1\text{,} \]
allows one to define a coboundary operator:

\[ \Delta_n : \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\text{.} \]
By composing \(\theta_n\) and \(\Delta_n\), one obtains a map:
\[ \delta_n : \operatorname{Br}(n,K) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\text{.} \]
One easily checks that the maps \(\delta_n\) are compatible with one another and define a homomorphism of groups:
\[ \delta : \operatorname{Br}(K) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\text{.} \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.3

The homomorphism \(\delta:\operatorname{Br}(K)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\) is bijective.
This results from the two following lemmas:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1.4

The map \(\Delta_n:\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\) is injective.

By [36], Cor. to Prop. I-44, it suffices to check that each time one twists the exact sequence (3.1.2.1) by an element of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right)\), the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\) of the middle group is trivial. This middle group is the group of \(\overline{K}\)-points of the multiplicative group of a central simple algebra \(A\) of rank \(n^2\) over \(K\). To prove that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(G,A_{\overline{K}}^\times) = 0\), one interprets \(A^\times\) as the group of automorphisms of the free \(A\)-module \(L\) of rank \(1\), and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\) as the set of “forms” of \(L\) – the \(A\)-modules of rank \(n^2\) over \(K\), which are automatically free.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1.5

Let \(\alpha\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times)\), \(K'\) a finite extension of \(K\) contained in \(\overline{K}\), \(n=[K':K]\), and \(G'=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K')\). If the image of \(\alpha\) in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G',\overline{K}^\times)\) is zero, then \(\alpha\) belongs to the image of \(\Delta_n\).
Let us first note that one has:
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G',\overline{K}^\times) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2\left(G,(\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times\right)\text{.} \]

(From a geometric point of view, if one denotes \(x=\operatorname{Spec}(K)\), \(x'=\operatorname{Spec}(K')\) and \(\pi:x'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} x\) the canonical morphism, one has \(\mathsf{R}^q \pi_*(\mathbb{G}_{m,x'}) = 0\) for \(q>0\), and consequently \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(x',\mathbb{G}_{m,X'})\simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(x,\pi_*\mathbb{G}_{m,X'})\) for \(q\geqslant 0\)).
Moreover, the choice of a basis of \(K'\) as a vector space over \(K\) allows one to define a homomorphism
\[ (\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{gl}(n,\overline{K}) \]
which, to an element \(x\), associates the endomorphism of multiplication by \(x\) of \(\overline{K}\otimes_K K'\). One then has a commutative diagram with exact rows:

\[ \xymatrix{ 1 \ar[r] & \overline{K}^\times \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & (\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times \ar[r] \ar[d] & (\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times / \overline{K}^\times \ar[r] \ar[d] & 1 \\ 1 \ar[r] & \overline{K}^\times \ar[r] & \operatorname{gl}(n,\overline{K}) \ar[r] & \operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K}) \ar[r] & 1 } \]
The lemma results from the commutative diagram deduced from it by passing to cohomology:

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,(\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times/\overline{K}^\times\right) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2\left(G,(\overline{K}\otimes_K K')^\times\right) \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(G,\operatorname{PGL}(n,\overline{K})\right) \ar[r]^-{\Delta_n} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(G,\overline{K}^\times) . } \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.6

Let \(K\) be a field, \(\overline{K}\) an algebraic closure of \(K\) and \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)\). Suppose that, for every finite extension \(K'\) of \(K\), one has \(\operatorname{Br}(K')=0\). Then one has:

  1. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(G,\overline{K}^\times) = 0\) for every \(q>0\).

  2. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(G,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for every torsion \(G\)-module \(\mathscr{F}\) and for every \(q\geqslant 2\).
(For the proof, cf. [36]).
3.2 Tsen's theorem

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.2.1

One says that a field \(K\) is \(C_1\) if every non-constant homogeneous polynomial \(f(x_1,\dotsc,x_n)\) of degree \(d<n\) has a nontrivial zero.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2.2

If a field \(K\) is \(C_1\), one has \(\operatorname{Br}(K)=0\).

It is a matter of showing that every skew field \(D\) with centre \(K\) and finite over \(K\) is equal to \(K\). Let \(r^2\) be the degree of \(D\) over \(K\) and \(\operatorname{Nrd}:D\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K\) the reduced norm.

(Locally for the étale topology on \(K\), \(D\) is isomorphic – not canonically – to a matrix algebra \(M_r\), and the reduced norm coincides with the determinant map. The latter is well defined, independently of the isomorphism chosen between \(D\) and \(M_r\), since every automorphism of \(M_r\) is inner and two similar matrices have the same determinant. This map, defined locally for the étale topology, descends, because of its local uniqueness, to a map \(\operatorname{Nrd}:D\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K\)).

The only zero of \(\operatorname{Nrd}\) is the zero element of \(D\), since, if \(x\ne 0\), one has \(\operatorname{Nrd}(x)\cdot \operatorname{Nrd}(x^{-1}) = 1\). On the other hand, if \(\{e_1,\dotsc,e_{r^2}\}\) is a basis of \(D\) over \(K\) and if \(x=\sum x_i e_i\), the function \(\operatorname{Nrd}(x)\) is written as a homogeneous polynomial \(\operatorname{Nrd}(x_1,\dotsc,x_{r^2})\) of degree \(r\) (this is clear locally for the étale topology). Since \(K\) is \(C_1\), one has \(r^2\leqslant r\), that is, \(r=1\) and \(D=K\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.2.3 (Tsen)

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(K\) an extension of transcendence degree \(1\) of \(k\). Then \(K\) is \(C_1\).
Let us first suppose that \(K=k(X)\). Let
\[ f(T) = \sum a_{i_1,\dotsc i_n} T_1^{i_1} \dotsm T_n^{i_n} \]

be a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(d<n\) with coefficients in \(k(X)\). After multiplying the coefficients by a common denominator if necessary, one may assume that they lie in \(k[X]\). Let then \(\delta=\sup\deg(a_{i_1\dotsc i_n})\). One seeks a nontrivial zero in \(k[X]\) by the method of undetermined coefficients, writing each \(T_i\) (\(i=1,\dotsc,n\)) as a polynomial of degree \(N\) in \(X\). Then the equation \(f(T)=0\) becomes a system of homogeneous equations in the \(n\times (N+1)\) coefficients of the polynomials \(T_i(X)\), expressing the vanishing of the coefficients of the polynomial in \(X\) obtained by replacing \(T_i\) by \(T_i(X)\). This polynomial is of degree at most \(\delta+N D\), so there are \(\delta+N d+1\) equations in \(n\times (N+1)\) variables. Since \(k\) is algebraically closed, this system has a nontrivial solution if \(n(N+1)>N d+\delta+1\), which will be the case for \(N\) large enough if \(d<n\).

It is clear that, to prove the theorem in the general case, it suffices to prove it when \(K\) is a finite extension of a purely transcendental extension \(k(X)\) of \(k\). Let \(f(T)=f(T_1,\dotsc,T_n)\) be a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(d<n\) with coefficients in \(K\). Let \(a=[K:k(X)]\) and \(e_1,\dotsc,e_s\) a basis of \(K\) over \(k(X)\). Let us introduce new variables \(U_{i j}\), \(s n\) in number, such that \(T_i=\sum U_{i j}e_j\). For the polynomial \(f(T)\) to have a nontrivial zero in \(K\), it suffices that the polynomial \(g(X_{i j}) = N_{K/k}(f( T))\) have a nontrivial zero in \(k(X)\). Now \(g\) is a polynomial of degree \(s d\) in \(s n\) variables, whence the result.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.2.4

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(K\) an extension of transcendence degree \(1\) of \(k\). Then the étale cohomology groups \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\operatorname{Spec}(K),\mathbb{G}_m)\) are zero for every \(q>0\).
Cohomology of smooth curves
Henceforth, and unless expressly stated otherwise, the groups of cohomology considered are the étale cohomology groups.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3.1

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(X\) a connected non-singular projective curve over \(k\). Then one has:

\begin{align*} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathbb{G}_m) &= k^\times \text{,} \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{G}_m) &= \operatorname{Pic}(X) \text{,} \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{G}_m) &= 0 \text{ for } q\geqslant 2 \text{.} \end{align*}

Let \(\eta\) be the generic point of \(X\), \(j:\eta\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) the canonical morphism and \(\mathbb{G}_{m,X}\) the multiplicative group of the field of fractions \(K(X)\). For every closed point \(x\) of \(X\), let \(i_x:x\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) be the canonical immersion and \(\mathbb{Z}_x\) the constant sheaf with value \(\mathbb{Z}\) on \(x\). Thus \(j_*\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}\) is the sheaf of nonzero meromorphic functions on \(X\) and \(\oplus_{x\in X} i_{x_I}\mathbb{Z}_x\) the sheaf of divisors; one therefore has an exact sequence of sheaves:
\[ \tag{3.3.1.1} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r] & j_* \mathbb{G}_{m,\eta} \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{div}} \ar[r] & \displaystyle\bigoplus_{x\in X} i_{x*} \mathbb{Z}_x \ar[r] & 0. } \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.3.2

One has \(\mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{G}_{m,\eta} = 0\) for every \(q>0\).

It suffices to show that the stalk of this sheaf at every closed point \(x\) of \(X\) is zero. If \(\widetilde{\mathscr{O}}_{X,x}\) is the henselization of \(X\) at \(x\) and \(K\) the field of fractions of \(\widetilde{\mathscr{O}}_{X,x}\), one has
\[ \operatorname{Spec}(K) = \eta\times_X \operatorname{Spec}(\widetilde{\mathscr{O}}_{X,x})\text{,} \]
hence \((\mathsf{R}^qj_*\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta})_x = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\operatorname{Spec}(K),\mathbb{G}_m)\).
Now \(K\) is an algebraic extension of \(k(X)\), hence an extension of transcendence degree \(1\) of \(k\): the lemma results from (3.2.4).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.3.3

One has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X, j_*\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}) = 0\) for every \(q>0\).
Indeed, from (3.3.2) and the Leray spectral sequence for \(j\), one deduces:
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X, j_* \mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\eta,\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}) \]
for every \(q\geqslant 0\), and the right-hand side is zero for \(q>0\) by (3.2.4).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.3.4

One has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q\left(X,\bigoplus_{x\in X} i_{x*} \mathbb{Z}_x\right) = 0\) for every \(q>0\).
Indeed, for every closed point of \(X\), one has \(\mathsf{R}^q i_{x*}\mathbb{Z}_x 0\) for \(q>0\), since \(i_x\) is a finite morphism (2.3.6), and
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,i_{x*}\mathbb{Z}_x) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(x,\mathbb{Z}_x)\text{.} \]
The right-hand side is zero for every \(q>0\), since \(x\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field (One sees that the lemma is true more generally for every “skyscraper” sheaf on \(X\)).
From the preceding lemmas and the exact sequence (3.3.1.1) one deduces the equalities:
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{G}_m) = 0 \text{ for } q\geqslant 2 \text{,} \]
and an exact cohomology sequence in low degree:

\[ 1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathbb{G}_m) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X, j_*\mathbb{G}_{m,\eta}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\left(X,\bigoplus_{x\in X} i_{x*}\mathbb{Z}_x\right) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{G}_m) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 1 \]
which is none other than the exact sequence:

\[ 1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k(X)^\times\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Div}(X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}(X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 1\text{.} \]
From proposition 3.3.1 one deduces that the cohomology groups of \(X\) with values in \(\mathbb{Z}/n\), \(n\) prime to the characteristic of \(k\), have a reasonable value:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3.5

If \(X\) is of genus \(g\) and if \(n\) is invertible in \(k\), the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) are zero for \(q>2\), and free over \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) of rank \(1,2 g,1\) for \(q=0,1,2\). Replacing \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) by the isomorphic group \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\), one has canonical isomorphisms

\begin{align*} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) &= \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) &= \operatorname{Pic}^0(X)_n \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) &= \mathbb{Z}/n \text{.} \end{align*}
Since the field \(k\) is algebraically closed, \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) is isomorphic (not canonically) to \(\mu_n\). From the Kummer exact sequence:

\[ 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mu_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\text{,} \]
and from proposition 3.3.1, one deduces the equalities:
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0 \text{ for } q>2 \text{,} \]
and, in low degree, exact sequences:
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r] & k^\times \ar[r]^-n & k^\times \ar[r] & 0 } \]
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}(X) \ar[r]^-n & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r] & 0. } \]
Moreover, one has an exact sequence:
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}^0(X) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}(X) \ar[r]^-{\deg} & \mathbb{Z} \ar[r] & 0 , } \]

and \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\) is identified with the group of rational points over \(k\) of an abelian variety of dimension \(g\), the Jacobian of \(X\). In such a group, multiplication by \(n\) is surjective and its kernel is a free \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-module of rank \(2 g\) (since \(n\) is invertible in \(k\)); whence the corollary.
A clever dévissage, using the “trace method,” allows one to obtain as a corollary the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3.6 ([2])

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, \(X\) an algebraic curve over \(k\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then:

  1. One has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for \(q>2\).

  2. If \(X\) is affine, one even has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for \(q>1\).
For the proof, as well as for the exposition of the “trace method,” we refer to [2].
3.4 Dévissages

To compute the cohomology of varieties of dimension \(>1\), one uses fibrations by curves, which allows one to reduce to studying the morphisms whose fibres are of dimension \(\leqslant 1\). This principle has several variants; let us indicate a few of them.

Let \(A\) be a \(k\)-algebra of finite type and \(a_1,\dotsc,a_n\) generators of \(A\). If one sets \(X_0=\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(X_i=\operatorname{Spec}(k[a_1,\dotsc,a_i])\), \(X_n=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\), the canonical inclusions \(k[a_1,\dotsc,a_i]\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k[a_1,\dotsc,a_i,a_{i+1}]\) define morphisms \(X_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_{n-1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_0\) whose fibres are of dimension \(\leqslant 1\).

In the case of a smooth morphism, one can be more precise. We call an elementary fibration a morphism of schemes \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) that can be embedded in a commutative diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-j \ar[dr]_-f & \overline{X} \ar[d]^-{\overline{f}} & Y \ar@{_{(}->}[l]_-i \ar[dl]^-g\\ & S } \]
satisfying the following conditions:

1. \(j\) is an open immersion dense in each fibre and \(X=\overline{X} \setminus Y\).

  2. \(\overline{f}\) is smooth and projective, with irreducible geometric fibres of dimension \(1\).

  3. \(g\) is an étale covering and no fibre of \(g\) is empty.

A \(S\)-scheme \(X\) is called a good neighbourhood relative to \(S\) if there exist \(S\)-schemes \(X=X_n,\dotsc,X_0=S\) and elementary fibrations \(f_i:X_i\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_{i-1}\), \(i=1,\dotsc,n\). One can show [2] that if \(X\) is a smooth scheme over an algebraically closed field \(k\) every rational point of \(X\) has an open neighbourhood which is a good neighbourhood (relative to \(\operatorname{Spec}(K)\)).
One can carry out a dévissage of a proper morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) as follows. By Chow's lemma, there exists a commutative diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[dr]_-f & \overline{X} \ar[l]_-\pi \ar[d]^-{\overline{f}}\\ & S } \]

where \(\pi\) and \(\overline{f}\) are projective morphisms, \(\pi\) being moreover an isomorphism above a dense open subset of \(X\). Locally on \(S\), \(\overline{X}\) is a closed subscheme of a standard projective space \(\mathbb{P}_S^n\).

One carries out a dévissage of the latter by considering the projection \(\varphi:\mathbb{P}_S^n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{P}_S^1\) which sends the point with homogeneous coordinates \((x_0,x_1,\dotsc,x_n)\) to \((x_0,x_1)\). This is a rational map defined outside the closed subset \(Y\simeq \mathbb{P}_S^{n-2}\) of \(\mathbb{P}_S^n\) with homogeneous equations \(x_0=x_1=0\). Let \(u:P\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{P}_S^n\) be the blow-up with centre \(Y\); the fibres of \(u\) are of dimension \(\leqslant 1\). Moreover there exists a natural morphism \(v:P\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{P}_S^1\) which extends the rational map \(\varphi\) and \(v\) makes \(P\) into a \(\mathbb{P}_S^1\)-scheme locally isomorphic to the standard projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{n-1}\) which can in turn be projected onto a \(\mathbb{P}^1\), etc.

One can sweep out a smooth projective variety \(X\) by a Lefschetz pencil. The blow-up \(\widetilde X\) of the intersection of the axis of the pencil with \(X\) projects onto \(\mathbb{P}^1\) and the fibres of this projection are the hyperplane sections of \(X\) by the hyperplanes of the pencil.

pages.title: Base change theorem for a proper morphism
pages.html:
4 Base change theorem for a proper morphism

4.1 Introduction

This chapter is devoted to the proof and applications of the

Theorem 4.1.1

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper morphism of schemes and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion abelian sheaf on \(X\). Then, for every \(q\geqslant 0\), the stalk of \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\) at a geometric point \(s\) of \(S\) is isomorphic to the cohomology \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,\mathscr{F})\) of the fibre \(X_s=X\otimes_S \operatorname{Spec} k(s)\) of \(f\) at \(s\).

For \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a proper separated continuous map (separated means that the diagonal of \(X\times_S X\) is closed) between topological spaces, and \(\mathscr{F}\) an abelian sheaf on \(X\), the analogous result is well known and elementary: since \(f\) is closed, the \(f^{-1}(V)\) for \(V\) a neighbourhood of \(s\) form a fundamental system of neighbourhoods of \(X_s\), and one checks that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathscr{F}) = \varinjlim_U \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(U,\mathscr{F})\), for \(U\) running through the neighbourhoods of \(X_s\). In practice, \(X_s\) even has a fundamental system \(\mathscr{U}\) of neighbourhoods \(U\) of which it is a deformation retract and, for \(\mathscr{F}\) constant, one thus has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathscr{F})=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(U,\mathscr{F})\). In pictorial terms: the special fibre swallows the general fibre.

In the case of schemes the proof is more delicate and it is indispensable to assume that \(\mathscr{F}\) is torsion ([2]). Taking into account the description of the stalks of \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\) (2.3.3), the theorem (4.1.1) is essentially equivalent to

Theorem 4.1.2

Let \(A\) be a strictly henselian local ring and \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper morphism and \(X_0\) the closed fibre of \(f\). Then, for every torsion abelian sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) and every \(q\geqslant 0\), one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{F}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,\mathscr{F})\).

By passage to the limit one sees that it suffices to prove the theorem when \(A\) is the strict henselization of a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra of finite type at a prime ideal. One first treats the case \(q=0\) or \(1\) and \(\mathscr{F}=\mathbb{Z}/n\) (4.2). An argument based on the notion of constructible sheaf (4.3) shows moreover that it suffices to consider the case where \(\mathscr{F}\) is constant. On the other hand the dévissage (3.4.3) allows one to assume that \(X_0\) is a curve; in this case it only remains to prove the theorem for \(q=2\) (4.4).

Among other applications (4.6), the theorem allows one to define the notion of cohomology with proper support (4.5).

4.2 Proof for \(q=0\) or \(1\) and \(\mathscr{F}=\mathbb{Z}/n\)

The result for \(q=0\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) constant is equivalent to the following proposition (Zariski's connectedness theorem):

Proposition 4.2.1

Let \(A\) be a noetherian henselian local ring and \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper morphism and \(X_0\) the closed fibre of \(f\). Then the sets of connected components \(\pi_0(X)\) and \(\pi_0(X_0)\) are in bijection.

It amounts to the same to show that the sets of subsets that are at once open and closed \(\operatorname{Of}(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Of}(X_0)\) are in bijection. It is known that the set \(\operatorname{Of}(X)\) corresponds bijectively to the set of idempotents of \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)\), likewise \(\operatorname{Of}(X_0)\) corresponds bijectively to the set of idempotents of \(\Gamma(X_0,\mathscr{O}_{X_0})\). It is therefore a matter of showing that the canonical map

\[ \operatorname{Idem} \Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Idem}\Gamma(X_0,\mathscr{O}_{X_0}) \]

is bijective.

We denote by \(\mathfrak{m}\) the maximal ideal of \(A\), by \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)^\wedge\) the completion of \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)\) for the \(\mathfrak{m}\)-adic topology and, for every integer \(n\geqslant 0\), \(X_n=X\otimes_A A/\mathfrak{m}^{n+1}\). By the finiteness theorem for proper morphisms [20], \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)\) is a finite \(A\)-algebra; since \(A\) is henselian, it follows that the canonical map

\[ \operatorname{Idem} \Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Idem}\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)^\wedge \]

is bijective. In particular the canonical map

\[ \operatorname{Idem} \Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)^\wedge \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \varprojlim \operatorname{Idem}\Gamma(X_n,\mathscr{O}_{X_n}) \]

is bijective. But, since \(X_n\) and \(X_0\) have the same underlying topological space, the canonical map

\[ \operatorname{Idem}\Gamma(X_n,\mathscr{O}_{X_n}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Idem} \Gamma(X_0,\mathscr{O}_{X_0}) \]

is bijective for every \(n\), which completes the proof.

Since \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) is in bijection with the set of isomorphism classes of Galois étale coverings of \(X\) with group \(\mathbb{Z}/n\), the theorem for \(q=1\) and \(\mathscr{F}=\mathbb{Z}/n\) follows from the following proposition.

Proposition 4.2.2

Let \(A\) be a noetherian henselian local ring and \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper morphism and \(X_0\) the closed fibre of \(f\). Then the restriction functor

\[ \operatorname{Rev.et}(X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Rev.et}(X_0) \]

is an equivalence of categories.

(If \(X_0\) is connected and if a geometric point of \(X_0\) has been chosen as base point, this amounts to saying that the canonical map \(\pi_1(X_0)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \pi_1(X)\) on the (profinite) fundamental groups is bijective).

Proposition (4.2.1) shows that this functor is fully faithful. Indeed, if \(X'\) and \(X''\) are two étale coverings of \(X\), a \(X\)-morphism from \(X'\) to \(X''\) is determined by its graph, which is an open and closed subset of \(X'\times_X X''\).

It is therefore a matter of showing that every étale covering \(X_0'\) of \(X_0\) extends to an étale covering of \(X\). It is known that étale coverings do not depend on the nilpotent elements [23], consequently \(X_0'\) lifts uniquely to an étale covering \(X_n'\) of \(X_n\) for every \(n\geqslant 0\), in other words to an étale covering \(\mathfrak{X}'\) of the formal scheme \(\mathfrak{X}\), the completion of \(X\) along \(X_0\). By Grothendieck's algebraization theorem for formal coherent sheaves (existence theorem, [20]), \(\mathfrak{X}'\) is the formal completion of an étale covering \(\overline{X}'\), of \(\overline{X}=X\otimes_A \widehat{A}\).

By passage to the limit, it suffices to prove the proposition in the case where \(A\) is the henselization of a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra of finite type. One can then apply Artin's approximation theorem to the functor \(\mathscr{F}:(A \textnormal{-algebras}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} (\textnormal{sets})\) which, to a \(A\)-algebra \(B\), associates the set of isomorphism classes of étale coverings of \(X\otimes_A B\). Indeed this functor is locally of finite presentation: if \(B_i\) is a filtered inductive system of \(A\)-algebras and if \(B=\varinjlim B_i\), one has \(\mathscr{F}(B) = \varinjlim \mathscr{F}(B_i)\). By Artin's theorem, given an element \(\xi\in \mathscr{F}(\widehat{A})\), in this case the isomorphism class of \(\overline{X}'\), there exists \(\xi\in \mathscr{F}(A)\) having the same image as \(\overline{\xi}\) in \(\mathscr{F}(A/\mathfrak{m})\). In other words there exists an étale covering \(X'\) of \(X\) whose restriction to \(X_0\) is isomorphic to \(X_0'\).

4.3 Constructible sheaves

In this section, we consider a noetherian scheme \(X\) and by a sheaf on \(X\) we mean an abelian sheaf on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\).

Definition 4.3.1

A sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) is said to be locally constant constructible (abbreviated l.c.c.) if it is represented by an étale covering of \(X\).

Definition 4.3.2

A sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) is said to be constructible if it satisfies the following equivalent conditions:

  1. There exists a finite surjective family of subschemes \(X_i\) of \(X\) such that the restriction of \(\mathscr{F}\) to \(X_i\) is l.c.c..

  2. There exists a finite family of finite morphisms \(p_i:X_i'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), for each \(i\) a constant constructible sheaf ( = defined by a finite abelian group) \(C_i\) on \(X_i'\), and a monomorphism \(\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \prod p_{i*} C_i\).

One checks easily that the category of constructible sheaves on \(X\) is an abelian category. Moreover, if \(u:\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{G}\) is a homomorphism of sheaves and if \(\mathscr{F}\) is constructible, the sheaf \(\operatorname{im}(u)\) is constructible.

Lemma 4.3.3

Every torsion sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) is a filtered inductive limit of constructible sheaves.

Indeed, if \(j:U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is an étale scheme of finite type over \(X\), an element \(\xi\in \mathscr{F}(U)\) such that \(n\xi=0\) defines a homomorphism of sheaves \(j_! \underline{\mathbb{Z}/n}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}\) whose image (the smallest subsheaf of \(\mathscr{F}\) of which \(\xi\) is a local section) is a constructible subsheaf of \(\mathscr{F}\). It is clear that \(\mathscr{F}\) is an inductive limit of such subsheaves.

Definition 4.3.4

Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be an abelian category and \(T\) a functor defined on \(\mathscr{C}\) with values in the category of abelian groups. We say that \(T\) is effaceable in \(\mathscr{C}\) if, for every object \(A\) of \(\mathscr{C}\) and every \(\alpha\in T(A)\), there exists a monomorphism \(u:A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\) in \(\mathscr{C}\) such that \(T(u)\alpha = 0\).

Lemma 4.3.5

The functors \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,-)\) for \(q>0\) are effaceable in the category of constructible sheaves on \(X\).

It suffices to remark that, if \(\mathscr{F}\) is a constructible sheaf, there necessarily exists an integer \(n>0\) such that \(\mathscr{F}\) is a sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules. Then there exists a monomorphism \(\mathscr{F}\hookrightarrow \mathscr{G}\), where \(\mathscr{G}\) is a sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{G}) = 0\) for every \(q>0\). One can for example take for \(\mathscr{G}\) the Godement resolution \(\prod_{x\in X} i_{x*} \mathscr{F}_{\overline{x}}\), where \(x\) runs through the points of \(X\) and \(i_x:\overline{x}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is a geometric point centred at \(X\). By (4.3.3) \(\mathscr{G}\) is an inductive limit of constructible sheaves, whence the lemma, since the functors \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,-)\) commute with inductive limits.

Lemma 4.3.6

Let \(\varphi^\bullet:T^\bullet\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} {T'}^\bullet\) be a morphism of cohomological functors defined on an abelian category \(\mathscr{C}\) and with values in the category of abelian groups. Suppose that \(T^q\) is effaceable for \(q>0\) and let \(\mathscr{E}\) be a subset of objects of \(\mathscr{C}\) such that every object of \(\mathscr{C}\) is contained in an object belonging to \(\mathscr{E}\). Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. \(\varphi^q(A)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\) and every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob} \mathscr{C}\).

  2. \(\varphi^0(M)\) is bijective and \(\varphi^q(M)\) surjective for every \(q>0\) and every \(M\in\mathscr{E}\).

  3. \(\varphi^0(A)\) is bijective for every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob} \mathscr{C}\) and \({T'}^q\) is effaceable for every \(q>0\).

The proof is by induction on \(q\) and presents no difficulties.

Proposition 4.3.7

Let \(X_0\) be a subscheme of \(X\). Suppose that, for every \(n\geqslant 0\) and for every scheme \(X'\) finite over \(X\), the canonical map

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X',\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0',\mathbb{Z}/n)\text{,} \]

where \(X_0' = X'\times_X X_0\), is bijective for \(q=0\) and surjective for \(q>0\). Then, for every torsion sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) and for every \(q\geqslant 0\), the canonical map

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,\mathscr{F}) \]

is bijective.

By passage to the limit, it suffices to prove the assertion for \(\mathscr{F}\) constructible. One applies lemma (4.3.6) taking for \(\mathscr{C}\) the category of constructible sheaves on \(X\), \(T^q=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,-)\), \({T'}^q=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,-)\), and \(\mathscr{E}\) the set of constructible sheaves of the form \(\prod p_{i*} C_i\), where \(p_i:X_i'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is a finite morphism and \(C_i\) a finite constant sheaf on \(X_i'\).

4.4 End of the proof

By the method of fibration by curves (3.4.3), one reduces to proving the theorem in relative dimension \(\leqslant 1\). By the previous section, it will suffice to show that, if \(S\) is the spectrum of a strictly henselian noetherian local ring, \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a proper morphism whose closed fibre \(X_0\) is of dimension \(\leqslant 1\) and \(n\) an integer \(\geqslant 0\), the canonical homomorphism

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,\mathbb{Z}/n) \]

is bijective for \(q=0\) and surjective for \(q>0\).

The cases \(q=0\) and \(1\) have been seen above and one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q\geqslant 3\); it therefore suffices to treat the case \(q=2\). One can evidently assume that \(n\) is a power of a prime number. If \(n=p^r\), where \(p\) is the characteristic of the residue field of \(S\), the Artin-Schreier theory shows that one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X_0,\mathbb{Z}/p^r) = 0\). If \(n=\ell^r\), \(\ell\ne p\), one deduces from Kummer theory a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ \operatorname{Pic}(X) \ar[d] \ar[r]^-\alpha & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X,\mathbb{Z}/\ell^r) \ar[d] \\ \operatorname{Pic}(X_0) \ar[r]^-\beta & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X_0,\mathbb{Z}/\ell^r) } \]

where the map \(\beta\) is surjective (This was seen in chapter 3 for a smooth curve over an algebraically closed field, but similar arguments apply to any curve over a separably closed field).

To conclude, it will therefore suffice to show:

Proposition 4.4.1

Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a noetherian henselian local ring and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a proper morphism whose closed fibre \(X_0\) is of dimension \(\leqslant 1\). Then the canonical restriction map

\[ \operatorname{Pic}(X)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}(X_0) \]

is surjective (It suffices moreover that the morphism \(f\) be separated of finite type).

To simplify the proof, we shall assume that \(X\) is integral, although this is not necessary. Every invertible sheaf on \(X_0\) is associated to a Cartier divisor (since \(X_0\) is a curve, hence quasi-projective), it therefore suffices to show that the canonical map \(\operatorname{Div}(X)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\operatorname{Div}(X_0)\) is surjective.

Every divisor on \(X_0\) is a linear combination of divisors whose support is concentrated at a single non-isolated closed point of \(X_0\). Let \(x\) be such a point, \(t_0\in\mathscr{O}_{X_0,x}\) a regular non-invertible element of \(\mathscr{O}_{X_0,x}\) and \(D_0\) the divisor concentrated at \(x\) with local equation \(t_0\). Let \(U\) be an open neighbourhood of \(x\) in \(X\) such that there exists a section \(t\in \Gamma(U,\mathscr{O}_U)\) lifting \(t_0\). Let \(Y\) be the closed subset of \(U\) with equation \(t=0\); by taking \(U\) small enough, one may assume that \(x\) is the only point of \(Y\cap X_0\). Then \(Y\) is quasi-finite over \(S\) at \(x\); since \(S\) is the spectrum of a henselian local ring, one deduces that \(Y=Y_1\amalg Y_2\), where \(Y_1\) is finite over \(S\) and where \(Y_2\) does not meet \(X_0\). Moreover, since \(X\) is separated over \(S\), \(Y_1\) is closed in \(X\).

By replacing \(U\) with a smaller open neighbourhood of \(x\), one may assume that \(Y=Y_1\), in other words that \(Y\) is closed in \(X\). One then defines a divisor \(D\) on \(X\) lifting \(D_0\) by setting \(D|X\setminus Y=0\) and \(D|U=\operatorname{div}(t)\), which makes sense since \(t\) is invertible on \(U\setminus Y\).

4.4.2 Remark

In the case where \(f\) is proper, one could also give a proof of the same style as that of proposition (4.2.2). Indeed, since \(X_0\) is a curve, there is no obstruction to lifting an invertible sheaf on \(X_0\) to the infinitesimal neighbourhoods \(X_n\) of \(X_0\), hence to the formal completion \(\mathfrak{X}\) of \(X\) along \(X_0\). One then concludes by applying successively Grothendieck's existence theorem and Artin's approximation theorem.

4.5 Cohomology with proper support

Definition 4.5.1

Let \(X\) be a separated scheme of finite type over a field \(k\). By a theorem of Nagata, there exists a scheme \(\overline{X}\) proper over \(k\) and an open immersion \(j:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\overline{X}\). For every torsion sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) one denotes by \(j_! \mathscr{F}\) the extension by \(0\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) to \(\overline{X}\) and one defines the groups of cohomology with proper support

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X,\mathscr{F})=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\overline{X}, j_! \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

Let us show that this definition is independent of the compactification \(j:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\overline{X}\) chosen. Let \(j_1:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{X}_1\) and \(j_2:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{X}_2\) be two compactifications. Then \(X\) maps into \(\overline{X}_1\times \overline{X}_2\) by \(x\mapsto (j_1(x),j_2(x))\) and the closed image \(\overline{X}_3\) of \(X\) under this map is a compactification of \(X\). We thus have a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ & \overline{X}_1 \\ X \ar[ur]^-{j_1} \ar[rr]^-{(j_1,j_2)} \ar[dr]_-{j_2} & & \overline{X}_3 \ar[ul]_-{p_1} \ar[dl]^-{p_2} \\ & \overline{X}_2 } \]

where \(p_1\) and \(p_2\), the restrictions of the natural projections to \(\overline{X}_3\), are proper morphisms. It therefore suffices to treat the case where one has a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[r]^-{j_2} \ar[dr]_-{j_1} & \overline{X}_2 \ar[d]^-p \\ & \overline{X}_1 } \]

with \(p\) a proper morphism.

Lemma 4.5.2

One has \(p_*(j_{2!} \mathscr{F}) = j_{1!} \mathscr{F}\) and \(\mathsf{R}^q p_*(j_{2!} \mathscr{F}) = 0\), for \(q>0\).

Let us note right away that the lemma suffices to conclude. Using the Leray spectral sequence of the morphism \(p\), one deduces that one has, for every \(q\geqslant 0\),

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\overline{X}_2, j_{2!} \mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\overline{X}_1, j_{1!} \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

To prove the lemma, one argues fibre by fibre using the base change theorem (4.1.1) for \(p\). The result is immediate, since, above a point of \(X\), \(p\) is an isomorphism and, above a point of \(\overline{X}_1\setminus X\), \(j_{2!} \mathscr{F}\) is zero on the fibre of \(p\).

4.5.3

Likewise, if \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is a separated morphism of finite type of schemes noetherian, there exists a proper morphism \(\overline{f}:\overline{X}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and an open immersion \(j:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{X}\). One then defines the higher direct images with proper support \(\mathsf{R}^q f_!\) by setting for every torsion sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\)

\[ \mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F} = \mathsf{R}^q f_*(j_! \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

One checks as before that this definition is independent of the compactification chosen.

Theorem 4.5.4

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a separated morphism of finite type of noetherian schemes and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then the stalk of \(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}\) at a geometric point \(s\) of \(S\) is isomorphic to the cohomology with proper support \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X_s,\mathscr{F})\) of the fibre \(X_s\) of \(f\) at \(s\).

This is a simple variant of the base change theorem for a proper morphism (4.1.1). More generally, if

\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]^-f & X' \ar[l]_-{g'} \ar[d]^-{f'} \\ S & S' \ar[l]^-g } \]

is a cartesian diagram, one has a canonical isomorphism

\[ \tag{4.5.4.1} g^* (\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}) \simeq \mathsf{R}^q f_!'({g'}^* \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

4.6 Applications

Theorem 4.6.1 (vanishing)

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a separated morphism of finite type whose fibres are of dimension \(\leqslant n\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then one has \(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F} = 0\) for \(q>2 n\).

By the base change theorem, one may assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of a separably closed field. If \(\dim X = n\), there exists an affine open \(U\) of \(X\) such that \(\dim(X\setminus U) < n\); one then has an exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}_U \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}_{X\setminus U} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) and, by induction on \(n\), it suffices to prove the theorem for \(X=U\) affine. Then the method of fibration by curves (3.4.1) and the base change theorem allow one to reduce to a curve over a separably closed field for which one deduces the desired result from Tsen's theorem (3.3.6).

Theorem 4.6.2 (finiteness)

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a separated morphism of finite type and \(\mathscr{F}\) a sheaf constructible on \(X\). Then the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}\) are constructible.

We consider only the case where \(\mathscr{F}\) is annihilated by an integer invertible on \(X\).

To prove the theorem one reduces to the case where \(\mathscr{F}\) is a constant sheaf \(\underline{\mathbb{Z}/n}\) and where \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is a proper and smooth morphism whose fibres are geometrically connected curves of genus \(g\). For \(n\) invertible on \(X\), the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\) are then locally free of finite rank, zero for \(q>2\) (4.6.1). Replacing \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) by the sheaf locally isomorphic (over \(S\)) \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\), one has canonically

\[ \tag{4.6.2.1} \begin{aligned} \mathsf{R}^0 f_* \boldsymbol{\mu}_n &= \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \\ \mathsf{R}^1 f_* \boldsymbol{\mu}_n &= \underline{\operatorname{Pic}}(X/S)_n \\ \mathsf{R}^2 f_* \boldsymbol{\mu}_n &= \mathbb{Z}/n \text{.} \end{aligned} \]
Theorem 4.6.3 (comparison with classical cohomology)

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a separated morphism of schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\), and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). We denote by a superscript \({(-)}^{\mathrm{an}}\) the functor of passage to the usual topological spaces, and by \(\mathsf{R}^q {f}^{\mathrm{an}}_!\) the derived functors of the direct image functor with proper support by \({f}^{\mathrm{an}}\). One has

\[ {(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F})}^{\mathrm{an}} \simeq \mathsf{R}^q {f}^{\mathrm{an}}_! {\mathscr{F}}^{\mathrm{an}} \text{.} \]

In particular, for \(S=\) a point and \(\mathscr{F}\) the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/n\),

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q({X}^{\mathrm{an}},\mathbb{Z}/n)\text{.} \]

Dévissages using the base change theorem reduce us to the case where \(X\) is a proper and smooth curve, where \(S=\) a point, and where \(\mathscr{F}=\mathbb{Z}/n\). The cohomology groups considered are then zero for \(q\ne 0,1,2\), and one invokes [32]: indeed, if \(X\) is proper over \(\mathbb{C}\), one has \(\pi_0(X) = \pi_0({X}^{\mathrm{an}})\) and \(\pi_1(X) = \) the profinite completion of \(\pi_1({X}^{\mathrm{an}})\), whence the assertion for \(q=0,1\). For \(q=2\), one uses the Kummer exact sequence and the fact that, by [32] again, \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\operatorname{Pic}({X}^{\mathrm{an}})\).

Theorem 4.6.4 (cohomological dimension of affine schemes)

Let \(X\) be an affine scheme of finite type over a separably closed field and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for \(q>\dim(X)\).

For the very pretty proof we refer to [2], XIV §2 and 3.

4.6.5 Remark

This theorem is in some sense a substitute for Morse theory. Consider indeed the classical case where \(X\) is smooth and affine over \(\mathbb{C}\), embedded in a standard affine space \(\mathbb{C}^N\). Then, for almost every point \(p\in\mathbb{C}^N\), the function “distance to \(p\)” on \(X\) is a Morse function and the indices of its critical points are smaller than \(\dim(X)\). Thus \(X\) is obtained by gluing handles of index smaller than \(\dim(X)\), whence the classical analogue of (4.6.4).

blocks.html: 4 Base change theorem for a proper morphism
4.1 Introduction
This chapter is devoted to the proof and applications of the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1.1

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper morphism of schemes and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion abelian sheaf on \(X\). Then, for every \(q\geqslant 0\), the stalk of \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\) at a geometric point \(s\) of \(S\) is isomorphic to the cohomology \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,\mathscr{F})\) of the fibre \(X_s=X\otimes_S \operatorname{Spec} k(s)\) of \(f\) at \(s\).

For \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a proper separated continuous map (separated means that the diagonal of \(X\times_S X\) is closed) between topological spaces, and \(\mathscr{F}\) an abelian sheaf on \(X\), the analogous result is well known and elementary: since \(f\) is closed, the \(f^{-1}(V)\) for \(V\) a neighbourhood of \(s\) form a fundamental system of neighbourhoods of \(X_s\), and one checks that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathscr{F}) = \varinjlim_U \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(U,\mathscr{F})\), for \(U\) running through the neighbourhoods of \(X_s\). In practice, \(X_s\) even has a fundamental system \(\mathscr{U}\) of neighbourhoods \(U\) of which it is a deformation retract and, for \(\mathscr{F}\) constant, one thus has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathscr{F})=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(U,\mathscr{F})\). In pictorial terms: the special fibre swallows the general fibre.

In the case of schemes the proof is more delicate and it is indispensable to assume that \(\mathscr{F}\) is torsion ([2]). Taking into account the description of the stalks of \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\) (2.3.3), the theorem (4.1.1) is essentially equivalent to

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1.2

Let \(A\) be a strictly henselian local ring and \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper morphism and \(X_0\) the closed fibre of \(f\). Then, for every torsion abelian sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) and every \(q\geqslant 0\), one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{F}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,\mathscr{F})\).

By passage to the limit one sees that it suffices to prove the theorem when \(A\) is the strict henselization of a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra of finite type at a prime ideal. One first treats the case \(q=0\) or \(1\) and \(\mathscr{F}=\mathbb{Z}/n\) (4.2). An argument based on the notion of constructible sheaf (4.3) shows moreover that it suffices to consider the case where \(\mathscr{F}\) is constant. On the other hand the dévissage (3.4.3) allows one to assume that \(X_0\) is a curve; in this case it only remains to prove the theorem for \(q=2\) (4.4).
Among other applications (4.6), the theorem allows one to define the notion of cohomology with proper support (4.5).
4.2 Proof for \(q=0\) or \(1\) and \(\mathscr{F}=\mathbb{Z}/n\)
The result for \(q=0\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) constant is equivalent to the following proposition (Zariski's connectedness theorem):

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.1

Let \(A\) be a noetherian henselian local ring and \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper morphism and \(X_0\) the closed fibre of \(f\).
