Then the sets of connected components \(\pi_0(X)\) and \(\pi_0(X_0)\) are in bijection.

It amounts to the same to show that the sets of subsets that are at once open and closed \(\operatorname{Of}(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Of}(X_0)\) are in bijection. It is known that the set \(\operatorname{Of}(X)\) corresponds bijectively to the set of idempotents of \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)\), likewise \(\operatorname{Of}(X_0)\) corresponds bijectively to the set of idempotents of \(\Gamma(X_0,\mathscr{O}_{X_0})\). It is therefore a matter of showing that the canonical map
\[ \operatorname{Idem} \Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Idem}\Gamma(X_0,\mathscr{O}_{X_0}) \]
is bijective.

We denote by \(\mathfrak{m}\) the maximal ideal of \(A\), by \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)^\wedge\) the completion of \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)\) for the \(\mathfrak{m}\)-adic topology and, for every integer \(n\geqslant 0\), \(X_n=X\otimes_A A/\mathfrak{m}^{n+1}\). By the finiteness theorem for proper morphisms [20], \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)\) is a finite \(A\)-algebra; since \(A\) is henselian, it follows that the canonical map
\[ \operatorname{Idem} \Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Idem}\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)^\wedge \]
is bijective. In particular the canonical map
\[ \operatorname{Idem} \Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_X)^\wedge \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \varprojlim \operatorname{Idem}\Gamma(X_n,\mathscr{O}_{X_n}) \]
is bijective. But, since \(X_n\) and \(X_0\) have the same underlying topological space, the canonical map
\[ \operatorname{Idem}\Gamma(X_n,\mathscr{O}_{X_n}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Idem} \Gamma(X_0,\mathscr{O}_{X_0}) \]
is bijective for every \(n\), which completes the proof.

Since \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) is in bijection with the set of isomorphism classes of Galois étale coverings of \(X\) with group \(\mathbb{Z}/n\), the theorem for \(q=1\) and \(\mathscr{F}=\mathbb{Z}/n\) follows from the following proposition.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.2

Let \(A\) be a noetherian henselian local ring and \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper morphism and \(X_0\) the closed fibre of \(f\). Then the restriction functor

\[ \operatorname{Rev.et}(X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Rev.et}(X_0) \]

is an equivalence of categories.

(If \(X_0\) is connected and if a geometric point of \(X_0\) has been chosen as base point, this amounts to saying that the canonical map \(\pi_1(X_0)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \pi_1(X)\) on the (profinite) fundamental groups is bijective).

Proposition (4.2.1) shows that this functor is fully faithful. Indeed, if \(X'\) and \(X''\) are two étale coverings of \(X\), a \(X\)-morphism from \(X'\) to \(X''\) is determined by its graph, which is an open and closed subset of \(X'\times_X X''\).

It is therefore a matter of showing that every étale covering \(X_0'\) of \(X_0\) extends to an étale covering of \(X\). It is known that étale coverings do not depend on the nilpotent elements [23], consequently \(X_0'\) lifts uniquely to an étale covering \(X_n'\) of \(X_n\) for every \(n\geqslant 0\), in other words to an étale covering \(\mathfrak{X}'\) of the formal scheme \(\mathfrak{X}\), the completion of \(X\) along \(X_0\). By Grothendieck's algebraization theorem for formal coherent sheaves (existence theorem, [20]), \(\mathfrak{X}'\) is the formal completion of an étale covering \(\overline{X}'\), of \(\overline{X}=X\otimes_A \widehat{A}\).

By passage to the limit, it suffices to prove the proposition in the case where \(A\) is the henselization of a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra of finite type. One can then apply Artin's approximation theorem to the functor \(\mathscr{F}:(A \textnormal{-algebras}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} (\textnormal{sets})\) which, to a \(A\)-algebra \(B\), associates the set of isomorphism classes of étale coverings of \(X\otimes_A B\). Indeed this functor is locally of finite presentation: if \(B_i\) is a filtered inductive system of \(A\)-algebras and if \(B=\varinjlim B_i\), one has \(\mathscr{F}(B) = \varinjlim \mathscr{F}(B_i)\). By Artin's theorem, given an element \(\xi\in \mathscr{F}(\widehat{A})\), in this case the isomorphism class of \(\overline{X}'\), there exists \(\xi\in \mathscr{F}(A)\) having the same image as \(\overline{\xi}\) in \(\mathscr{F}(A/\mathfrak{m})\). In other words there exists an étale covering \(X'\) of \(X\) whose restriction to \(X_0\) is isomorphic to \(X_0'\).
4.3 Constructible sheaves
In this section, we consider a noetherian scheme \(X\) and by a sheaf on \(X\) we mean an abelian sheaf on \({X}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.3.1

A sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) is said to be locally constant constructible (abbreviated l.c.c.) if it is represented by an étale covering of \(X\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.3.2

A sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) is said to be constructible if it satisfies the following equivalent conditions:

  1. There exists a finite surjective family of subschemes \(X_i\) of \(X\) such that the restriction of \(\mathscr{F}\) to \(X_i\) is l.c.c..

  2. There exists a finite family of finite morphisms \(p_i:X_i'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), for each \(i\) a constant constructible sheaf ( = defined by a finite abelian group) \(C_i\) on \(X_i'\), and a monomorphism \(\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \prod p_{i*} C_i\).

One checks easily that the category of constructible sheaves on \(X\) is an abelian category. Moreover, if \(u:\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{G}\) is a homomorphism of sheaves and if \(\mathscr{F}\) is constructible, the sheaf \(\operatorname{im}(u)\) is constructible.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.3.3

Every torsion sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) is a filtered inductive limit of constructible sheaves.

Indeed, if \(j:U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is an étale scheme of finite type over \(X\), an element \(\xi\in \mathscr{F}(U)\) such that \(n\xi=0\) defines a homomorphism of sheaves \(j_! \underline{\mathbb{Z}/n}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}\) whose image (the smallest subsheaf of \(\mathscr{F}\) of which \(\xi\) is a local section) is a constructible subsheaf of \(\mathscr{F}\). It is clear that \(\mathscr{F}\) is an inductive limit of such subsheaves.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.3.4

Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be an abelian category and \(T\) a functor defined on \(\mathscr{C}\) with values in the category of abelian groups. We say that \(T\) is effaceable in \(\mathscr{C}\) if, for every object \(A\) of \(\mathscr{C}\) and every \(\alpha\in T(A)\), there exists a monomorphism \(u:A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\) in \(\mathscr{C}\) such that \(T(u)\alpha = 0\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.3.5

The functors \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,-)\) for \(q>0\) are effaceable in the category of constructible sheaves on \(X\).

It suffices to remark that, if \(\mathscr{F}\) is a constructible sheaf, there necessarily exists an integer \(n>0\) such that \(\mathscr{F}\) is a sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules. Then there exists a monomorphism \(\mathscr{F}\hookrightarrow \mathscr{G}\), where \(\mathscr{G}\) is a sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{G}) = 0\) for every \(q>0\). One can for example take for \(\mathscr{G}\) the Godement resolution \(\prod_{x\in X} i_{x*} \mathscr{F}_{\overline{x}}\), where \(x\) runs through the points of \(X\) and \(i_x:\overline{x}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is a geometric point centred at \(X\). By (4.3.3) \(\mathscr{G}\) is an inductive limit of constructible sheaves, whence the lemma, since the functors \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,-)\) commute with inductive limits.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.3.6

Let \(\varphi^\bullet:T^\bullet\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} {T'}^\bullet\) be a morphism of cohomological functors defined on an abelian category \(\mathscr{C}\) and with values in the category of abelian groups. Suppose that \(T^q\) is effaceable for \(q>0\) and let \(\mathscr{E}\) be a subset of objects of \(\mathscr{C}\) such that every object of \(\mathscr{C}\) is contained in an object belonging to \(\mathscr{E}\). Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. \(\varphi^q(A)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\) and every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob} \mathscr{C}\).

  2. \(\varphi^0(M)\) is bijective and \(\varphi^q(M)\) surjective for every \(q>0\) and every \(M\in\mathscr{E}\).

  3. \(\varphi^0(A)\) is bijective for every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob} \mathscr{C}\) and \({T'}^q\) is effaceable for every \(q>0\).
The proof is by induction on \(q\) and presents no difficulties.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.3.7

Let \(X_0\) be a subscheme of \(X\). Suppose that, for every \(n\geqslant 0\) and for every scheme \(X'\) finite over \(X\), the canonical map

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X',\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0',\mathbb{Z}/n)\text{,} \]

where \(X_0' = X'\times_X X_0\), is bijective for \(q=0\) and surjective for \(q>0\). Then, for every torsion sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) and for every \(q\geqslant 0\), the canonical map

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,\mathscr{F}) \]

is bijective.

By passage to the limit, it suffices to prove the assertion for \(\mathscr{F}\) constructible. One applies lemma (4.3.6) taking for \(\mathscr{C}\) the category of constructible sheaves on \(X\), \(T^q=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,-)\), \({T'}^q=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,-)\), and \(\mathscr{E}\) the set of constructible sheaves of the form \(\prod p_{i*} C_i\), where \(p_i:X_i'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is a finite morphism and \(C_i\) a finite constant sheaf on \(X_i'\).
4.4 End of the proof

By the method of fibration by curves (3.4.3), one reduces to proving the theorem in relative dimension \(\leqslant 1\). By the previous section, it will suffice to show that, if \(S\) is the spectrum of a strictly henselian noetherian local ring, \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a proper morphism whose closed fibre \(X_0\) is of dimension \(\leqslant 1\) and \(n\) an integer \(\geqslant 0\), the canonical homomorphism
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,\mathbb{Z}/n) \]
is bijective for \(q=0\) and surjective for \(q>0\).

The cases \(q=0\) and \(1\) have been seen above and one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_0,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q\geqslant 3\); it therefore suffices to treat the case \(q=2\). One can evidently assume that \(n\) is a power of a prime number. If \(n=p^r\), where \(p\) is the characteristic of the residue field of \(S\), the Artin-Schreier theory shows that one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X_0,\mathbb{Z}/p^r) = 0\). If \(n=\ell^r\), \(\ell\ne p\), one deduces from Kummer theory a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ \operatorname{Pic}(X) \ar[d] \ar[r]^-\alpha & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X,\mathbb{Z}/\ell^r) \ar[d] \\ \operatorname{Pic}(X_0) \ar[r]^-\beta & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X_0,\mathbb{Z}/\ell^r) } \]
where the map \(\beta\) is surjective (This was seen in chapter 3 for a smooth curve over an algebraically closed field, but similar arguments apply to any curve over a separably closed field).
To conclude, it will therefore suffice to show:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.4.1

Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a noetherian henselian local ring and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a proper morphism whose closed fibre \(X_0\) is of dimension \(\leqslant 1\). Then the canonical restriction map

\[ \operatorname{Pic}(X)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}(X_0) \]

is surjective (It suffices moreover that the morphism \(f\) be separated of finite type).

To simplify the proof, we shall assume that \(X\) is integral, although this is not necessary. Every invertible sheaf on \(X_0\) is associated to a Cartier divisor (since \(X_0\) is a curve, hence quasi-projective), it therefore suffices to show that the canonical map \(\operatorname{Div}(X)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\operatorname{Div}(X_0)\) is surjective.

Every divisor on \(X_0\) is a linear combination of divisors whose support is concentrated at a single non-isolated closed point of \(X_0\). Let \(x\) be such a point, \(t_0\in\mathscr{O}_{X_0,x}\) a regular non-invertible element of \(\mathscr{O}_{X_0,x}\) and \(D_0\) the divisor concentrated at \(x\) with local equation \(t_0\). Let \(U\) be an open neighbourhood of \(x\) in \(X\) such that there exists a section \(t\in \Gamma(U,\mathscr{O}_U)\) lifting \(t_0\). Let \(Y\) be the closed subset of \(U\) with equation \(t=0\); by taking \(U\) small enough, one may assume that \(x\) is the only point of \(Y\cap X_0\). Then \(Y\) is quasi-finite over \(S\) at \(x\); since \(S\) is the spectrum of a henselian local ring, one deduces that \(Y=Y_1\amalg Y_2\), where \(Y_1\) is finite over \(S\) and where \(Y_2\) does not meet \(X_0\). Moreover, since \(X\) is separated over \(S\), \(Y_1\) is closed in \(X\).

By replacing \(U\) with a smaller open neighbourhood of \(x\), one may assume that \(Y=Y_1\), in other words that \(Y\) is closed in \(X\). One then defines a divisor \(D\) on \(X\) lifting \(D_0\) by setting \(D|X\setminus Y=0\) and \(D|U=\operatorname{div}(t)\), which makes sense since \(t\) is invertible on \(U\setminus Y\).

In the case where \(f\) is proper, one could also give a proof of the same style as that of proposition (4.2.2). Indeed, since \(X_0\) is a curve, there is no obstruction to lifting an invertible sheaf on \(X_0\) to the infinitesimal neighbourhoods \(X_n\) of \(X_0\), hence to the formal completion \(\mathfrak{X}\) of \(X\) along \(X_0\). One then concludes by applying successively Grothendieck's existence theorem and Artin's approximation theorem.
4.5 Cohomology with proper support

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.5.1

Let \(X\) be a separated scheme of finite type over a field \(k\). By a theorem of Nagata, there exists a scheme \(\overline{X}\) proper over \(k\) and an open immersion \(j:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\overline{X}\). For every torsion sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) one denotes by \(j_! \mathscr{F}\) the extension by \(0\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) to \(\overline{X}\) and one defines the groups of cohomology with proper support

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X,\mathscr{F})=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\overline{X}, j_! \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

Let us show that this definition is independent of the compactification \(j:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\overline{X}\) chosen. Let \(j_1:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{X}_1\) and \(j_2:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{X}_2\) be two compactifications. Then \(X\) maps into \(\overline{X}_1\times \overline{X}_2\) by \(x\mapsto (j_1(x),j_2(x))\) and the closed image \(\overline{X}_3\) of \(X\) under this map is a compactification of \(X\). We thus have a commutative diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ & \overline{X}_1 \\ X \ar[ur]^-{j_1} \ar[rr]^-{(j_1,j_2)} \ar[dr]_-{j_2} & & \overline{X}_3 \ar[ul]_-{p_1} \ar[dl]^-{p_2} \\ & \overline{X}_2 } \]
where \(p_1\) and \(p_2\), the restrictions of the natural projections to \(\overline{X}_3\), are proper morphisms. It therefore suffices to treat the case where one has a commutative diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[r]^-{j_2} \ar[dr]_-{j_1} & \overline{X}_2 \ar[d]^-p \\ & \overline{X}_1 } \]
with \(p\) a proper morphism.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.5.2

One has \(p_*(j_{2!} \mathscr{F}) = j_{1!} \mathscr{F}\) and \(\mathsf{R}^q p_*(j_{2!} \mathscr{F}) = 0\), for \(q>0\).
Let us note right away that the lemma suffices to conclude. Using the Leray spectral sequence of the morphism \(p\), one deduces that one has, for every \(q\geqslant 0\),
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\overline{X}_2, j_{2!} \mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\overline{X}_1, j_{1!} \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

To prove the lemma, one argues fibre by fibre using the base change theorem (4.1.1) for \(p\). The result is immediate, since, above a point of \(X\), \(p\) is an isomorphism and, above a point of \(\overline{X}_1\setminus X\), \(j_{2!} \mathscr{F}\) is zero on the fibre of \(p\).

Likewise, if \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is a separated morphism of finite type of schemes noetherian, there exists a proper morphism \(\overline{f}:\overline{X}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and an open immersion \(j:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{X}\). One then defines the higher direct images with proper support \(\mathsf{R}^q f_!\) by setting for every torsion sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\)
\[ \mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F} = \mathsf{R}^q f_*(j_! \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]
One checks as before that this definition is independent of the compactification chosen.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.5.4

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a separated morphism of finite type of noetherian schemes and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then the stalk of \(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}\) at a geometric point \(s\) of \(S\) is isomorphic to the cohomology with proper support \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X_s,\mathscr{F})\) of the fibre \(X_s\) of \(f\) at \(s\).
This is a simple variant of the base change theorem for a proper morphism (4.1.1). More generally, if
\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]^-f & X' \ar[l]_-{g'} \ar[d]^-{f'} \\ S & S' \ar[l]^-g } \]
is a cartesian diagram, one has a canonical isomorphism
\[ \tag{4.5.4.1} g^* (\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}) \simeq \mathsf{R}^q f_!'({g'}^* \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]
4.6 Applications

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.6.1 (vanishing)

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a separated morphism of finite type whose fibres are of dimension \(\leqslant n\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then one has \(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F} = 0\) for \(q>2 n\).

By the base change theorem, one may assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of a separably closed field. If \(\dim X = n\), there exists an affine open \(U\) of \(X\) such that \(\dim(X\setminus U) < n\); one then has an exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}_U \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}_{X\setminus U} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) and, by induction on \(n\), it suffices to prove the theorem for \(X=U\) affine. Then the method of fibration by curves (3.4.1) and the base change theorem allow one to reduce to a curve over a separably closed field for which one deduces the desired result from Tsen's theorem (3.3.6).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.6.2 (finiteness)

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a separated morphism of finite type and \(\mathscr{F}\) a sheaf constructible on \(X\). Then the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}\) are constructible.
We consider only the case where \(\mathscr{F}\) is annihilated by an integer invertible on \(X\).

To prove the theorem one reduces to the case where \(\mathscr{F}\) is a constant sheaf \(\underline{\mathbb{Z}/n}\) and where \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is a proper and smooth morphism whose fibres are geometrically connected curves of genus \(g\). For \(n\) invertible on \(X\), the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\) are then locally free of finite rank, zero for \(q>2\) (4.6.1). Replacing \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) by the sheaf locally isomorphic (over \(S\)) \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\), one has canonically

\[ \tag{4.6.2.1} \begin{aligned} \mathsf{R}^0 f_* \boldsymbol{\mu}_n &= \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \\ \mathsf{R}^1 f_* \boldsymbol{\mu}_n &= \underline{\operatorname{Pic}}(X/S)_n \\ \mathsf{R}^2 f_* \boldsymbol{\mu}_n &= \mathbb{Z}/n \text{.} \end{aligned} \]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.6.3 (comparison with classical cohomology)

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a separated morphism of schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\), and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). We denote by a superscript \({(-)}^{\mathrm{an}}\) the functor of passage to the usual topological spaces, and by \(\mathsf{R}^q {f}^{\mathrm{an}}_!\) the derived functors of the direct image functor with proper support by \({f}^{\mathrm{an}}\). One has

\[ {(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F})}^{\mathrm{an}} \simeq \mathsf{R}^q {f}^{\mathrm{an}}_! {\mathscr{F}}^{\mathrm{an}} \text{.} \]

In particular, for \(S=\) a point and \(\mathscr{F}\) the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/n\),

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q({X}^{\mathrm{an}},\mathbb{Z}/n)\text{.} \]

Dévissages using the base change theorem reduce us to the case where \(X\) is a proper and smooth curve, where \(S=\) a point, and where \(\mathscr{F}=\mathbb{Z}/n\). The cohomology groups considered are then zero for \(q\ne 0,1,2\), and one invokes [32]: indeed, if \(X\) is proper over \(\mathbb{C}\), one has \(\pi_0(X) = \pi_0({X}^{\mathrm{an}})\) and \(\pi_1(X) = \) the profinite completion of \(\pi_1({X}^{\mathrm{an}})\), whence the assertion for \(q=0,1\). For \(q=2\), one uses the Kummer exact sequence and the fact that, by [32] again, \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\operatorname{Pic}({X}^{\mathrm{an}})\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.6.4 (cohomological dimension of affine schemes)

Let \(X\) be an affine scheme of finite type over a separably closed field and \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion sheaf on \(X\). Then one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for \(q>\dim(X)\).
For the very pretty proof we refer to [2], XIV §2 and 3.

This theorem is in some sense a substitute for Morse theory. Consider indeed the classical case where \(X\) is smooth and affine over \(\mathbb{C}\), embedded in a standard affine space \(\mathbb{C}^N\). Then, for almost every point \(p\in\mathbb{C}^N\), the function “distance to \(p\)” on \(X\) is a Morse function and the indices of its critical points are smaller than \(\dim(X)\). Thus \(X\) is obtained by gluing handles of index smaller than \(\dim(X)\), whence the classical analogue of (4.6.4).

pages.title: Local acyclicity of smooth morphisms
pages.html:
5 Local acyclicity of smooth morphisms

Let \(X\) be a complex analytic variety and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} D\) a morphism of \(X\) into the disc. We denote by \([0,t]\) the closed line segment with endpoints \(0\) and \(t\) in \(D\) and by \((0,t]\) the half-open segment. If \(f\) is smooth, the inclusion

\[ j : f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right) \hookrightarrow f^{-1}\left([0,t]\right) \]

is a homotopy equivalence; one can push the special fibre \(X_0=f^{-1}(0)\) into \(f^{-1}([0,t])\).

In practice, for \(t\) small enough, \(f^{-1}((0,t])\) will be a fibre bundle over \((0,t]\) so that the inclusion

\[ X_t = f^{-1}(t) \hookrightarrow f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right) \]

will also be a homotopy equivalence. One then calls cospecialization morphism the homotopy class of maps:

\[ \operatorname{cosp} : X_0 \hookrightarrow f^{-1}\left([0,t]\right) \xleftarrow{\sim} f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right) \xleftarrow{\sim} X_t \text{.} \]

One can express this construction in pictorial terms by saying that, for a smooth morphism, the general fibre swallows the special fibre.

Let us no longer assume \(f\) necessarily smooth (but assume that \(f^{-1}((0,t])\) is a fibre bundle over \((0,t]\)). One can still define a morphism \(\operatorname{cosp}^\bullet\) in cohomology as soon as \(j_* \mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{Z} = 0\) for \(q>0\). Under these hypotheses, the Leray spectral sequence for \(j\) shows that one has

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(f^{-1}\left([0,t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \]

and \(\operatorname{cosp}^\bullet\) is the composite morphism:

\[ \operatorname{cosp}^\bullet : \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_t,\mathbb{Z}) \xleftarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \xleftarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(f^{-1}\left([0,t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_0,\mathbb{Z}) \]

The stalk of \(\mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{Z}\) at a point \(x\in X_0\) is computed as follows. In an ambient space one takes a ball \(B_\varepsilon\) with centre \(x\) and radius \(\varepsilon\) small enough, and for \(\eta\) small enough, one sets \(E=X\cap B_\varepsilon \cap f^{-1}(\eta t)\); this is the variety of vanishing cycles at \(x\). One has

\[ (\mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{Z})_x \xleftarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q\left(X\cap B_\varepsilon\cap f^{-1}\left((0,\eta t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(E,\mathbb{Z}) \]

and the cospecialization morphism is defined in cohomology as soon as the varieties of vanishing cycles are acyclic (\(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(E,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(E,\mathbb{Z}) = 0\) for \(q>0\)), which is expressed by saying that \(f\) is locally acyclic.

This chapter is devoted to the analogue of this situation for a morphism smooth of schemes for étale cohomology. However it is indispensable in this framework to restrict to coefficients of torsion and of order prime to the residue characteristics. Section 5.1 is devoted to generalities on locally acyclic morphisms and the cospecialization arrows. In section 5.2, we prove that a smooth morphism is locally acyclic. In section 5.3, we join this result to those of the previous chapter to deduce two applications: a specialization theorem for the cohomology groups (the cohomology of the geometric fibres of a proper and smooth morphism is locally constant) and a base change theorem by a smooth morphism.

In all that follows, we fix an integer \(n\) and “scheme” means “scheme over which \(n\) is invertible.” “Geometric point” will always mean “algebraic geometric point” (2.3.1) \(x:\operatorname{Spec}(k)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), with \(k\) algebraically closed.

5.1 Locally acyclic morphisms

5.1.1 Notation

Given a scheme \(S\) and a geometric point \(s\) of \(S\), we denote by \(\widetilde S^s\) the spectrum of the strict localization of \(S\) at \(s\).

Definition 5.1.2

We say that a geometric point \(t\) of \(S\) is a generization of \(s\) if it is defined by an algebraic closure of the residue field of a point of \(\widetilde S^s\). We also say that \(s\) is a specialization of \(t\), and the \(S\)-morphism \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \widetilde S^s\) is called the specialization arrow.

Definition 5.1.3

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a morphism of schemes. Let \(s\) be a geometric point of \(S\), \(t\) a generization of \(s\), \(x\) a geometric point of \(X\) above \(s\), and \(\widetilde X_t^x = \widetilde X^x\times_{\widetilde S^s} t\). Then we say that \(\widetilde X_t^x\) is a variety of vanishing cycles of \(f\) at the point \(x\).

We say that \(f\) is locally acyclic if the reduced cohomology of every variety of vanishing cycles \(\widetilde X_t^x\) is zero:

\[ \tag{5.1.3.1} \widehat{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^\bullet(\widetilde X_t^x,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\text{,} \]

i.e., \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\left(X_t^x,\mathbb{Z}/n\right) = \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\widetilde X_t^x,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q>0\).

Lemma 5.1.4

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a locally acyclic morphism and \(g:S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a quasi-finite morphism (or a projective limit of quasi-finite morphisms). Then the morphism \(f':X'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S'\) deduced from \(f\) by base change is locally acyclic.

Indeed, one checks that every variety of vanishing cycles of \(f'\) is a variety of vanishing cycles of \(f\).

Lemma 5.1.5

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a locally acyclic morphism. For every geometric point \(t\) of \(S\), giving rise to a cartesian diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X_t \ar[r]^-{\varepsilon'} \ar[d] & X \ar[d]^-f \\ t \ar[r]^-\varepsilon & S } \]

we have \(\varepsilon_*' \mathbb{Z}/n = f^*\varepsilon_* \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\mathsf{R}^q \varepsilon_*'\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(q>0\).

Let \(\overline{S}\) be the closure of \(\varepsilon(t)\), \(S'\) the normalization of \(\overline{S}\) in \(k(t)\), and the cartesian diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X_t \ar[r]^-{f'} \ar[d] & X' \ar[r]^-{\alpha'} \ar[d]^-{f'} & X \ar[d]^-f \\ t \ar[r]^-i & S' \ar[r]^-\alpha & S } \]

The local rings of \(S'\) are normal with separably closed field of fractions. They are therefore strictly henselian, and the local acyclicity of \(f'\) (5.1.4) yields \(f_*'\mathbb{Z}/n = \mathbb{Z}/n\), \(\mathsf{R}^qi_*'\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) for \(q>0\). Since \(\alpha\) is integral, we then have

\[ \mathsf{R}^q\varepsilon_*'\mathbb{Z}/n = \alpha_*' \mathsf{R}^q i_*' \mathbb{Z}/n = \alpha_*' {f'}^* \mathsf{R}^q i_* \mathbb{Z}/n = f^* \alpha_* \mathsf{R}^q i_* \mathbb{Z}/n = f^* \mathsf{R}^q \varepsilon_* \mathbb{Z}/n \text{,} \]

and the lemma follows.

5.1.6

Given a locally acyclic morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and a specialization arrow \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \widetilde S^s\), we shall define canonical homomorphisms, called cospecialization arrows

\[ \operatorname{cosp}^\bullet : \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n)\text{,} \]

relating the cohomology of the general fibre \(X_t=X\times_S t\) to that of the special fibre \(X_s=X\times_X s\).

Consider the cartesian diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X_t \ar[d] \ar[r]^-{\varepsilon'} & \widetilde X \ar[d]^-{f'} & X_s \ar[d] \ar[l]\\ t \ar[r]^-\varepsilon & \widetilde S^s & s \ar[l]} \]

deduced from \(f\) by base change. By (5.1.4), \(f'\) is again locally acyclic. From the definition of local acyclicity, one immediately deduces that the restriction to \(X_s\) of the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^q \varepsilon_*' \mathbb{Z}/n\) is \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) for \(q=0\), and \(0\) for \(q>0\). By (5.1.5) we even know that \(\mathsf{R}^q \varepsilon_*'\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) for \(q>0\). One defines \(\operatorname{cosp}^\bullet\) as the composite arrow

\[ \tag{5.1.6.1} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\varepsilon_*' \mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n) \text{.} \]

Variant

Let \(\overline{S}\) be the closure of \(\varepsilon(t)\) in \(\widetilde S^s\), \(S'\) the normalization of \(\overline{S}\) in \(k(t)\), and \(X'/S'\) deduced from \(X/S\) by base change. The diagram (5.1.6.1) can also be written

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X',\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n) \text{.} \]
Theorem 5.1.7

Let \(S\) be a locally noetherian scheme, \(s\) a geometric point of \(S\), and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a morphism. Assume

  1. the morphism \(f\) is locally acyclic,

  2. for every specialization morphism \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \widetilde S^s\) and for every \(q\geqslant 0\), the cospecialization arrows \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) are bijective.

Then the canonical homomorphism \((\mathsf{R}^q f_*\mathbb{Z}/n)_s\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\).

To prove the theorem, it is clear that we may assume \(S=\widetilde S^s\). We shall in fact show that, for every sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-modules \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(S\), the canonical homomorphism \(\varphi^q(\mathscr{F}):(\mathsf{R}^q f_* f^* \mathscr{F})_s \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,f^*\mathscr{F})\) is bijective.

Every sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) is a filtered inductive limit of constructible sheaves of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-modules (4.3.3). Moreover, every constructible sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-modules embeds in a sheaf of the form \(\prod i_{\lambda *} C_\lambda\), where \(i_\lambda:t_\lambda\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is a finite family of generizations of \(s\) and \(C_\lambda\) a free \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-module of finite rank on \(t_\lambda\). By the definition of the cospecialization arrows, condition b) means that the homomorphisms \(\varphi^q(\mathscr{F})\) are bijective if \(\mathscr{F}\) is of this form.

We conclude with the aid of a variant of the lemma (4.3.6):

Lemma 5.1.8

Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be an abelian category in which filtered inductive limits exist. Let \(\varphi^\bullet:T^\bullet\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{T'}^\bullet\) be a morphism of cohomological functors commuting with filtered inductive limits, defined on \(\mathscr{C}\) and with values in the category of abelian groups. Suppose that there exist two subsets \(\mathscr{D}\) and \(\mathscr{E}\) of objects of \(\mathscr{C}\) such that:

  1. every object of \(\mathscr{C}\) is a filtered inductive limit of objects belonging to \(\mathscr{D}\),

  2. every object belonging to \(\mathscr{D}\) is contained in an object belonging to \(\mathscr{E}\).

Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. \(\varphi^q(A)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\) and every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{C}\).

  2. \(\varphi^q(M)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\) and every \(M\in\mathscr{E}\).

The proof of the lemma is carried out by passage to the inductive limit, induction on \(q\), and repeated application of the five lemma to the diagram of exact cohomology sequences deduced from an exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} A'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\), with \(A\in\mathscr{D}\), \(M\in\mathscr{E}\), \(A'\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{C}\).

Corollary 5.1.9

Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a strictly henselian noetherian local ring and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a locally acyclic morphism. Suppose that, for every geometric point \(t\) of \(S\), one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q>0\) (in other words, the geometric fibres of \(f\) are acyclic). Then we have \(f_* \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\mathsf{R}^qf_*\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) for \(q>0\).

Corollary 5.1.10

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) and \(g:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) be morphisms of locally noetherian schemes. Then, if \(f\) and \(g\) are locally acyclic, so is \(g\circ f\).

We may assume that \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) are strictly local and that \(f\) and \(g\) are local morphisms. It then remains to show that, if \(z\) is an algebraic geometric point of \(Z\), one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X_z,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_z,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q>0\).

Since \(g\) is locally acyclic, one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(Y_z,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n\), and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(Y_z,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q>0\). Moreover, the morphism \(f_z:X_z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_z\) is locally acyclic (5.1.4) and its geometric fibres are acyclic, since they are varieties of vanishing cycles of \(f\). By (5.1.9), we therefore have \(\mathsf{R}^q {f_z}_*\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) for \(q>0\). Moreover, \({f_z}_*\mathbb{Z}/n\) is constant with fibre \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) on \(Y_z\). We conclude with the aid of the Leray spectral sequence of \(f_z\).

5.2 Local acyclicity of a smooth morphism

Theorem 5.2.1

A smooth morphism is locally acyclic.

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a smooth morphism. The assertion is local for the étale topology on \(X\) and \(S\), so we may assume that \(X\) is the standard affine space of dimension \(d\) over \(S\). By passage to the limit, we may assume that \(S\) is noetherian, and the transitivity of local acyclicity (5.1.10) shows that it suffices to treat the case \(d=1\).

Let \(s\) be a geometric point of \(S\) and \(x\) a geometric point of \(X\) centred at a closed point of \(X_s\). We must show that the geometric fibres of the morphism \(\widetilde X^x\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \widetilde S^s\) are acyclic. From now on we set \(S=\widetilde S^s=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(X=\widetilde X^x\). We have \(X\simeq \operatorname{Spec} A\{T\}\), where \(A\{T\}\) is the henselization of \(A[T]\) at the point \(T=0\) above \(s\).

If \(t\) is a geometric point of \(S\), the fibre \(X_t\) is a projective limit of affine curves smooth over \(t\). We therefore have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q\geqslant 0\), and it suffices to show that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(n\) prime to the residue characteristic of \(S\). This follows from the two following propositions.

Proposition 5.2.2

Let \(A\) be a strictly henselian local ring, \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(X=\operatorname{Spec} A\{T\}\). Then the geometric fibres of \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) are connected.

By passage to the limit, we may reduce to the case where \(A\) is a strict henselization of a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra of finite type.

Let \(\overline{t}\) be a geometric point of \(S\), localized at \(t\), and \(k'\) a finite separable extension of \(k(t)\) in \(k(\overline{t})\). Set \(t'=\operatorname{Spec}(k')\) and \(X_{t'} = X\times_S\operatorname{Spec}(k')\). We must check that, whatever \(\overline{t}\) and \(t'\) may be, \(X_{t'}\) is connected (by which we mean connected and nonempty). Let \(A'\) be the normalization of \(A\) in \(k'\), i.e., the ring of elements of \(k'\) integral over the image of \(A\) in \(k(t)\). We have \(A\{t\}\otimes_A A'\xrightarrow{\sim} A'\{T\}\): indeed, the left-hand side is henselian local (since \(A'\) is finite over \(A\), and local) and a limit of local algebras étale over \(A'\{T\}=A\{T\}\otimes_A A'\). The scheme \(X_{t'}\) is therefore again the fibre at \(t'\) of \(X=\operatorname{Spec}\left(A'\{T\}\right)\) over \(S'=\operatorname{Spec}(A')\). The local scheme \(X'\) is normal, hence integral; its localization \(X_{t'}\) is again integral, a fortiori connected.

Proposition 5.2.3

Let \(A\) be a strictly henselian local ring, \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(X=\operatorname{Spec}\left(A\{T\}\right)\). Let \(\overline{t}\) be a geometric point of \(S\) and \(X_{\overline{t}}\) the corresponding geometric fibre. Then every Galois étale covering of \(X_{\overline{t}}\) of order prime to the characteristic of the residue field of \(A\) is trivial.

Lemma 5.2.4 (Zariski-Nagata purity theorem in dimension \(2\))

Let \(C\) be a regular local ring of dimension \(2\) and \(C'\) a finite normal \(C\)-algebra, étale above the open complement of the closed point of \(\operatorname{Spec}(C)\). Then \(C'\) is étale over \(C\).

Indeed, \(C'\) is normal of dimension \(2\), hence \(\operatorname{prof}(C')=2\). Since \(\operatorname{prof}(C')+\dim\operatorname{proj}(C') = \dim(C)=2\), we conclude that \(C'\) is free over \(C\). Then the set of points of \(C\) where \(C'\) is ramified is defined by a single equation, the discriminant; since it contains no point of height \(1\), it is empty.

Lemma 5.2.5 (special case of Abhyankar's lemma)

Let \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(V)\) be a trait, \(\pi\) a uniformizer, \(\eta\) the point generic of \(S\), \(X\) smooth over \(S\), irreducible, of relative dimension \(1\), \(\widetilde X_\eta\) a Galois étale covering of \(X_\eta\), of degree \(n\) invertible on \(S\), and \(S_1=\operatorname{Spec}\left(V[\pi^{1/n}]\right)\). Denote by a subscript \((-)_1\) the base change from \(S\) to \(S_1\). Then \(\widetilde X_{1\eta}\) extends to an étale covering of \(X_1\).

Let \(\widetilde X_1\) be the normalization of \(X_1\) in \(\widetilde X_{1\eta}\). Given the structure of the tame inertia groups of the discrete valuation rings obtained by localizing \(X\) at the generic points of the special fibre \(X_s\), \(\widetilde X_1\) is étale over \(X_1\) on the general fibre, and at the points generic of the special fibre. By (5.2.4), it is étale everywhere.

5.2.6

Denote by \(t\) the point at which \(\overline{t}\) is localized. We are free to replace \(A\) by the normalization of \(A\) in a finite separable extension \(k(t')\) of \(k(t)\) in \(k(\overline{t})\) (cf. 5.2.2). This, together with a preliminary passage to the limit, allows us to assume that

  1. \(A\) is normal noetherian, and \(t\) is the generic point of \(S\).

  2. The étale covering of \(X_{\overline{t}}\) under consideration comes from an étale covering of \(X_t\).

  3. It comes from an étale covering \(\widetilde X_U\) of the inverse image \(X_U\) of a nonempty open set \(U\) of \(S\) (this follows from b): \(t\) is the limit of the \(U\)).

  4. The complement of \(U\) is of codimension \(\geqslant 2\) (this at the cost of enlarging \(k(t)\), by applying (5.2.5) to the discrete valuation rings obtained by localizing \(S\) at the points of \(S\setminus U\) of codimension \(1\) in \(S\); these points are finite in number).

  5. The covering \(\widetilde X_U\) is trivial above the subscheme \(T=0\). (This, at the cost of enlarging \(k(t)\) again.)

When these conditions are fulfilled, we shall see that the covering \(\widetilde X_U\) is trivial.

Lemma 5.2.7

Let \(A\) be a strictly henselian, normal, noetherian local ring, \(U\) an open set of \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) whose complement is of codimension \(\geqslant 2\), \(V\) its inverse image in \(X=\operatorname{Spec}\left(A\{T\}\right)\) and \(V'\) an étale covering of \(V\). If \(V'\) is trivial above \(T=0\), then \(V'\) is trivial.

Let \(B=\Gamma(V',\mathscr{O})\). Since \(V'\) is the inverse image of \(V\) in \(\operatorname{Spec}(B)\), it suffices to see that \(B\) is finite étale over \(A\{T\}\) (hence split, since \(A\{T\}\) is strictly henselian). Let \(\widehat X=A[\![ T]\!]\), and denote by \((-)^\wedge\) the base change from \(X\) to \(\widehat X\). The scheme \(\widehat X\) is faithfully flat over \(X\). We therefore have \(\Gamma(\widehat V',\mathscr{O}) = B\otimes_{A\{T\}} A[\![ T]\!]\), and it suffices to see that this ring \(\widehat B\) is finite étale over \(A[\![ T]\!]\).

Let \(V_m\) (resp. \(V_m'\)) be the subscheme of \(\widehat V\) (resp. \(\widehat V'\)) defined by the equation \(T^{m+1} = 0\). By hypothesis, \(V_0'\) is a trivial covering of \(V_0\): a sum of \(n\) copies of \(V_0\). The same holds for \(V_m'/V_m\), since étale coverings are insensitive to nilpotents. From this we obtain

\[ \varphi : \Gamma(\widehat V',\mathscr{O}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \varprojlim_m \Gamma(V_m',\mathscr{O}) = \left(\varprojlim_m \Gamma(V,\mathscr{O})\right)^n \text{.} \]

By hypothesis, the complement of \(U\) is of depth \(\geqslant 2\): we have \(\Gamma(V_m,\mathscr{O})=A[T]/(T^{m+1})\), and \(\varphi\) is a homomorphism from \(\widehat B\) into \(A[\![ T]\!]^n\). Above \(U\), it provides \(n\) distinct sections of \(\widehat V'/\widehat V\): \(\widehat V'\) is therefore trivial, a sum of \(n\) copies of \(\widehat V\). Since the complement of \(\widehat V\) in \(\widehat X\) is again of codimension \(\geqslant 2\) (hence of depth \(\geqslant 2\)), we deduce that \(\widehat B=A[\![ T]\!]^n\), whence the lemma.

5.3 Applications

Theorem 5.3.1 (specialization of cohomology groups)

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper and locally acyclic morphism, for example a proper and smooth morphism. Then the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^q f_*\mathbb{Z}/n\) are locally constant constructible, and for every specialization arrow \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\widetilde S^s\), the cospecialization arrows \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) are bijective.

This follows immediately from the definition of the cospecialization arrows and from the finiteness and base change theorems for proper morphisms.

Theorem 5.3.2 (base change by a smooth morphism)

Consider a cartesian diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X' \ar[r]^-{g'} \ar[d]^-{f'} & X \ar[d]^-f \\ S' \ar[r]^-{g} & S } \]

with \(g\) smooth. For every sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\), of torsion and prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\), we have

\[ g^* \mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}^q f_*'({g'}^* \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

By taking an open covering of \(X\), we reduce to the case where \(X\) is affine, then by a passage to the limit to the case where \(X\) is of finite type over \(S\). Then \(f\) factors as an open immersion \(j:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{X}\) and a proper morphism \(\overline{f}:\overline{X}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\). From the Leray spectral sequence for \(\overline{f}\circ j\) and the base change theorem for proper morphisms, we deduce that it suffices to prove the theorem in the case where \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is an open immersion.

In this case, if \(\mathscr{F}\) is of the form \(\varepsilon_* C\), where \(\varepsilon:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is a geometric point of \(X\), the theorem is a corollary of (5.1.5). The general case follows from it by the lemma (5.1.8).

Corollary 5.3.3

Let \(K/k\) be an extension of separably closed fields, \(X\) a \(k\)-scheme and \(n\) an integer prime to the characteristic of \(k\). Then the canonical map \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_K,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\).

It suffices to remark that \(\overline{K}\) is an inductive limit of smooth \(\overline{k}\)-algebras.

Theorem 5.3.4 (relative purity)

Consider a commutative diagram

\[ \tag{5.3.4.1}\xymatrix{ U \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-j \ar[dr] & X \ar[d]^-f & Y \ar[dl]^-h \ar@{_{(}->}[l]_-i\\ & S } \]

with \(f\) smooth, purely of relative dimension \(N\), \(h\) smooth, purely of relative dimension \(N-1\), \(i\) a closed embedding, and \(U=X\setminus Y\). For \(n\) prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\), we have

\[ \begin{aligned} j_* \mathbb{Z}/n &= \mathbb{Z}/n \\ \mathsf{R}^1 j_*\mathbb{Z}/n &= \mathbb{Z}/n(-1)_Y \\ \mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n &= 0 \qquad \text{for } q\geqslant 2 \end{aligned} \]

In these formulas, \(\mathbb{Z}/n(-1)\) denotes the \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-dual of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\). If \(t\) is a local equation for \(Y\), the isomorphism \(\mathsf{R}^1j_*\mathbb{Z}/n\simeq\mathbb{Z}/n(-1)_Y\) is defined by the map \(a:\mathbb{Z}/n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}^1j_*\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\) which sends \(1\) to the class of the \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\)-torsor of the \(n\)-th roots of \(t\).

The question is local in nature. This allows us to replace \((X,Y)\) by a locally isomorphic pair, for example

\[ \xymatrix{ \mathbb{A}_T^1 \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-j \ar[dr]_-g & \mathbb{P}_T^1 \ar[d]^-f & T \ar[dl] \ar@{_{(}->}[l]_-i\\ & T } \]

with \(T=\mathbb{A}_S^{n-1}\) and \(i=\) the section at infinity. The corollary (5.1.9) applies to \(g\), and yields \(\mathsf{R}^q g_ \mathbb{Z}/n=\mathbb{Z}/n\) for \(q=0\), \(0\) for \(q>0\). For \(f\), we have moreover (4.6.2.1)

\[ \mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathbb{Z}/n = \mathbb{Z}/n,0,\mathbb{Z}/n(-1),0 \text{ for } q>2 \text{.} \]

One easily checks that \(j_* \mathbb{Z}/n = \mathbb{Z}/n\), and that the \(\mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) are concentrated on \(i(T)\) for \(q>0\). The Leray spectral sequence \(E_2^{pq} = \mathsf{R}^p f_* \mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n \Rightarrow \mathsf{R}^{p+q}g_* \mathbb{Z}/n\) therefore reduces to

\[ \xymatrix{ i^* \mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{Z}/n & 0 & \cdots \\ i^* \mathsf{R}^1 j_* \mathbb{Z}/n \ar[drr]^-{d_2} & 0 & \cdots \\ \mathbb{Z}/n & 0 & \mathbb{Z}/n(-1) & 0 & \cdots } \]

\(\mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(q\geqslant 0\), and \(\mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n\) is the extension by zero of a locally free sheaf of rank one on \(T\) (isomorphic, via \(d_2\), to \(\mathbb{Z}/n(-1)\)). Since the map \(a\), defined above, is injective (as one checks fibre by fibre), it is an isomorphism, and this proves (5.3.4).

5.3.5

We refer to [2] for the proof of the following applications of the acyclicity theorem (5.2.1).

Theorem 5.3.6

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a morphism of schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a constructible sheaf on \(X\). Then

\[ {(\mathsf{R}^q f_*\mathscr{F})}^{\mathrm{an}} \sim \mathsf{R}^q {f}^{\mathrm{an}}_* ({\mathscr{F}}^{\mathrm{an}}) \]

(cf. 4.6.3: in ordinary cohomology, it is necessary to assume \(\mathscr{F}\) constructible and not merely of torsion).

Theorem 5.3.7

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a morphism of schemes of finite type over a field \(k\) of characteristic \(0\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a constructible sheaf on \(X\). Then the \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\) are also constructible.

The proof uses resolution of singularities and (5.3.4). It is generalized to the case of a morphism of finite type of excellent schemes of characteristic \(0\) in [2]. Another proof, independent of resolution, is given in this volume (VII, 1.1)

it applies to a morphism of schemes of finite type over a field or over a Dedekind ring.

blocks.html: 5 Local acyclicity of smooth morphisms

Let \(X\) be a complex analytic variety and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} D\) a morphism of \(X\) into the disc. We denote by \([0,t]\) the closed line segment with endpoints \(0\) and \(t\) in \(D\) and by \((0,t]\) the half-open segment. If \(f\) is smooth, the inclusion
\[ j : f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right) \hookrightarrow f^{-1}\left([0,t]\right) \]
is a homotopy equivalence; one can push the special fibre \(X_0=f^{-1}(0)\) into \(f^{-1}([0,t])\).
In practice, for \(t\) small enough, \(f^{-1}((0,t])\) will be a fibre bundle over \((0,t]\) so that the inclusion
\[ X_t = f^{-1}(t) \hookrightarrow f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right) \]
will also be a homotopy equivalence. One then calls cospecialization morphism the homotopy class of maps:
\[ \operatorname{cosp} : X_0 \hookrightarrow f^{-1}\left([0,t]\right) \xleftarrow{\sim} f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right) \xleftarrow{\sim} X_t \text{.} \]
One can express this construction in pictorial terms by saying that, for a smooth morphism, the general fibre swallows the special fibre.

Let us no longer assume \(f\) necessarily smooth (but assume that \(f^{-1}((0,t])\) is a fibre bundle over \((0,t]\)). One can still define a morphism \(\operatorname{cosp}^\bullet\) in cohomology as soon as \(j_* \mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{Z} = 0\) for \(q>0\). Under these hypotheses, the Leray spectral sequence for \(j\) shows that one has
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(f^{-1}\left([0,t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \]
and \(\operatorname{cosp}^\bullet\) is the composite morphism:

\[ \operatorname{cosp}^\bullet : \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_t,\mathbb{Z}) \xleftarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(f^{-1}\left((0,t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \xleftarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\left(f^{-1}\left([0,t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_0,\mathbb{Z}) \]

The stalk of \(\mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{Z}\) at a point \(x\in X_0\) is computed as follows. In an ambient space one takes a ball \(B_\varepsilon\) with centre \(x\) and radius \(\varepsilon\) small enough, and for \(\eta\) small enough, one sets \(E=X\cap B_\varepsilon \cap f^{-1}(\eta t)\); this is the variety of vanishing cycles at \(x\). One has

\[ (\mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{Z})_x \xleftarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q\left(X\cap B_\varepsilon\cap f^{-1}\left((0,\eta t]\right),\mathbb{Z}\right) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(E,\mathbb{Z}) \]

and the cospecialization morphism is defined in cohomology as soon as the varieties of vanishing cycles are acyclic (\(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(E,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(E,\mathbb{Z}) = 0\) for \(q>0\)), which is expressed by saying that \(f\) is locally acyclic.

This chapter is devoted to the analogue of this situation for a morphism smooth of schemes for étale cohomology. However it is indispensable in this framework to restrict to coefficients of torsion and of order prime to the residue characteristics. Section 5.1 is devoted to generalities on locally acyclic morphisms and the cospecialization arrows. In section 5.2, we prove that a smooth morphism is locally acyclic. In section 5.3, we join this result to those of the previous chapter to deduce two applications: a specialization theorem for the cohomology groups (the cohomology of the geometric fibres of a proper and smooth morphism is locally constant) and a base change theorem by a smooth morphism.

In all that follows, we fix an integer \(n\) and “scheme” means “scheme over which \(n\) is invertible.” “Geometric point” will always mean “algebraic geometric point” (2.3.1) \(x:\operatorname{Spec}(k)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), with \(k\) algebraically closed.
5.1 Locally acyclic morphisms
Given a scheme \(S\) and a geometric point \(s\) of \(S\), we denote by \(\widetilde S^s\) the spectrum of the strict localization of \(S\) at \(s\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.1.2

We say that a geometric point \(t\) of \(S\) is a generization of \(s\) if it is defined by an algebraic closure of the residue field of a point of \(\widetilde S^s\). We also say that \(s\) is a specialization of \(t\), and the \(S\)-morphism \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \widetilde S^s\) is called the specialization arrow.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.1.3

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a morphism of schemes. Let \(s\) be a geometric point of \(S\), \(t\) a generization of \(s\), \(x\) a geometric point of \(X\) above \(s\), and \(\widetilde X_t^x = \widetilde X^x\times_{\widetilde S^s} t\). Then we say that \(\widetilde X_t^x\) is a variety of vanishing cycles of \(f\) at the point \(x\).

We say that \(f\) is locally acyclic if the reduced cohomology of every variety of vanishing cycles \(\widetilde X_t^x\) is zero:

\[ \tag{5.1.3.1} \widehat{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^\bullet(\widetilde X_t^x,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\text{,} \]

i.e., \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\left(X_t^x,\mathbb{Z}/n\right) = \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\widetilde X_t^x,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q>0\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.1.4

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a locally acyclic morphism and \(g:S'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a quasi-finite morphism (or a projective limit of quasi-finite morphisms). Then the morphism \(f':X'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S'\) deduced from \(f\) by base change is locally acyclic.
Indeed, one checks that every variety of vanishing cycles of \(f'\) is a variety of vanishing cycles of \(f\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.1.5

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a locally acyclic morphism. For every geometric point \(t\) of \(S\), giving rise to a cartesian diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X_t \ar[r]^-{\varepsilon'} \ar[d] & X \ar[d]^-f \\ t \ar[r]^-\varepsilon & S } \]

we have \(\varepsilon_*' \mathbb{Z}/n = f^*\varepsilon_* \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\mathsf{R}^q \varepsilon_*'\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(q>0\).
Let \(\overline{S}\) be the closure of \(\varepsilon(t)\), \(S'\) the normalization of \(\overline{S}\) in \(k(t)\), and the cartesian diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ X_t \ar[r]^-{f'} \ar[d] & X' \ar[r]^-{\alpha'} \ar[d]^-{f'} & X \ar[d]^-f \\ t \ar[r]^-i & S' \ar[r]^-\alpha & S } \]

The local rings of \(S'\) are normal with separably closed field of fractions. They are therefore strictly henselian, and the local acyclicity of \(f'\) (5.1.4) yields \(f_*'\mathbb{Z}/n = \mathbb{Z}/n\), \(\mathsf{R}^qi_*'\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) for \(q>0\). Since \(\alpha\) is integral, we then have

\[ \mathsf{R}^q\varepsilon_*'\mathbb{Z}/n = \alpha_*' \mathsf{R}^q i_*' \mathbb{Z}/n = \alpha_*' {f'}^* \mathsf{R}^q i_* \mathbb{Z}/n = f^* \alpha_* \mathsf{R}^q i_* \mathbb{Z}/n = f^* \mathsf{R}^q \varepsilon_* \mathbb{Z}/n \text{,} \]
and the lemma follows.

Given a locally acyclic morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and a specialization arrow \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \widetilde S^s\), we shall define canonical homomorphisms, called cospecialization arrows

\[ \operatorname{cosp}^\bullet : \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n)\text{,} \]
relating the cohomology of the general fibre \(X_t=X\times_S t\) to that of the special fibre \(X_s=X\times_X s\).
Consider the cartesian diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ X_t \ar[d] \ar[r]^-{\varepsilon'} & \widetilde X \ar[d]^-{f'} & X_s \ar[d] \ar[l]\\ t \ar[r]^-\varepsilon & \widetilde S^s & s \ar[l]} \]

deduced from \(f\) by base change. By (5.1.4), \(f'\) is again locally acyclic. From the definition of local acyclicity, one immediately deduces that the restriction to \(X_s\) of the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^q \varepsilon_*' \mathbb{Z}/n\) is \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) for \(q=0\), and \(0\) for \(q>0\). By (5.1.5) we even know that \(\mathsf{R}^q \varepsilon_*'\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) for \(q>0\). One defines \(\operatorname{cosp}^\bullet\) as the composite arrow

\[ \tag{5.1.6.1} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\varepsilon_*' \mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n) \text{.} \]
Variant

Let \(\overline{S}\) be the closure of \(\varepsilon(t)\) in \(\widetilde S^s\), \(S'\) the normalization of \(\overline{S}\) in \(k(t)\), and \(X'/S'\) deduced from \(X/S\) by base change. The diagram (5.1.6.1) can also be written

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) \simeq \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X',\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n) \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.1.7

Let \(S\) be a locally noetherian scheme, \(s\) a geometric point of \(S\), and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a morphism. Assume

  1. the morphism \(f\) is locally acyclic,

  2. for every specialization morphism \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \widetilde S^s\) and for every \(q\geqslant 0\), the cospecialization arrows \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) are bijective.

Then the canonical homomorphism \((\mathsf{R}^q f_*\mathbb{Z}/n)_s\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\).

To prove the theorem, it is clear that we may assume \(S=\widetilde S^s\). We shall in fact show that, for every sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-modules \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(S\), the canonical homomorphism \(\varphi^q(\mathscr{F}):(\mathsf{R}^q f_* f^* \mathscr{F})_s \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,f^*\mathscr{F})\) is bijective.

Every sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) is a filtered inductive limit of constructible sheaves of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-modules (4.3.3). Moreover, every constructible sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-modules embeds in a sheaf of the form \(\prod i_{\lambda *} C_\lambda\), where \(i_\lambda:t_\lambda\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is a finite family of generizations of \(s\) and \(C_\lambda\) a free \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)-module of finite rank on \(t_\lambda\). By the definition of the cospecialization arrows, condition b) means that the homomorphisms \(\varphi^q(\mathscr{F})\) are bijective if \(\mathscr{F}\) is of this form.
We conclude with the aid of a variant of the lemma (4.3.6):

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.1.8

Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be an abelian category in which filtered inductive limits exist. Let \(\varphi^\bullet:T^\bullet\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{T'}^\bullet\) be a morphism of cohomological functors commuting with filtered inductive limits, defined on \(\mathscr{C}\) and with values in the category of abelian groups. Suppose that there exist two subsets \(\mathscr{D}\) and \(\mathscr{E}\) of objects of \(\mathscr{C}\) such that:

  1. every object of \(\mathscr{C}\) is a filtered inductive limit of objects belonging to \(\mathscr{D}\),

  2. every object belonging to \(\mathscr{D}\) is contained in an object belonging to \(\mathscr{E}\).

Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. \(\varphi^q(A)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\) and every \(A\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{C}\).

  2. \(\varphi^q(M)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\) and every \(M\in\mathscr{E}\).

The proof of the lemma is carried out by passage to the inductive limit, induction on \(q\), and repeated application of the five lemma to the diagram of exact cohomology sequences deduced from an exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} A'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\), with \(A\in\mathscr{D}\), \(M\in\mathscr{E}\), \(A'\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{C}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.1.9

Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a strictly henselian noetherian local ring and \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) a locally acyclic morphism. Suppose that, for every geometric point \(t\) of \(S\), one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q>0\) (in other words, the geometric fibres of \(f\) are acyclic). Then we have \(f_* \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\mathsf{R}^qf_*\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) for \(q>0\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.1.10

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) and \(g:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) be morphisms of locally noetherian schemes. Then, if \(f\) and \(g\) are locally acyclic, so is \(g\circ f\).

We may assume that \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) are strictly local and that \(f\) and \(g\) are local morphisms. It then remains to show that, if \(z\) is an algebraic geometric point of \(Z\), one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X_z,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_z,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q>0\).

Since \(g\) is locally acyclic, one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(Y_z,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n\), and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(Y_z,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q>0\). Moreover, the morphism \(f_z:X_z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_z\) is locally acyclic (5.1.4) and its geometric fibres are acyclic, since they are varieties of vanishing cycles of \(f\). By (5.1.9), we therefore have \(\mathsf{R}^q {f_z}_*\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) for \(q>0\). Moreover, \({f_z}_*\mathbb{Z}/n\) is constant with fibre \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) on \(Y_z\). We conclude with the aid of the Leray spectral sequence of \(f_z\).
5.2 Local acyclicity of a smooth morphism

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.2.1

A smooth morphism is locally acyclic.

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a smooth morphism. The assertion is local for the étale topology on \(X\) and \(S\), so we may assume that \(X\) is the standard affine space of dimension \(d\) over \(S\). By passage to the limit, we may assume that \(S\) is noetherian, and the transitivity of local acyclicity (5.1.10) shows that it suffices to treat the case \(d=1\).

Let \(s\) be a geometric point of \(S\) and \(x\) a geometric point of \(X\) centred at a closed point of \(X_s\). We must show that the geometric fibres of the morphism \(\widetilde X^x\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \widetilde S^s\) are acyclic. From now on we set \(S=\widetilde S^s=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(X=\widetilde X^x\). We have \(X\simeq \operatorname{Spec} A\{T\}\), where \(A\{T\}\) is the henselization of \(A[T]\) at the point \(T=0\) above \(s\).

If \(t\) is a geometric point of \(S\), the fibre \(X_t\) is a projective limit of affine curves smooth over \(t\). We therefore have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(q\geqslant 0\), and it suffices to show that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(n\) prime to the residue characteristic of \(S\). This follows from the two following propositions.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2.2

Let \(A\) be a strictly henselian local ring, \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(X=\operatorname{Spec} A\{T\}\). Then the geometric fibres of \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) are connected.
By passage to the limit, we may reduce to the case where \(A\) is a strict henselization of a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra of finite type.

Let \(\overline{t}\) be a geometric point of \(S\), localized at \(t\), and \(k'\) a finite separable extension of \(k(t)\) in \(k(\overline{t})\). Set \(t'=\operatorname{Spec}(k')\) and \(X_{t'} = X\times_S\operatorname{Spec}(k')\). We must check that, whatever \(\overline{t}\) and \(t'\) may be, \(X_{t'}\) is connected (by which we mean connected and nonempty). Let \(A'\) be the normalization of \(A\) in \(k'\), i.e., the ring of elements of \(k'\) integral over the image of \(A\) in \(k(t)\). We have \(A\{t\}\otimes_A A'\xrightarrow{\sim} A'\{T\}\): indeed, the left-hand side is henselian local (since \(A'\) is finite over \(A\), and local) and a limit of local algebras étale over \(A'\{T\}=A\{T\}\otimes_A A'\). The scheme \(X_{t'}\) is therefore again the fibre at \(t'\) of \(X=\operatorname{Spec}\left(A'\{T\}\right)\) over \(S'=\operatorname{Spec}(A')\). The local scheme \(X'\) is normal, hence integral; its localization \(X_{t'}\) is again integral, a fortiori connected.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2.3

Let \(A\) be a strictly henselian local ring, \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(X=\operatorname{Spec}\left(A\{T\}\right)\). Let \(\overline{t}\) be a geometric point of \(S\) and \(X_{\overline{t}}\) the corresponding geometric fibre. Then every Galois étale covering of \(X_{\overline{t}}\) of order prime to the characteristic of the residue field of \(A\) is trivial.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.2.4 (Zariski-Nagata purity theorem in dimension \(2\))

Let \(C\) be a regular local ring of dimension \(2\) and \(C'\) a finite normal \(C\)-algebra, étale above the open complement of the closed point of \(\operatorname{Spec}(C)\). Then \(C'\) is étale over \(C\).

Indeed, \(C'\) is normal of dimension \(2\), hence \(\operatorname{prof}(C')=2\). Since \(\operatorname{prof}(C')+\dim\operatorname{proj}(C') = \dim(C)=2\), we conclude that \(C'\) is free over \(C\). Then the set of points of \(C\) where \(C'\) is ramified is defined by a single equation, the discriminant; since it contains no point of height \(1\), it is empty.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.2.5 (special case of Abhyankar's lemma)

Let \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(V)\) be a trait, \(\pi\) a uniformizer, \(\eta\) the point generic of \(S\), \(X\) smooth over \(S\), irreducible, of relative dimension \(1\), \(\widetilde X_\eta\) a Galois étale covering of \(X_\eta\), of degree \(n\) invertible on \(S\), and \(S_1=\operatorname{Spec}\left(V[\pi^{1/n}]\right)\). Denote by a subscript \((-)_1\) the base change from \(S\) to \(S_1\). Then \(\widetilde X_{1\eta}\) extends to an étale covering of \(X_1\).

Let \(\widetilde X_1\) be the normalization of \(X_1\) in \(\widetilde X_{1\eta}\). Given the structure of the tame inertia groups of the discrete valuation rings obtained by localizing \(X\) at the generic points of the special fibre \(X_s\), \(\widetilde X_1\) is étale over \(X_1\) on the general fibre, and at the points generic of the special fibre. By (5.2.4), it is étale everywhere.

Denote by \(t\) the point at which \(\overline{t}\) is localized. We are free to replace \(A\) by the normalization of \(A\) in a finite separable extension \(k(t')\) of \(k(t)\) in \(k(\overline{t})\) (cf. 5.2.2). This, together with a preliminary passage to the limit, allows us to assume that

1. \(A\) is normal noetherian, and \(t\) is the generic point of \(S\).

  2. The étale covering of \(X_{\overline{t}}\) under consideration comes from an étale covering of \(X_t\).

  3. It comes from an étale covering \(\widetilde X_U\) of the inverse image \(X_U\) of a nonempty open set \(U\) of \(S\) (this follows from b): \(t\) is the limit of the \(U\)).

  4. The complement of \(U\) is of codimension \(\geqslant 2\) (this at the cost of enlarging \(k(t)\), by applying (5.2.5) to the discrete valuation rings obtained by localizing \(S\) at the points of \(S\setminus U\) of codimension \(1\) in \(S\); these points are finite in number).

  5. The covering \(\widetilde X_U\) is trivial above the subscheme \(T=0\). (This, at the cost of enlarging \(k(t)\) again.)
When these conditions are fulfilled, we shall see that the covering \(\widetilde X_U\) is trivial.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.2.7

Let \(A\) be a strictly henselian, normal, noetherian local ring, \(U\) an open set of \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) whose complement is of codimension \(\geqslant 2\), \(V\) its inverse image in \(X=\operatorname{Spec}\left(A\{T\}\right)\) and \(V'\) an étale covering of \(V\). If \(V'\) is trivial above \(T=0\), then \(V'\) is trivial.

Let \(B=\Gamma(V',\mathscr{O})\). Since \(V'\) is the inverse image of \(V\) in \(\operatorname{Spec}(B)\), it suffices to see that \(B\) is finite étale over \(A\{T\}\) (hence split, since \(A\{T\}\) is strictly henselian). Let \(\widehat X=A[\![ T]\!]\), and denote by \((-)^\wedge\) the base change from \(X\) to \(\widehat X\). The scheme \(\widehat X\) is faithfully flat over \(X\). We therefore have \(\Gamma(\widehat V',\mathscr{O}) = B\otimes_{A\{T\}} A[\![ T]\!]\), and it suffices to see that this ring \(\widehat B\) is finite étale over \(A[\![ T]\!]\).

Let \(V_m\) (resp. \(V_m'\)) be the subscheme of \(\widehat V\) (resp. \(\widehat V'\)) defined by the equation \(T^{m+1} = 0\). By hypothesis, \(V_0'\) is a trivial covering of \(V_0\): a sum of \(n\) copies of \(V_0\). The same holds for \(V_m'/V_m\), since étale coverings are insensitive to nilpotents. From this we obtain

\[ \varphi : \Gamma(\widehat V',\mathscr{O}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \varprojlim_m \Gamma(V_m',\mathscr{O}) = \left(\varprojlim_m \Gamma(V,\mathscr{O})\right)^n \text{.} \]

By hypothesis, the complement of \(U\) is of depth \(\geqslant 2\): we have \(\Gamma(V_m,\mathscr{O})=A[T]/(T^{m+1})\), and \(\varphi\) is a homomorphism from \(\widehat B\) into \(A[\![ T]\!]^n\). Above \(U\), it provides \(n\) distinct sections of \(\widehat V'/\widehat V\): \(\widehat V'\) is therefore trivial, a sum of \(n\) copies of \(\widehat V\). Since the complement of \(\widehat V\) in \(\widehat X\) is again of codimension \(\geqslant 2\) (hence of depth \(\geqslant 2\)), we deduce that \(\widehat B=A[\![ T]\!]^n\), whence the lemma.
5.3 Applications

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.3.1 (specialization of cohomology groups)

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a proper and locally acyclic morphism, for example a proper and smooth morphism. Then the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^q f_*\mathbb{Z}/n\) are locally constant constructible, and for every specialization arrow \(t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\widetilde S^s\), the cospecialization arrows \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_t,\mathbb{Z}/n)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_s,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) are bijective.
This follows immediately from the definition of the cospecialization arrows and from the finiteness and base change theorems for proper morphisms.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.3.2 (base change by a smooth morphism)

Consider a cartesian diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ X' \ar[r]^-{g'} \ar[d]^-{f'} & X \ar[d]^-f \\ S' \ar[r]^-{g} & S } \]

with \(g\) smooth. For every sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\), of torsion and prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\), we have

\[ g^* \mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}^q f_*'({g'}^* \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

By taking an open covering of \(X\), we reduce to the case where \(X\) is affine, then by a passage to the limit to the case where \(X\) is of finite type over \(S\). Then \(f\) factors as an open immersion \(j:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{X}\) and a proper morphism \(\overline{f}:\overline{X}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\). From the Leray spectral sequence for \(\overline{f}\circ j\) and the base change theorem for proper morphisms, we deduce that it suffices to prove the theorem in the case where \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is an open immersion.

In this case, if \(\mathscr{F}\) is of the form \(\varepsilon_* C\), where \(\varepsilon:t\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is a geometric point of \(X\), the theorem is a corollary of (5.1.5). The general case follows from it by the lemma (5.1.8).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3.3

Let \(K/k\) be an extension of separably closed fields, \(X\) a \(k\)-scheme and \(n\) an integer prime to the characteristic of \(k\). Then the canonical map \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(X_K,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) is bijective for every \(q\geqslant 0\).
It suffices to remark that \(\overline{K}\) is an inductive limit of smooth \(\overline{k}\)-algebras.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.3.4 (relative purity)

Consider a commutative diagram

\[ \tag{5.3.4.1}\xymatrix{ U \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-j \ar[dr] & X \ar[d]^-f & Y \ar[dl]^-h \ar@{_{(}->}[l]_-i\\ & S } \]

with \(f\) smooth, purely of relative dimension \(N\), \(h\) smooth, purely of relative dimension \(N-1\), \(i\) a closed embedding, and \(U=X\setminus Y\). For \(n\) prime to the residue characteristics of \(S\), we have

\[ \begin{aligned} j_* \mathbb{Z}/n &= \mathbb{Z}/n \\ \mathsf{R}^1 j_*\mathbb{Z}/n &= \mathbb{Z}/n(-1)_Y \\ \mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n &= 0 \qquad \text{for } q\geqslant 2 \end{aligned} \]

In these formulas, \(\mathbb{Z}/n(-1)\) denotes the \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-dual of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\).
