If \(t\) is a local equation for \(Y\), the isomorphism \(\mathsf{R}^1j_*\mathbb{Z}/n\simeq\mathbb{Z}/n(-1)_Y\) is defined by the map \(a:\mathbb{Z}/n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}^1j_*\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\) which sends \(1\) to the class of the \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\)-torsor of the \(n\)-th roots of \(t\).
The question is local in nature. This allows us to replace \((X,Y)\) by a locally isomorphic pair, for example
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathbb{A}_T^1 \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-j \ar[dr]_-g & \mathbb{P}_T^1 \ar[d]^-f & T \ar[dl] \ar@{_{(}->}[l]_-i\\ & T } \]

with \(T=\mathbb{A}_S^{n-1}\) and \(i=\) the section at infinity. The corollary (5.1.9) applies to \(g\), and yields \(\mathsf{R}^q g_ \mathbb{Z}/n=\mathbb{Z}/n\) for \(q=0\), \(0\) for \(q>0\). For \(f\), we have moreover (4.6.2.1)
\[ \mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathbb{Z}/n = \mathbb{Z}/n,0,\mathbb{Z}/n(-1),0 \text{ for } q>2 \text{.} \]

One easily checks that \(j_* \mathbb{Z}/n = \mathbb{Z}/n\), and that the \(\mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) are concentrated on \(i(T)\) for \(q>0\). The Leray spectral sequence \(E_2^{pq} = \mathsf{R}^p f_* \mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n \Rightarrow \mathsf{R}^{p+q}g_* \mathbb{Z}/n\) therefore reduces to
\[ \xymatrix{ i^* \mathsf{R}^q j_* \mathbb{Z}/n & 0 & \cdots \\ i^* \mathsf{R}^1 j_* \mathbb{Z}/n \ar[drr]^-{d_2} & 0 & \cdots \\ \mathbb{Z}/n & 0 & \mathbb{Z}/n(-1) & 0 & \cdots } \]

\(\mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n=0\) for \(q\geqslant 0\), and \(\mathsf{R}^q j_*\mathbb{Z}/n\) is the extension by zero of a locally free sheaf of rank one on \(T\) (isomorphic, via \(d_2\), to \(\mathbb{Z}/n(-1)\)). Since the map \(a\), defined above, is injective (as one checks fibre by fibre), it is an isomorphism, and this proves (5.3.4).
We refer to [2] for the proof of the following applications of the acyclicity theorem (5.2.1).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.3.6

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a morphism of schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a constructible sheaf on \(X\). Then

\[ {(\mathsf{R}^q f_*\mathscr{F})}^{\mathrm{an}} \sim \mathsf{R}^q {f}^{\mathrm{an}}_* ({\mathscr{F}}^{\mathrm{an}}) \]

(cf. 4.6.3: in ordinary cohomology, it is necessary to assume \(\mathscr{F}\) constructible and not merely of torsion).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.3.7

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a morphism of schemes of finite type over a field \(k\) of characteristic \(0\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a constructible sheaf on \(X\). Then the \(\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}\) are also constructible.

The proof uses resolution of singularities and (5.3.4). It is generalized to the case of a morphism of finite type of excellent schemes of characteristic \(0\) in [2]. Another proof, independent of resolution, is given in this volume (VII, 1.1)
it applies to a morphism of schemes of finite type over a field or over a Dedekind ring.

pages.title: Poincaré duality
pages.html:
Poincaré duality

6.1 Introduction

Let \(X\) be an oriented topological variety, purely of dimension \(N\), and suppose that \(X\) admits a finite open covering \(\mathscr{U}=(U_i)_{1\leqslant i\leqslant K}\), such that the nonempty intersections of open sets \(U_i\) are homeomorphic to balls. For such a variety, the Poincaré duality theorem can be presented as follows:

  1. The cohomology of \(X\) is the Čech cohomology corresponding to the covering \(\mathscr{U}\). It is the cohomology of the complex

    \[ \tag{1} 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}^{A_0} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}^{A_1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \]

    where \(A_k=\{(i_0,\dotsc,i_k) : i_0<\cdots<i_k\text{ and } U_{i_0}\cap \cdots \cap U_{i_k} \ne \varnothing\}\).

  2. For \(a\in A_k\), \(a=(i_0,\dotsc,i_k)\), let \(U_a=U_{i_1}\cap \cdots \cap U_{i_k}\) and let \(j_a\) be the inclusion of \(U_a\) in \(X\). The constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}\) on \(X\) admits the (left) resolution

    \[ \tag{2} \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & \displaystyle\bigoplus_{a\in A_1} j_{a!}\mathbb{Z} \ar[r] & \displaystyle\bigoplus_{a\in A_0} j_{a!} \mathbb{Z} \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ & & \mathbb{Z} . } \]

    The cohomology with compact support \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,j_{a!}\mathbb{Z})\) is nothing but the cohomology with proper support of the (oriented) ball \(U_a\):

    \[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,j_{a!}\mathbb{Z}) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i\ne N \\ \mathbb{Z} & \text{if } i = N \end{cases} \]

The hypercohomology spectral sequence, for the complex (2), and the cohomology with proper support, therefore asserts that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X)\) is the \((i-N)\)-th cohomology group of a complex

\[ \tag{3} \cdots \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}^{A_1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}^{A_0} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0 \text{.} \]

This complex is the dual of the complex (1), whence Poincaré duality.

The essential points of this construction are

  1. the existence of a theory of cohomology with proper support:

  2. the fact that every point \(x\) of a variety \(X\) purely of dimension \(N\) has a fundamental system of open neighbourhoods \(U\) for which

    \[ \tag{4} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(U) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } i\ne N \text{,} \\ \mathbb{Z} & \text{for } i=N \text{.} \end{cases} \]

Poincaré duality in étale cohomology can be constructed on this model. For \(X\) smooth, purely of dimension \(N\) over \(k\) algebraically closed, \(n\) invertible on \(X\) and \(x\) a closed point of \(X\), the key point is to compute the projective limit, extended over the étale neighbourhoods \(U\) of \(x\)

\[ \tag{5} \varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(U,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i\ne 2N \\ \mathbb{Z}/n & \text{if } i=2N \text{.} \end{cases} \]

Just as for topological varieties one must first treat directly the case of an open ball (or even simply that of the interval \((0,1)\)), here one must first treat directly the case of curves (6.2). The theorem of local acyclicity of smooth morphisms then allows one to reduce (5) to this special case (6.3).

The isomorphisms (4) and (5) are not canonical: they depend on the choice of an orientation of \(X\). For \(n\) invertible on a scheme \(X\), \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\) is a sheaf of free \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules of rank one. We denote by \(\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\) its \(N\)-th tensor power (\(N\in\mathbb{Z}\)). The intrinsic form of the second line of (5) is

\[ \tag{6} \varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2N} \left(U,\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\right) = \mathbb{Z}/n \text{,} \]

and \(\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\) is called the orientation sheaf of \(X\); since the sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\) is constant, isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\), one can take it out of the sign \(N\) and write instead

\[ \tag{7} \varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2N} (U,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n(-N) \text{,} \]

and Poincaré duality will take the form of a perfect duality, with values in \(\mathbb{Z}/n(-N)\), between \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2N-i}(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\).

6.2 The case of curves

6.2.1

Let \(\overline{X}\) be a projective smooth curve over \(k\) algebraically closed, and \(n\) invertible on \(\overline{X}\). The proof of (3.3.5) provides, for \(\overline{X}\) connected, a canonical isomorphism

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(\overline{X},\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \operatorname{Pic}(\overline{X})/n\operatorname{Pic}(\overline{X}) \ar[r]^-{\deg}_-{\sim} & \mathbb{Z}/n } \]

Let \(D\) be a reduced divisor of \(\overline{X}\) and \(X=\overline{X}\setminus D\)

\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-j & \overline{X} & D . \ar@{_{(}->}[l]_-i} \]

The exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} j_! \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \boldsymbol{\mu}_n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} i_* \boldsymbol{\mu}_n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) and the fact that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},i_*\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(D,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)=0\) for \(i>0\) provide an isomorphism

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(\overline{X},j_! \boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r]^-\sim & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(\overline{X},\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r]^-\sim & \mathbb{Z}/n . } \]

For \(\overline{X}\) disconnected, we likewise have

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = (\mathbb{Z}/n)^{\pi_0(X)} \]

and one defines the trace morphism as the sum

\[ \xymatrix{ \operatorname{tr} : \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n)^{\pi_0(X)} \ar[r]^-\Sigma & \mathbb{Z}/n. } \]
Theorem 6.2.2

The form \(\operatorname{tr}(a\smallsmile b)\) identifies each of the two groups \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2-i}(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) with the dual (with values in \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)) of the other.

Transcendental proof. If \(\overline{X}\) is a projective smooth curve over a trait \(S\), and \(j:X\hookrightarrow \overline{X}\) is the inclusion of the complement of a divisor \(D\) étale over \(S\), the cohomologies (resp. the cohomologies with proper support) of the special and generic geometric fibres of \(X/S\) are “the same,” i.e., the fibres of sheaves locally constant on \(S\). This follows from the analogous facts for \(\overline{X}\) and \(D\), via the exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} j_! \mathbb{Z}/n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{Z}/n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} {\mathbb{Z}/n}_D\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) (for cohomology with proper support) and the formulas \(j_*\mathbb{Z}/n = \mathbb{Z}/n\), \(\mathsf{R}^1 j_* \mathbb{Z}/n \simeq {\mathbb{Z}/n}_D(-1)\), \(\mathsf{R}^i j_*\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) (\(i\geqslant 2\)) (for ordinary cohomology) (5.3.4).

This specialization principle reduces (6.2.2) to the case where \(k\) is of characteristic \(0\). By (5.3.3), this case reduces to the one where \(k=\mathbb{C}\). Finally, for \(k=\mathbb{C}\), the groups \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) coincide with the groups of the same name, computed for the classical topological space \(X_{\textnormal{cl}}\) and, via the isomorphism \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \boldsymbol{\mu}_n: x\mapsto \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i x}{n}\right)\), the trace morphism is identified with “integration over the fundamental class,” so that (6.2.2) follows from Poincaré duality for \(X_{\textnormal{cl}}\).

6.2.3 Algebraic proof

For a very economical proof, see (V, §2).

Here is another, connected with the autoduality of the Jacobian.

We resume the notation of (6.2.1). We may assume — and we do assume — that \(X\) is connected. The cases \(i=0\) and \(i=2\) being trivial, we also assume that \(i=1\). We define \(_D\mathbb{G}_m\) by the exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} _D\mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} i_*\mathbb{G}_m\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) (sections of \(\mathbb{G}_m\) congruent to \(1\mod D\)). The group \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(\overline{X}, _D\mathbb{G}_m)\) classifies the invertible sheaves on \(\overline{X}\) trivialized on \(D\). It is the group of points of \(\operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X})\), an extension of \(\mathbb{Z}\) (the degree) by the group of points of a generalized Jacobian of Rosenlicht (corresponding to conductor \(1\) at each point of \(D\)) \(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})\), itself an extension of the abelian variety \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(\overline{X})\) by the torus \(\mathbb{G}_m^D/(\mathbb{G}_m \text{ diagonal})\).

  1. The exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} _D\mathbb{G}_m \xrightarrow{n} _D\mathbb{G}_m\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) yields an isomorphism

    \[ \tag{6.2.3.1} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n \text{.} \]

  2. The map which assigns to \(x\in X(k)\) the class of the invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{O}(x)\) on \(\overline{X}\), trivialized by \(1\) on \(D\), arises from a morphism

    \[ f:X \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X}) \text{.} \]

For the sequel, we fix a base point \(0\) and set \(f_0(x)=f(x)-f(0)\). For every homomorphism \(v:\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\), let \(\overline{v}\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}),\mathbb{Z}/n\right)\) be the image under \(v\) of the class in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}),\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n\right)\) of the torsor defined by the extension

\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}) \ar[r]^-n & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}) \ar[r] & 0 } \]

Geometric class field theory (as presented in Serre [33]) shows that the map \(v\mapsto f_0^*(\overline{v})\):

\[ \tag{6.2.3.2} \hom\left(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n,\mathbb{Z}/n\right) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) \]

is an isomorphism. To deduce (6.2.2) from (6.2.3.1) and (6.2.3.2), it remains to know that

\[ \tag{6.2.2.3} \operatorname{tr}\left(u \smallsmile f_0^*(\overline{v})\right) = -v(u) \text{.} \]

6.3 The general case

Let \(X\) be a smooth algebraic variety, purely of dimension \(N\), over \(k\) algebraically closed. To state the Poincaré duality theorem, one must first define the trace morphism

\[ \operatorname{tr} : \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2N}\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\right) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\text{.} \]

The definition is a tedious dévissage starting from the case of curves [2]. One then has

Theorem 6.3.1

The form \(\operatorname{tr}(a\smallsmile b)\) identifies each of the groups \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i\left(X,\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\right)\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2 N-i}(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) with the dual of the other.

Let \(x\in X\) be a closed point and \(X_x\) the strict localization of \(X\) at \(x\). We set, for \(U\) ranging over the étale neighbourhoods of \(x\)

\[ \tag{6.3.1.1} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X_x,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(U,\mathbb{Z}/n) \text{.} \]

It would be preferable to consider instead the pro-object \(\text{``}\varprojlim\text{''} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(U,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) but, the groups involved being finite, the difference is inessential. As we have tried to explain in the introduction, (6.3.1) follows from the fact that

\[ \tag{6.3.1.2} \begin{aligned} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X_x,\mathbb{Z}/n) &= 0 \text{ for } i\ne 2N \text{ and that } \\ \operatorname{tr} : \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2 N}\left(X_x, \mathbb{Z}/n(N)\right) &\xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{Z}/n \text{ is an isomorphism.} \end{aligned} \]

The case where \(N=0\) is trivial. If \(N>0\), let \(Y_y\) be the strict localization at a closed point of a scheme \(Y\) that is smooth, purely of dimension \(N-1\), and let \(f:X_x\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_y\) be an essentially smooth morphism (of relative dimension one). The proof uses the Leray spectral sequence in cohomology with proper support for \(f\), in order to reduce to the case of curves. Since the “cohomology with proper support” under consideration are defined as limits (6.3.1.1), the existence of such a spectral sequence raises various problems of passage to the limit, treated in too much detail in [2]. For every geometric point \(z\) of \(Y_y\), one has

\[ (\mathsf{R}^if_! \mathbb{Z}/n)_z = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(f^{-1}(z),\mathbb{Z}/n) \text{.} \]

The geometric fibre \(f^{-1}(z)\) is a projective limit of smooth curves over an algebraically closed field. It satisfies Poincaré duality. Its ordinary cohomology is given by the local acyclicity theorem for smooth morphisms:

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(f^{-1}(z),\mathbb{Z}/n) = \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z}/n & \text{for } i=0 \\ 0 & \text{for } i>0 \text{.} \end{cases} \]

By duality, one has

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(f^{-1}(z),\mathbb{Z}/n) = \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z}/n(-1) & \text{for } i=2 \\ 0 & \text{for } i\ne 2 \text{.} \end{cases} \]

and the Leray spectral sequence reads

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i\left(X_x,\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\right) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{i-2}\left(Y_y,\mathbb{Z}/n(N-1)\right) \text{.} \]

We conclude by induction on \(N\).

6.4 Variants and applications

One can construct, in étale cohomology, a “duality formalism” (\(=\) functors \(\mathsf{R} f_!\), \(\mathsf{R} f_!\), \(\mathsf{R} f^!\) satisfying various compatibilities and adjunction formulas) parallel to the one that exists in coherent cohomology. In this language, the results of the preceding section can be transcribed as follows: if \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is smooth and purely of relative dimension \(N\), and \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), with \(k\) algebraically closed, then

\[ \mathsf{R} f^! \mathbb{Z}/n = \mathbb{Z}/n [2N](N) \text{.} \]

This result holds without any hypothesis on \(S\). It admits the following

Corollary 6.4.1

If \(f\) is smooth and purely of relative dimension \(N\), and the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^i f_! \mathbb{Z}/n\) are locally constant, then the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^i f_* \mathbb{Z}/n\) are also locally constant, and

\[ \mathsf{R}^i f_* \mathbb{Z}/n = \underline{\hom}\left(\mathsf{R}^{2 N-i} f_! \mathbb{Z}/n(N),\mathbb{Z}/n\right)\text{.} \]

In particular, under the hypotheses of the corollary, the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^i f_* \mathbb{Z}/n\) are constructible. Starting from this, one can show that, if \(S\) is of finite type over the spectrum of a field or of a Dedekind ring, then, for every morphism of finite type \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) and every constructible sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\), the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^i f_* \mathscr{F}\) are constructible (VII, 1.1).

blocks.html: Poincaré duality
6.1 Introduction

Let \(X\) be an oriented topological variety, purely of dimension \(N\), and suppose that \(X\) admits a finite open covering \(\mathscr{U}=(U_i)_{1\leqslant i\leqslant K}\), such that the nonempty intersections of open sets \(U_i\) are homeomorphic to balls. For such a variety, the Poincaré duality theorem can be presented as follows:

1. The cohomology of \(X\) is the Čech cohomology corresponding to the covering \(\mathscr{U}\). It is the cohomology of the complex

    \[ \tag{1} 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}^{A_0} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}^{A_1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \]

    where \(A_k=\{(i_0,\dotsc,i_k) : i_0<\cdots<i_k\text{ and } U_{i_0}\cap \cdots \cap U_{i_k} \ne \varnothing\}\).

  2. For \(a\in A_k\), \(a=(i_0,\dotsc,i_k)\), let \(U_a=U_{i_1}\cap \cdots \cap U_{i_k}\) and let \(j_a\) be the inclusion of \(U_a\) in \(X\). The constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}\) on \(X\) admits the (left) resolution

    \[ \tag{2} \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & \displaystyle\bigoplus_{a\in A_1} j_{a!}\mathbb{Z} \ar[r] & \displaystyle\bigoplus_{a\in A_0} j_{a!} \mathbb{Z} \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ & & \mathbb{Z} . } \]

    The cohomology with compact support \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,j_{a!}\mathbb{Z})\) is nothing but the cohomology with proper support of the (oriented) ball \(U_a\):

    \[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,j_{a!}\mathbb{Z}) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i\ne N \\ \mathbb{Z} & \text{if } i = N \end{cases} \]

The hypercohomology spectral sequence, for the complex (2), and the cohomology with proper support, therefore asserts that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X)\) is the \((i-N)\)-th cohomology group of a complex

\[ \tag{3} \cdots \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}^{A_1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}^{A_0} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0 \text{.} \]
This complex is the dual of the complex (1), whence Poincaré duality.
The essential points of this construction are

1. the existence of a theory of cohomology with proper support:

  2. the fact that every point \(x\) of a variety \(X\) purely of dimension \(N\) has a fundamental system of open neighbourhoods \(U\) for which

    \[ \tag{4} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(U) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } i\ne N \text{,} \\ \mathbb{Z} & \text{for } i=N \text{.} \end{cases} \]

Poincaré duality in étale cohomology can be constructed on this model. For \(X\) smooth, purely of dimension \(N\) over \(k\) algebraically closed, \(n\) invertible on \(X\) and \(x\) a closed point of \(X\), the key point is to compute the projective limit, extended over the étale neighbourhoods \(U\) of \(x\)
\[ \tag{5} \varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(U,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i\ne 2N \\ \mathbb{Z}/n & \text{if } i=2N \text{.} \end{cases} \]

Just as for topological varieties one must first treat directly the case of an open ball (or even simply that of the interval \((0,1)\)), here one must first treat directly the case of curves (6.2). The theorem of local acyclicity of smooth morphisms then allows one to reduce (5) to this special case (6.3).

The isomorphisms (4) and (5) are not canonical: they depend on the choice of an orientation of \(X\). For \(n\) invertible on a scheme \(X\), \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\) is a sheaf of free \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules of rank one. We denote by \(\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\) its \(N\)-th tensor power (\(N\in\mathbb{Z}\)). The intrinsic form of the second line of (5) is
\[ \tag{6} \varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2N} \left(U,\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\right) = \mathbb{Z}/n \text{,} \]

and \(\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\) is called the orientation sheaf of \(X\); since the sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/n(N)\) is constant, isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\), one can take it out of the sign \(N\) and write instead
\[ \tag{7} \varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2N} (U,\mathbb{Z}/n) = \mathbb{Z}/n(-N) \text{,} \]

and Poincaré duality will take the form of a perfect duality, with values in \(\mathbb{Z}/n(-N)\), between \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2N-i}(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\).
6.2 The case of curves

Let \(\overline{X}\) be a projective smooth curve over \(k\) algebraically closed, and \(n\) invertible on \(\overline{X}\). The proof of (3.3.5) provides, for \(\overline{X}\) connected, a canonical isomorphism
\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(\overline{X},\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \operatorname{Pic}(\overline{X})/n\operatorname{Pic}(\overline{X}) \ar[r]^-{\deg}_-{\sim} & \mathbb{Z}/n } \]
Let \(D\) be a reduced divisor of \(\overline{X}\) and \(X=\overline{X}\setminus D\)
\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-j & \overline{X} & D . \ar@{_{(}->}[l]_-i} \]

The exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} j_! \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \boldsymbol{\mu}_n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} i_* \boldsymbol{\mu}_n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) and the fact that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},i_*\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(D,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)=0\) for \(i>0\) provide an isomorphism

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(\overline{X},j_! \boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r]^-\sim & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(\overline{X},\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r]^-\sim & \mathbb{Z}/n . } \]
For \(\overline{X}\) disconnected, we likewise have
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = (\mathbb{Z}/n)^{\pi_0(X)} \]
and one defines the trace morphism as the sum
\[ \xymatrix{ \operatorname{tr} : \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n)^{\pi_0(X)} \ar[r]^-\Sigma & \mathbb{Z}/n. } \]

blocks.html:
Theorem 6.2.2

The form \(\operatorname{tr}(a\smallsmile b)\) identifies each of the two groups \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2-i}(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) with the dual (with values in \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)) of the other.

Transcendental proof. If \(\overline{X}\) is a projective smooth curve over a trait \(S\), and \(j:X\hookrightarrow \overline{X}\) is the inclusion of the complement of a divisor \(D\) étale over \(S\), the cohomologies (resp. the cohomologies with proper support) of the special and generic geometric fibres of \(X/S\) are “the same,” i.e., the fibres of sheaves locally constant on \(S\). This follows from the analogous facts for \(\overline{X}\) and \(D\), via the exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} j_! \mathbb{Z}/n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{Z}/n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} {\mathbb{Z}/n}_D\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) (for cohomology with proper support) and the formulas \(j_*\mathbb{Z}/n = \mathbb{Z}/n\), \(\mathsf{R}^1 j_* \mathbb{Z}/n \simeq {\mathbb{Z}/n}_D(-1)\), \(\mathsf{R}^i j_*\mathbb{Z}/n = 0\) (\(i\geqslant 2\)) (for ordinary cohomology) (5.3.4).

This specialization principle reduces (6.2.2) to the case where \(k\) is of characteristic \(0\). By (5.3.3), this case reduces to the one where \(k=\mathbb{C}\). Finally, for \(k=\mathbb{C}\), the groups \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) coincide with the groups of the same name, computed for the classical topological space \(X_{\textnormal{cl}}\) and, via the isomorphism \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \boldsymbol{\mu}_n: x\mapsto \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i x}{n}\right)\), the trace morphism is identified with “integration over the fundamental class,” so that (6.2.2) follows from Poincaré duality for \(X_{\textnormal{cl}}\).
6.2.3 Algebraic proof
For a very economical proof, see (V, §2).
Here is another, connected with the autoduality of the Jacobian.

We resume the notation of (6.2.1). We may assume — and we do assume — that \(X\) is connected. The cases \(i=0\) and \(i=2\) being trivial, we also assume that \(i=1\). We define \(_D\mathbb{G}_m\) by the exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} _D\mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} i_*\mathbb{G}_m\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) (sections of \(\mathbb{G}_m\) congruent to \(1\mod D\)). The group \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(\overline{X}, _D\mathbb{G}_m)\) classifies the invertible sheaves on \(\overline{X}\) trivialized on \(D\). It is the group of points of \(\operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X})\), an extension of \(\mathbb{Z}\) (the degree) by the group of points of a generalized Jacobian of Rosenlicht (corresponding to conductor \(1\) at each point of \(D\)) \(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})\), itself an extension of the abelian variety \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(\overline{X})\) by the torus \(\mathbb{G}_m^D/(\mathbb{G}_m \text{ diagonal})\).

1. The exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} _D\mathbb{G}_m \xrightarrow{n} _D\mathbb{G}_m\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) yields an isomorphism

    \[ \tag{6.2.3.1} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n \text{.} \]

  2. The map which assigns to \(x\in X(k)\) the class of the invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{O}(x)\) on \(\overline{X}\), trivialized by \(1\) on \(D\), arises from a morphism

    \[ f:X \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X}) \text{.} \]

For the sequel, we fix a base point \(0\) and set \(f_0(x)=f(x)-f(0)\). For every homomorphism \(v:\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\), let \(\overline{v}\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}),\mathbb{Z}/n\right)\) be the image under \(v\) of the class in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}),\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n\right)\) of the torsor defined by the extension
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}) \ar[r]^-n & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}) \ar[r] & 0 } \]
Geometric class field theory (as presented in Serre [33]) shows that the map \(v\mapsto f_0^*(\overline{v})\):

\[ \tag{6.2.3.2} \hom\left(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n,\mathbb{Z}/n\right) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) \]
is an isomorphism. To deduce (6.2.2) from (6.2.3.1) and (6.2.3.2), it remains to know that
\[ \tag{6.2.2.3} \operatorname{tr}\left(u \smallsmile f_0^*(\overline{v})\right) = -v(u) \text{.} \]
